t.historic centre of krakow@50.1,19.9:
Every hour, a trumpeter plays a short melody from the taller tower of St Mary's Basilica on Kraków's market square, and every time the tune breaks off abruptly mid-phrase. Legend says it commemorates a watchman shot by a Tatar arrow in the throat as he sounded the alarm in the thirteenth century, and the hejnał has been played that way ever since, broadcast daily on Polish radio at noon. It is a fitting introduction to a city that wears its history so openly. The Rynek Główny, the main square, is one of the largest medieval squares in Europe, with the Renaissance Cloth Hall in the middle, and the historic centre, including Wawel Hill and the Jewish quarter of Kazimierz, was among the first sites ever placed on the UNESCO list in 1978.

Wawel Castle, the residence of Polish kings for centuries, stands on a hill above the Vistula with its cathedral, where kings and national heroes are buried. Kazimierz, once a separate town and later the heart of Jewish life in Kraków, has synagogues, cemeteries and a vibrant scene of cafés, bars and galleries. Kraków escaped major destruction in the Second World War, but the memory of the Holocaust is ever present, and Auschwitz-Birkenau is about an hour away.

Riding into Kraków means dealing with city traffic, trams and cobbles. The old town is largely closed to traffic, and parking is restricted, so leave the bike in a secure garage and explore on foot. The surroundings offer some fine riding: south toward the Tatra mountains and Zakopane, with winding roads through the hills; west through the Jura Krakowsko-Częstochowska, a limestone upland with rocks and castles on the Trail of the Eagles' Nests; and east to the salt mine of Wieliczka, with its underground chapels carved from salt.

Kraków has every service, and it is an excellent place to eat: pierogi, dumplings with all kinds of fillings, żurek, a sour rye soup served in a bread bowl, obwarzanki, the ring-shaped bread sold from carts on every corner, and zapiekanki, open sandwiches from the stands in Kazimierz. Summers are warm and lively, winters cold but atmospheric, especially during the Christmas market.
t.fujisan@35.4,138.7:
At 3,776 metres, Mount Fuji is the highest mountain in Japan, and its almost perfectly symmetrical cone has been a sacred symbol and an artistic inspiration for centuries. UNESCO listed Fujisan in 2013 as a cultural site, a place of worship and source of artistic inspiration, rather than for its natural beauty alone, recognising the shrines, pilgrim trails, lakes and springs around the mountain, and the woodblock prints of Hokusai and Hiroshige that made its image famous around the world.

The mountain is an active volcano, which last erupted in 1707, and its slopes are covered with lava flows, forests and lakes. The Fuji Five Lakes on the northern side offer classic views of the mountain reflected in the water, especially at Lake Kawaguchi, and the Aokigahara forest, growing on an old lava flow, is dense, dark and eerie.

You cannot ride to the summit. Roads climb to the fifth stations on several sides of the mountain, at around two thousand metres or higher, where the climbing trails begin. The Fuji Subaru Line from Fujiyoshida to the Yoshida trail's fifth station is the most popular, a winding road through forests with views over the lakes, and the Fujisan Skyline on the southern side climbs to the Fujinomiya fifth station. During the summer climbing season, private vehicles are restricted on some of these roads, and the access roads close in winter because of snow, so check the rules before setting out. The climbing season itself runs roughly from July to early September, and climbers now face fees and entry controls on some trails.

Fujiyoshida, about eleven kilometres away, has fuel, shops, restaurants and accommodation, including traditional inns that once housed pilgrims. The area around the lakes offers great riding, with roads circling the lakes and winding through the hills, though weekend traffic can be heavy. Local food includes hōtō, thick noodles in a miso stew with pumpkin and vegetables, and Yoshida udon, notably chewy noodles. The mountain is often hidden by clouds, especially in summer; early mornings in autumn and winter offer the clearest views.
t.fuji sengen jinja shrine@35.4,138.9:
On the eastern side of Mount Fuji, in the village of Subashiri, a shrine has stood at the start of the pilgrims' path for more than a thousand years. The Fuji Sengen shrine, often called Higashiguchi Hongū, the eastern main shrine, marks the beginning of the Subashiri trail to the summit, and pilgrims traditionally prayed here before starting their climb. The shrine is set in a forest of tall cedars and old trees, with a red gate, wooden halls and a quiet, spiritual atmosphere, and it is one of the components of the Fujisan UNESCO site, recognised as part of the mountain's cultural and religious landscape.

The Sengen shrines are dedicated to Konohanasakuya-hime, the goddess of Mount Fuji, a blossom princess associated with cherry trees and volcanoes, and the worship of the mountain, Fuji-kō, was a popular religious movement in the Edo period, when groups of pilgrims from Edo, now Tokyo, made the climb as a spiritual practice. Their names and marks can still be found on stones and lanterns around the shrine.

The riding around this side of Fuji is excellent. From Gotemba, roads climb toward Subashiri and the fifth station of the Subashiri trail, through forests and with views of the mountain, and the road is open to private vehicles outside the climbing season restrictions, which apply to some roads in summer. The Lake Yamanaka area, north of Subashiri, has roads circling the lake and climbing over the Kagosaka pass, and the Hakone area to the southeast, with its winding roads, hot springs and views of Fuji over Lake Ashi, is a famous riding destination. Traffic can be heavy on weekends and holidays, and the weather on the mountain changes quickly, with fog and rain common. Winter brings snow and road closures at higher altitudes.

Gotemba, about nine kilometres away, is a city with fuel, shops, restaurants and a huge outlet mall that draws crowds from Tokyo. Subashiri has small shops and restaurants near the shrine, selling local specialities like grilled river fish and soba noodles. Hot spring baths in the area are a wonderful way to relax after a ride, though some do not admit people with tattoos, so check beforehand.
t.architectonic ensemble of the town of na:
Nazas is a small town on the river of the same name in the north of the state of Durango, where the Sierra Madre Occidental gives way to the high, dry basins of the Mexican interior. It sits on the route of the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the old royal road that ran north from Mexico City to Santa Fe, carrying silver, mercury, goods and settlers for nearly three centuries. A group of its historic buildings, around the main square and church, was included in the UNESCO listing of the Camino Real in 2010.

The town is quiet and modest, with low adobe and stone buildings, a church and a plaza shaded by trees. Its importance lay in water. The Nazas river flows out of the mountains and into the desert, and its waters made possible the oases and cotton fields of the Laguna region downstream, around Torreón and Gómez Palacio. Farmers here have depended on the river for centuries, and its floods and droughts shaped the history of the region, including struggles over land and water that fed into the Mexican Revolution.

The landscape around is wide and spare: desert scrub, cacti, mesquite and distant ranges, with green strips of farmland along the river. The light is intense, the sky enormous, and the night stars are spectacular. Summer days are very hot, while winter nights can be cold, and storms in the rainy season can flood roads quickly.

Riding in this part of Mexico means long distances, straight roads and few services. Highways are generally good, but minor roads can be rough, with potholes, gravel and livestock wandering freely. Topes, the speed bumps found in every village, can be brutal if you miss them. Durango is also famous for one of Mexico's great motorcycle roads, the highway over the Sierra Madre to Mazatlán, known for its twists and the dramatic stretch called the Devil's Backbone, though that lies a long way south-west of Nazas.

There is no large town nearby, so fuel planning is essential. Fill up in the last city on your way in and carry a reserve. Check current security advice for the state before travelling, as conditions vary by area. Local food is hearty: try gorditas, carne asada and Durango's famous dried meat, washed down with a cold drink in the shade of the plaza.
t.stretch of the camino real between nazas:
For nearly three centuries, the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro was the royal road linking Mexico City with Santa Fe in New Mexico, a route some 2,600 kilometres long that carried silver south and settlers, missionaries, soldiers and goods north. In the state of Durango, it crossed a vast semi-desert of scrub, cactus and rocky hills, and the stretch between Nazas and San Pedro del Gallo is one of the sections inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2010. Along the road, haciendas, chapels and waystations grew up wherever water could be found.

Today, the landscape is much as travellers on the Camino Real would have seen it: wide, empty and sunbaked, with dry riverbeds, creosote bushes and distant mountain ranges shimmering in the heat. Nazas, a small town of about thirty-six hundred people on the river of the same name, is one of the few green spots, with cottonwoods and irrigated fields along the water. The river was historically vital for agriculture in the Laguna region downstream.

Riding here is about distance and solitude. The roads are long and straight, with occasional curves over low passes, and traffic is light. Surfaces are generally paved, but expect potholes, loose gravel on the edges and livestock wandering across, especially at night. Fuel stations are far apart, and there is no town of five thousand people nearby, so fill up whenever you can and carry extra water. Summer heat is intense, often over forty degrees, so ride early and rest in the shade.

The nearest larger cities are Gómez Palacio and Torreón to the east, and Durango city to the south-west, each a few hours away. In the small towns, simple restaurants serve gorditas, carne asada and the local cheese. Take your time, stop at the old chapels and haciendas along the way, and imagine the mule trains and ox carts that once crawled across this landscape on their way to the silver mines and the far northern frontier.
t.tajima yahei sericulture farm@36.2,139.2:
Silk transformed modern Japan, and Gunma Prefecture was its heartland. In the village of Shimamura, now part of Isesaki, on the north bank of the Tone River, stands the farmhouse of Tajima Yahei, a sericulturist who developed a method of raising silkworms in the nineteenth century. He built a two-storey house with a ventilation structure on the roof, allowing air to circulate through the upper floor where the silkworms were kept, and his design was widely copied across Japan.

The farm is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the Tomioka Silk Mill and Related Sites, inscribed in 2014, which tells the story of how Japan modernized silk production and became the world's largest exporter of raw silk in the early twentieth century. The Tomioka mill, founded by the government in 1872 with French expertise, is the centrepiece, but the farmhouses where silkworms were raised are just as important. Shimamura still has many houses with the characteristic roof ventilators, and walking through the village is like stepping into the past.

The riding in this part of the Kanto plain is flat and mostly urban or agricultural, with roads running between rice fields, vegetable plots and towns. It is not dramatic, but the views of the mountains to the north, especially Mount Akagi, are fine on clear days. Within an hour you can reach the mountains of Gunma, with winding roads through forests and hot spring towns such as Kusatsu and Ikaho. Remember to drive on the left and to respect the low speed limits. Summers are hot and humid, winters cold and dry with strong winds, known locally as karakkaze, blowing down from the mountains.

The farm is about two kilometres from Sakai-nakajima and close to the cities of Honjo and Isesaki, which have fuel and all services. Convenience stores are everywhere in Japan, offering food, coffee and clean toilets. The local cuisine includes okkirikomi, a thick noodle stew, and yakimanju, grilled buns with miso sauce, both Gunma specialties. In late spring, mulberry trees, whose leaves feed the silkworms, still grow in some fields, a reminder of the industry that once shaped this landscape.
t.chapel of the refugio of the former haci:
Hacienda chapels tell you a lot about colonial Mexico. They were built by landowners who controlled vast estates of cattle, crops or mines, and they served as places of worship for the owners, their families and the workers who lived and laboured on the estate. The Chapel of the Refugio, once part of a hacienda near Cuencamé in the state of Durango, is one of the sites included in the UNESCO listing of the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the royal road that ran from Mexico City to Santa Fe and carried silver, goods, missionaries and settlers across the northern frontier for nearly three centuries.

The chapel stands in a landscape of dry plains and low mountains, with mesquite, creosote bush and cactus, and the remains of the hacienda buildings around it hint at a time when this was a busy, self-contained world. Many haciendas declined after the Mexican Revolution of 1910, when land reform broke up the great estates, and today their chapels are often the best-preserved parts.

The riding in this part of Durango is open and spacious, with long straight roads crossing high desert, mountains on the horizon and wide skies overhead. The main highway between Torreón and Durango passes nearby and is busy with trucks, while smaller roads to villages are quieter but rougher, with potholes, gravel and topes. Watch for livestock on the road, especially at night, and avoid riding after dark if you can.

Pedriceña and Velardeña, the nearest villages, are small, with basic shops. Velardeña has a long mining history. For reliable fuel and food, Cuencamé, about twenty-six kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, and the city of Durango or Gómez Palacio offer every service. Local food includes caldillo durangueño, a hearty beef and chile stew, and gorditas, and the region is known for its mezcal.

Come in the cooler months, from October to April, when days are warm and nights cold. Summers can be very hot, and the rainy season brings afternoon storms. It is a small, plain building, and that is its charm: a whitewashed refuge in a hard country, exactly as its name suggests.
t.town of san pedro del gallo@25.6,-104.3:
San Pedro del Gallo is a very small town in a very big landscape, and that is precisely its appeal. Fewer than a thousand people live here, in the high desert of northern Durango, among dry plains, low mountains and endless sky, and the town grew up as a stop on the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the royal road that linked Mexico City with the northern frontier and Santa Fe. San Pedro del Gallo is one of the places included in the UNESCO listing of the Camino Real, with its church, simple adobe houses and the quiet atmosphere of a place where time moves slowly.

The church and the old houses around the plaza are modest but authentic, built of adobe and stone to withstand heat, cold and wind. The surrounding desert is home to mesquite, creosote bush, cholla and prickly pear, and the light changes from harsh white at midday to soft gold and violet at dusk. The stars at night are spectacular, thanks to the clear dry air and the lack of light pollution.

Riding here means long distances on quiet roads, often straight, sometimes rough, with very few services. The surface can vary from good asphalt to potholed and patched sections, and loose gravel and livestock on the road are common hazards. Wind can be strong, and temperatures swing widely between day and night. Carry plenty of water, make sure someone knows your plans and avoid riding after dark.

Fuel is the main practical concern. San Pedro del Gallo itself has very limited services, and the nearest town of any size is a long way off, so fill up in a larger town such as Cuencamé, Gómez Palacio or Durango before heading out, and plan your route carefully. Small village stores may sell snacks and cold drinks, and you might find a local family serving simple meals of beans, tortillas and meat.

Come in the cooler months, from October to April, when days are warm and nights cold. Summers can be very hot, and storms in the rainy season can flood roads and tracks. Sit on a bench in the plaza in the evening, listen to the silence broken only by a dog barking or a radio playing, and you will feel how far the royal road reached into the empty north.
t.oshino hakkai@35.5,138.8:
Eight ponds of astonishingly clear water lie in the village of Oshino, at the northern foot of Mount Fuji, and the water in them is snowmelt from the mountain, filtered for many years through layers of volcanic rock before welling up here. The Oshino Hakkai, the eight seas of Oshino, were once part of a lake that dried up, and they became places of pilgrimage for people climbing Fuji, who purified themselves in the springs before their ascent. They are included in UNESCO's inscription of Fujisan as a place of worship and source of artistic inspiration.

The village is pretty, with thatched-roof houses, water wheels and small shops selling soba noodles, tofu and grilled fish. On a clear day, Fuji rises behind, perfectly reflected in the ponds, and the water is so clear that you can see every pebble and fish on the bottom. It can be crowded with tour groups, especially at weekends, so come early or late. Nearby, Fujiyoshida is the traditional starting point for the climb, with the Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen shrine among giant cedars, and the Chureito pagoda, framed by cherry blossoms in spring, is one of the most famous views in Japan.

The riding around Fuji is excellent. The roads around the Fuji Five Lakes, such as Kawaguchi and Yamanaka, are scenic and well-maintained, with views of the mountain at every turn. The Fuji Subaru Line, a toll road, climbs to the fifth station on the northern slope, at about two thousand three hundred metres, and is open to motorcycles outside the busiest periods. Traffic can be heavy on weekends and holidays, and the weather changes quickly, with cloud often hiding the mountain. Winter brings snow and ice, and some roads close.

Fujiyoshida has fuel, shops and restaurants. Local food includes Yoshida udon, thick and chewy noodles, and hoto, a hearty noodle soup with pumpkin and vegetables. Japanese convenience stores are a rider's friend, with good coffee, snacks and clean toilets. Remember that Japan drives on the left. At Oshino Hakkai, walk around the ponds slowly, look into the deep blue of the largest one, and drink a cup of the spring water from a public fountain; it is cold, clean and tastes faintly of stone.
t.fujisan hongu sengen taisha shrine@35.2,:
Mount Fuji has been worshipped as a sacred mountain for as long as people have lived beneath it, and the Fujisan Hongū Sengen Taisha in Fujinomiya is the head shrine of that worship, the principal sanctuary of over a thousand Sengen shrines across Japan. Its main hall, rebuilt in the early seventeenth century under the patronage of Tokugawa Ieyasu, has an unusual two-storey design, painted in vermilion and set among tall trees. The shrine is dedicated to Konohanasakuya-hime, a goddess associated with the mountain, with blossoms and with fire.

On a clear day, the view of Fuji from the shrine grounds is magnificent, the great cone rising above the town. In the grounds is Wakutama Pond, fed by springs of crystal-clear water that has filtered through the volcanic rock of the mountain for years. The water is cold and pure, and locals fill bottles there. Remarkably, the shrine also owns the summit of Fuji itself, above the eighth station, a fact recognised by the Japanese courts. The shrine is part of the Fujisan UNESCO World Heritage site, listed in 2013 as a place of worship and source of artistic inspiration.

Fujinomiya is a pleasant small city, famous across Japan for its yakisoba, fried noodles with a chewy texture, sold in stalls around town. Try them at lunchtime, preferably with a view of the mountain.

The riding around Fuji is spectacular. The Fuji Skyline climbs from the Fujinomiya side up to the fifth station on the mountain's southern flank, a superb road with hairpins and views; it is open only in the summer climbing season, and access to the upper part may be restricted to shuttle buses at peak times. Route 139 runs north across the Asagiri plateau, with dairy farms and wide views of the mountain, towards the Fuji Five Lakes. The roads around the lakes are popular and can be busy at weekends, but the scenery is extraordinary.

Fujinomiya has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. The weather around Fuji is changeable: the mountain often hides in cloud, especially in summer, and the best views are in the clear, cold air of winter mornings, though the higher roads may be closed by snow and ice. Spring and autumn offer pleasant riding temperatures. Arrive early to see Fuji before the clouds gather.
t.takayama sha sericulture school@36.2,139:
Silk built modern Japan, and the hills of Gunma prefecture were its engine room. In the second half of the nineteenth century, farmhouses across this region raised silkworms on the upper floors, and the quality of the cocoons decided the fortunes of families and, eventually, of the nation's exports. At the Takayama-sha site in Fujioka, a farmer named Takayama Chōgorō developed a method of raising silkworms that balanced ventilation and temperature, and he trained students from across Japan in his large farmhouse. You can still see the building, with its distinctive roof vents running along the ridge, designed to let warm, moist air escape.

It is one of four components of the UNESCO World Heritage site of the Tomioka Silk Mill and Related Sites, listed in 2014. The mill itself, in nearby Tomioka, was founded by the Meiji government in 1872 with the help of French engineers and was one of the first large modern factories in Japan. Its long brick buildings, a blend of Japanese and Western techniques, are remarkably well preserved and are the obvious next stop. The story of the young women who came to work there, learning to reel silk on French machines, is told in the exhibitions.

The surrounding country is a pleasant mix of rice paddies, mulberry fields, small towns and wooded hills, with the jagged peaks of Myōgi rising to the west. The Arafune cold storage site, another part of the heritage group, sits in the hills near Shimonita, where natural cold air flowing from rock crevices was used to store silkworm eggs.

The riding is excellent in the hills. The roads around Mount Myōgi are narrow and twisting, with sharp bends, rock faces and dense forest, and views of the strange, eroded peaks. Further west, the old Usui pass road towards Karuizawa climbs through 184 bends, passing the Megane-bashi, a brick railway viaduct built in the Meiji era. Traffic is light on weekdays, though the passes attract riders and drivers at weekends. Watch for fallen leaves, moss and gravel on the narrow roads.

Fujioka has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. Try Shimonita's famous thick leeks and konnyaku, a specialty of the area, if you pass that way. Summers are hot and humid; spring and autumn are the best seasons for riding. Remember to drive on the left and carry the correct international driving permit.
t.nirayama reverbatory furnaces@35.0,139.0:
Two pairs of tall brick chimneys stand in a quiet suburb at the base of the Izu Peninsula, looking strangely European against the green hills. They belong to the Nirayama reverberatory furnace, built in the 1850s to melt iron for casting cannons, at a time when Japan felt threatened by Western warships arriving in its waters. The project was led by Egawa Hidetatsu, the local magistrate, a forward-thinking official who studied Western military technology from Dutch books. He died before it was completed, and his son finished the work. It is the only surviving reverberatory furnace of its era in Japan that was actually used for casting, and since 2015 it has been part of the UNESCO site of the Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution.

The furnaces are made of firebrick, with a structure of stone and iron to hold them together, and they have been restored. A small visitor centre explains how they worked and the story of the Egawa family. There is also a tea plantation on the hillside behind, where you can taste local green tea while looking at the chimneys.

The Izu Peninsula is one of the most popular riding areas near Tokyo, and with good reason. The Izu Skyline, a toll road along the spine of the mountains, offers flowing bends and views of Mount Fuji and Sagami Bay. The west coast road, Route 136, winds along cliffs and coves, with views of Fuji across Suruga Bay on clear days. Inland, the old Amagi pass road climbs through forest past waterfalls, and the Kawazu Nanadaru loop bridge, a double spiral of road, is a highlight on the descent towards the east coast. Traffic can be heavy at weekends and holidays, especially in spring and summer.

The peninsula is famous for its hot springs. Shuzenji, a short ride south of Nirayama, is a charming onsen town with a temple, a bamboo forest and a river running through the centre. Soaking in a hot spring after a day of riding is one of the great pleasures of touring in Japan.

Izunokuni and nearby Mishima and Numazu have fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. Numazu is known for its fresh seafood, especially horse mackerel. The weather is mild compared with Tokyo, but rain is frequent in early summer, and typhoons can bring heavy storms in late summer and autumn.
t.tomioka silk mill and related sites@36.3:
In 1872, barely four years after the Meiji Restoration had ended the rule of the shoguns, Japan's new government opened a model silk-reeling mill in the small town of Tomioka in Gunma prefecture. It hired a French engineer, Paul Brunat, imported French machinery, and recruited young women from across the country to learn the new techniques and take them home. The long brick buildings, a curious mix of Japanese timber framing and European brick, still stand, and the mill operated until 1987. In 2014 it was inscribed on the UNESCO list together with related sericulture sites, such as farms where silkworm rearing methods were improved and a cold storage cave used to control the hatching of eggs.

Silk was Japan's great export in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, paying for the country's modernisation, and Gunma was at the heart of the industry. Many old farmhouses in the area have distinctive raised roofs with ventilation sections built for raising silkworms in the attic. The mill tour explains the process, from cocoon to thread, and the scale of the buildings gives a sense of the ambition of the early Meiji state.

The riding around Tomioka is a pleasant mix of valley and mountain. The town sits in the Kabura river valley on the edge of the Kanto plain, with the strange, jagged peaks of Mount Myogi rising to the west. The Myogi area has some excellent twisty roads, climbing through forest with tight corners and great views of the rock pinnacles. Further west, the road toward Karuizawa and the Usui pass climbs into the mountains, with famous hairpins on the old pass road. Traffic on weekends can be heavy, and summer is hot and humid, but spring and autumn are lovely.

Tomioka has around fifty thousand inhabitants, with fuel stations, convenience stores and restaurants. Look out for local specialities such as konnyaku, made from the root of a plant grown in Gunma, and hearty udon noodles. The mill is right in the town, with paid parking nearby; plan for at least an hour to walk around the buildings and see the reeling machines. Then head for Myogi in the afternoon for a ride through the pinnacles before the light goes.
t.auschwitz@50.0,19.2:
This is a stop to make in silence. Auschwitz was the largest of the Nazi German concentration and extermination camps, built in occupied Poland on the edge of the town of Oświęcim, and between 1940 and 1945 around 1.1 million people were murdered here, the vast majority of them Jews from across Europe, along with Poles, Roma, Soviet prisoners of war and others. The memorial and museum, which includes the original camp, Auschwitz I, and the vast camp at Birkenau, Auschwitz II, about three kilometres away, was listed by UNESCO in 1979 as a reminder of the cruelty of humanity.

A visit is overwhelming. At Auschwitz I, the brick barracks hold exhibitions with personal belongings of the victims: shoes, suitcases, glasses, hair. At Birkenau, the scale is staggering: rows of wooden and brick barracks, the railway tracks leading through the gate to the ramp where people were selected for death or forced labour, and the ruins of the gas chambers and crematoria, blown up by the Germans before they retreated. Allow several hours, and take your time.

Entry to the memorial is free, but reservations are required, and during the busiest hours visitors must join guided tours, which are available in many languages and are worth taking. Book well in advance, especially in summer. There are car parks at both sites, and motorcycles can be parked there. Dress respectfully and remember that it is a cemetery.

Oświęcim is a town of over forty thousand people, and it has a life beyond the camp, with a castle, a market square and a Jewish Centre, with a restored synagogue and a museum about the Jewish community that lived in the town before the war, when more than half the population was Jewish. It is worth visiting to understand what was lost.

The surrounding area is flat, with the Vistula and Soła rivers meeting nearby, and the roads are generally good, though traffic can be heavy, especially around Kraków, about sixty kilometres to the east. To the south, the Beskid mountains offer winding roads through forests and hills, a place to clear your head after the visit.

Oświęcim has fuel, shops and restaurants. Many visitors find they need time alone after the visit, and a quiet ride through the countryside, or a walk by the river, can help. Whatever you feel, it is important to have come.
t.enryaku ji@35.1,135.8:
Mount Hiei rises between Kyoto and Lake Biwa, and in 788 a young monk named Saichō built a small hermitage on its slopes. It grew into Enryaku-ji, the headquarters of the Tendai school of Buddhism and one of the most powerful religious institutions in Japanese history. Many of the founders of later Buddhist schools, including Hōnen, Shinran, Dōgen and Nichiren, studied here. At its height, the mountain held thousands of temples, and the monastery maintained an army of warrior monks who regularly descended on Kyoto to intimidate the court. In 1571, the warlord Oda Nobunaga, tired of their political meddling, attacked the mountain, burned the temples and killed thousands of people. The monastery was rebuilt in the following decades, and today its halls are spread across the forested summit in three main areas, connected by footpaths and roads. The main hall, the Konpon Chūdō, houses a lamp said to have burned continuously for over a thousand years. Enryaku-ji is part of the UNESCO listing of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto.

The mountain is still a place of rigorous practice. A small number of monks undertake the kaihōgyō, a pilgrimage of a thousand days spread over seven years, walking enormous distances around the mountain, sometimes the equivalent of a marathon a day, in straw sandals. Those who complete it are revered as living saints.

The ride up is a joy. The Hieizan Driveway, a toll road, climbs from the Kyoto side in a series of smooth, well-cambered bends through cedar forest, with views over the city, and continues as the Okuhiei Driveway along the ridge to the north, with views over Lake Biwa, the largest lake in Japan. The surface is excellent, the traffic light on weekdays, and the scenery superb. Watch for deer and monkeys, especially at dawn and dusk. Ōtsu, on the shore of the lake, is the other gateway to the mountain, with a cable car up from Sakamoto, a village of old stone walls built by the monks' masons.

Ōtsu and Kyoto have fuel and every service; there is little on the mountain itself. Winter brings snow to the summit, and the toll roads may close. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and the forest is cool even in summer.
t.arafune cold storage@36.2,138.6:
High in the mountains of southwestern Gunma, near the border with Nagano, a series of stone-walled pits sit among the trees on a hillside. They look like ruins, and in a sense they are, but in their day they were cutting-edge technology. The Arafune cold storage, built in the early twentieth century, used the cold air flowing out of crevices in a rocky slope, a natural wind cave or fuketsu, to keep silkworm eggs cool and delay their hatching. This allowed silk farmers to raise several batches of silkworms a year instead of just one, greatly increasing production. At its peak, the facility stored eggs for farmers from across Japan and even abroad. It is part of the UNESCO listing of the Tomioka Silk Mill and Related Sites, inscribed in 2014, which tells the story of how Japan became the world's largest exporter of raw silk.

The Tomioka Silk Mill itself, founded by the Meiji government in 1872 with French engineers and machinery, stands in the town of Tomioka, about twenty-five kilometres away, a huge complex of brick buildings that remained in operation until 1987. Together with the cold storage and two sericulture farms, it shows the whole chain of silk production, from egg to thread.

The cold storage is in the town of Shimonita, famous throughout Japan for two products: konnyaku, a jelly made from the corm of the devil's tongue plant, and Shimonita negi, thick, sweet leeks that are prized in winter hot pots. Roadside shops sell both, and konnyaku dishes appear on every menu.

The riding is mountainous and beautiful. Route 254 climbs from Shimonita through forests to the Uchiyama pass and descends into the Saku basin in Nagano, with tight bends and views over the ridges. The roads around Arafune itself are narrow and steep, with a final access road to the site that requires care. The Myōgi mountains, a range of jagged volcanic peaks, rise to the east, with a famous winding road along their flanks. The surface is excellent, traffic light, and the scenery superb, especially in autumn, when the maples turn red.

Shimonita and Tomioka have fuel and convenience stores, and Saku has more services on the Nagano side. The site sits at high altitude and is cold even in summer, which was precisely the point; bring a layer.
t.landscape for breeding and training of c:
Kladruby nad Labem is a horse village in the flat country of the Elbe valley in eastern Bohemia, and its stud farm is among the oldest in the world. It was founded in the sixteenth century to breed carriage horses for the Habsburg court, and the Kladruber, a large, elegant horse that is usually white or black, is still bred here. The landscape, with its stables, riding grounds, pastures, avenues of trees and farm buildings laid out as a single working system, was added to the UNESCO list in 2019 as a cultural landscape.

The horses were bred for ceremony. Emperors rode in carriages drawn by teams of white Kladrubers for state occasions, and the black horses were used for funerals and high-ranking processions, and the combination of strength, height and a calm temperament made them prized across Europe. The stud has survived wars, changes of regime and many threats, and today it is a national cultural monument, which you can visit to see the stables and the horses in their paddocks. A foal in the spring, with its dark coat that will lighten over years, is a memorable sight.

The riding in the region is gentle. Roads run through flat farmland, past ponds and woods, and along the Elbe, with long straights and a few bends, and the surface is generally good. Traffic is light on the minor roads, though tractors and cyclists appear without warning, and on summer weekends the stud draws visitors. Spring and early autumn are best, with fresh green fields or golden leaves, and you may smell hay, horses and wet earth on the breeze. It is an easy place to combine with a visit to the nearby towns of Pardubice and Kutná Hora.

Přelouč, about six kilometres away, has fuel stations, shops and cafés, and Pardubice, a short ride further, is known for its gingerbread, called perník, and for a famous steeplechase. In the villages you can find simple Czech food: goulash with dumplings, fried cheese, and a glass of good lager. Visitors to the stud are usually asked to book or arrive at set times, so check ahead, and keep voices low and bikes parked at a distance, since horses are sensitive to engine noise.
t.oshi lodging house@35.5,138.8:
Mount Fuji has been a place of pilgrimage for a thousand years, and the lodging houses in Fujiyoshida are what the pilgrims used. Believers in the Fuji cult, called the Fuji-kō, travelled in confraternities from Edo and farther away, and when they reached the foot of the mountain they stayed with an oshi, a guide and priest who arranged their prayers, their meals and their climb. The streets of old Kamiyoshida still have a few of these houses, with deep entrances, long rooms and a small shrine inside, designed for groups to eat, sleep and prepare. UNESCO lists one of them as part of the Fujisan cultural landscape.

The setting helps. From the long straight main street of Fujiyoshida, Fuji rises at the end of the road, cone-shaped and enormous, with a water channel running beside the pavement and a sense that the whole town was laid out to face the mountain. Nearby is the Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen shrine, with cedar trunks wider than a person, from where the old pilgrim trail up the Yoshida route begins. In late August the Fire Festival lights the streets with giant torches, a spectacle worth seeing, though crowded.

Fujiyoshida is a proper town of nearly fifty thousand, so fuel, convenience stores and cafes are everywhere. The local speciality is Yoshida udon, a chewy noodle served with cabbage and a spicy miso sauce, cheap and filling. Fujikawaguchiko, on the lake shore to the south, is the tourist magnet, and you can reach the Five Lakes region in minutes.

The riding is lovely, though it needs timing. The Fuji Subaru Line climbs up the mountain to the fifth station, with long bends through larch and pine, but it has toll fees, seasonal restrictions on traffic and is closed for winter, so check its status. Around the lakes the roads are smooth, wind in gentle curves and give views of the peak that are frequently hidden by cloud. Fuji hides on most summer afternoons, so ride early. Autumn and early winter are clearest, when the air is dry, but cold, and the first snow turns the summit white. Summer weekends bring buses and heavy traffic.
t.murayama sengen jinja shrine@35.3,138.7:
Murayama Sengen-jinja is the quieter ancestor of the Fuji pilgrimage. Long before the climbers of Edo came in crowds, ascetic mountain priests of Shugendō trained at Murayama on the southern slope of Mount Fuji, and the shrine stood at the beginning of a trail up the mountain. The old name for the place is a reminder that this was a monastery as much as a shrine, a base of mountain monks who practised purification and climbed in rigorous seasons. Large cedars shade the grounds, and a stone path leads between moss-covered stones and old wooden buildings, so the place feels more like a forest sanctuary than a tourist stop.

The Murayama route up the mountain was one of the old ways to the summit, though it has long been overshadowed by the more popular trails, and it is not marked for the average walker. The shrine is better treated as a place to understand why Fuji has been sacred rather than as a trailhead.

Fujinomiya, the nearest city, has more than a hundred thousand people, with fuel, restaurants and every service, and it is famous for its fried noodle dish, yakisoba, which you can eat at stalls and diners. The great Fuji-san Hongū Sengen Taisha, the head shrine of all Sengen shrines, stands in the centre of town, and water from the mountain's snowmelt wells up in a pool beside it. Fuji city to the south is an industrial place with paper mills and a view of the volcano from every road.

For riders, the southern side of Fuji is the less crowded side, with wide, quiet roads that climb through forest and open grassland, such as the Asagiri highland, where dairy farms spread out under the cone and the air smells of cut grass. The surface is good, the corners are gentle and the views, when the weather allows, are enormous. Cloud hides the summit more often than not, especially in summer, so early morning in late autumn or winter gives the clearest views. Mihonomatsubara, the pine grove on the Shimizu coast, is the other piece of the day, a long beach of black sand and wind-bent pines looking back across the bay to the mountain.
t.chapel of the former hacienda of la inma:
Out in the dry heart of northern Mexico, among the creosote bushes and distant mountains of the Chihuahuan Desert, stand the ruins and chapels of old haciendas, great estates that shaped the history of the country. The chapel at the former Hacienda de la Inmaculada Concepción in Durango is one of them, a small whitewashed church standing in an empty landscape, with a bell tower and a simple interior built for the workers who lived and laboured on the estate. A hacienda was a world of its own, with a main house, a granary, a store, stables, workers' homes and a chapel, and the owners often held enormous areas, producing cattle, cotton, maize or minerals.

The region is high desert, around a thousand metres, with scrub, cactus, dry riverbeds and wide valleys edged by purple ranges. The nearby Bolsón de Mapimí is a vast basin of desert with a biosphere reserve, home to a rare desert tortoise and some unusual creatures. The Zona del Silencio, a spot where radio signals are said to fade, draws curious visitors, though much of the legend is exaggerated.

Towns here are small. Rodeo, with about four and a half thousand people, has shops and fuel, and Nogales, much smaller, a store or two. The larger cities of Gómez Palacio and Torreón are a long way off, so fill up whenever you see a pump, and carry water and a spare litre or two of fuel, since gaps can be over a hundred kilometres. Mobile coverage is patchy, so tell someone your route.

The riding is wide open, with long straight highways, big skies and little traffic, apart from trucks, and the main danger is wind, loose animals and long hours of sameness. Roads between small places can be rough, with potholes and sand drift, and unmarked dips after rain. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with warm days and cool nights, while summer is very hot and brings fierce thunderstorms. Winter nights can be freezing. Eat burritos, cheese and machaca, the dried and shredded beef of the north, in a small roadside kitchen, and stop for the sunset, which is long, red and silent.
t.fuji omuro segen jinja shrine@35.5,138.7:
There is a good argument that this is the most atmospheric shrine at the foot of Mount Fuji, and it has nothing to do with the view. Omuro Sengen-jinja stands in a grove of huge old cedars on the northern side, close to the lake town of Kawaguchiko, and the trees are so tall and so quiet that the sound of the road disappears within a few steps of the torii. The shrine is attached to the cult of Fuji itself, the idea that the mountain is a goddess to be placated, and it is part of the World Heritage listing for Fujisan as a sacred place and not simply a pretty one.

The history is volcanic. A great eruption on the mountain's flank in the ninth century sent lava into the area now known as Aokigahara and dammed lakes, and shrines like this one were built to calm the deity. Centuries later, the Fuji-ko brotherhoods of Edo pilgrims climbed the mountain in white robes and used cave sites in the lava fields as places of prayer and rest, which is what the neighbouring Hitoana label points to. Today the shrine is quiet, with a small wooden hall, mossy lanterns, and a path that leads to the edge of the forest.

For the rider, the area is a pleasure, if you time it right. The roads around Lake Kawaguchi have good surfaces, gentle climbs and long open bends with a clear view of the mountain, and the Fuji Subaru Line climbs toward the fifth station through forest and then bare cinders. It is a toll road and it is closed by snow for much of the winter, so check before you point a bike at it. Weekends in summer and on public holidays bring an immense amount of traffic, and the best hours are early in the morning, when mist hangs over the lake and the cone is sharp against a pale sky.

Fuel and food are straightforward. Fujikawaguchiko and Fujiyoshida are both real towns with stations, convenience stores and good bowls of houtou, the thick miso noodle stew that Yamanashi lives on. Bring a layer: at this altitude the temperature drops fast after sunset, even in July.
t.kozan ji@35.1,135.7:
Kozan-ji hangs on a forested ridge in the Toganoo hills, north-west of Kyoto, and the way there is the best part. Route 162, the old Shuzan Kaido, follows the Kiyotaki river up from the city through a narrow valley of cedar and maple, past the villages of Takao, Makino and Toganoo. The road is narrow and winding, with tight bends and blind corners, and it moves quickly from city to deep woods. In autumn the maples turn scarlet and the traffic can be heavy, so go on a weekday morning, or in early spring when the valley is nearly empty.

The temple is old, though most of what you see is a later rebuilding. It was restored in the early thirteenth century by the monk Myoe, who made it a centre of strict Buddhist study, and it is best known today for the Choju-jinbutsu-giga, a set of ink scrolls from the twelfth and thirteenth centuries in which frogs, rabbits and monkeys behave like humans, wrestling, bathing and mocking monks. They are often called the first manga, and the originals are now in museums, but the temple holds the memory. The Sekisui-in hall, with its wide wooden veranda, is a National Treasure and a lovely place to sit with a cup of tea.

Tea is the other story here. Myoe was a friend of the monk Eisai, who brought tea seeds back from China, and Toganoo is traditionally the place where tea was first grown in Japan. A small plot is still said to hold the oldest tea plants in the country, which is a charming claim whether or not you check the botany. It is a quiet, damp, mossy place, and the sound of the river is constant.

For practicalities, bring fuel from the city, since the valley is thin on stations; Arashiyama and Kamigyo-ku are the nearest large districts. A small shop or two near the Takao bus stop sells snacks. Parking for motorcycles is limited and the entrance is a short climb on stone steps, which is a good test for riding boots. Summer is humid; winter mornings can be icy in the shadows.
t.yamamiya sengen jinja shrine@35.3,138.6:
Fuji does not need an introduction, but the shrines around its foot deserve one. Yamamiya Sengen-jinja stands on the southwest side of the mountain at the edge of Fujinomiya, in Shizuoka Prefecture, and it is one of the old shrines dedicated to Konohanasakuya-hime, the blossoming princess who is the deity of Mount Fuji, and her cult spread to the whole country as the Sengen shrines. The Yamamiya precinct is a calm, cedar-shaded compound where the mountain presides from behind, and the main buildings stand in the old Edo-period style, with dark wood and copper roofing, and the mood of a place that has served pilgrims for centuries.

The pilgrimage was serious business. Climbers called fujiko, members of devotional clubs, walked from Edo and elsewhere, purified themselves at shrines like this one and then went up in white robes, chanting a mantra about clean senses and a clear mountain. It was this long religious and artistic relationship with the volcano that persuaded UNESCO in 2013 to inscribe Fujisan as a cultural landscape, not a natural site, and the shrines are an important part of that. The pure spring water that wells up in the town, filtered through ancient lava for decades, feeds ponds and streams and is part of the same sacred picture.

Riding here is easy to love. Fujinomiya is a town of about one hundred and twenty thousand people, with plenty of fuel, convenience stores and a famous local fried noodle dish, yakisoba, made with a firm noodle and cabbage and topped with a powder of dried fish. The mountain roads that climb to the fifth stations, the starting points for climbers, are scenic but subject to seasonal traffic regulations, and in the climbing season private vehicles may be restricted, so check the current rules before heading up. The stretch of Route 139 along the western flank passes the Shiraito Falls, a curtain of fine water pouring over a lava lip, and the open grassland of the Asagiri Plateau, where cattle graze below the volcano.

Fuji hides itself in cloud more often than visitors expect, and the clearest views come on cold, dry mornings in winter and in late autumn. Summers are hazy, humid, and brief on the summit. If the mountain shows itself, stop wherever you can safely park, and look. If it does not, the shrine and its forest are consolation.
t.rokuon ji@35.0,135.7:
The Golden Pavilion has been burned down at least once, and that is part of why it feels so intense. Rokuon-ji, the temple most people call Kinkaku-ji, began as the retirement villa of the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, who built it in the 1390s on the hillside of Kitayama in the north-west of Kyoto, and left instructions that after his death it should become a Zen temple. The three-storey pavilion on the lake is covered in gold leaf above the ground floor, each storey in a different architectural style, and topped with a bronze phoenix. In calm weather the reflection in the pond is perfect, and in winter, with snow on the roof, it is almost too much.

The old building was destroyed in 1950 when a young monk who was obsessed by the building set fire to it, a story that Yukio Mishima turned into one of the best-known Japanese novels of the twentieth century. The pavilion was rebuilt in the mid-1950s, and later regilded with a thicker layer of gold leaf in the 1980s. The garden around it, a carefully arranged stroll garden with islands, rocks and pine trees shaped like clouds, preserves the planning of Yoshimitsu's age, the Muromachi period, when Kyoto was at the height of its tea, noh and ink-painting culture.

On a bike, Kyoto is a city for patience. The streets are laid out on a grid that was copied from ancient Chinese capitals, and that makes navigation simple, but traffic is dense, buses and taxis dominate, and the cycling lanes get crowded. Speed limits are low and enforced. Parking for motorcycles near the temple is limited, so use a designated car park and walk. Arrive when the gates open and the light is soft, and you can see the pavilion before the tour coaches arrive. Autumn leaves in November and the quiet of a snowy morning are the best moments, and the heat of summer makes the gold almost painful to look at.

Kyoto has about one and a half million people, so fuel, food and everything else are easy, though petrol stations in the centre are fewer than you might expect. Beyond the city the hills to the north, along the Kitayama cedar roads and past Kurama and Kibune, offer narrow, twisting, forested riding, with tiny villages and cool air in summer. Come back to the lanes near the temple for a bowl of udon or a sweet of matcha and red bean, and you have a good day.
t.kiyomizu dera@35.0,135.8:
On the eastern hills of Kyoto, the great wooden veranda of Kiyomizu-dera juts out over a slope of maple and cherry, held up by a forest of pillars. The stage is about thirteen metres above the ground, and there is a Japanese saying, to jump off the stage of Kiyomizu, that means to take a bold, irreversible step. In the Edo period, people did really jump, hoping that survival would grant a wish, and a surprising number survived. The temple was founded in 778, and the present buildings date mainly from the 1630s, built without nails, using interlocking beams of Japanese zelkova and cypress.

Below the main hall, the Otowa waterfall splits into three streams, and visitors queue with long-handled cups to drink from them, each stream said to bring a different blessing, health, success or long life. Wisely, you are supposed to drink from only one. The name Kiyomizu means pure water, and this spring is the reason the temple stands where it does. Nearby is the little Jishu shrine, dedicated to love and matchmaking, with a pair of stones set several metres apart, and the tradition that if you can walk from one to the other with your eyes closed, your love will come true.

The approach is a lively, steep street of ceramics shops, sweet sellers and pickle merchants, running up from the district of Higashiyama through the lanes of Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka, where wooden houses have been preserved. It is magnificent early in the morning, and almost unbearable in the middle of a spring or autumn day, when crowds fill the slope. Go at opening time, or in the evening during the special illuminations, when the hall glows above the dark trees.

For a rider, the district is best reached by leaving the bike in a car park on the edge of the old city and walking uphill, as the lanes are narrow, partly pedestrian and busy with visitors. Kyoto's roads are slow and tidy, with low limits, and cameras and patrols enforce them. Fuel is available throughout the city of nearly one and a half million people, though stations are fewer in the old centre. Outside the city, the mountain roads north towards Kurama and Ohara and east over the hills towards Lake Biwa give real riding, with shaded forests of cedar, tight bends and quiet temples. Autumn leaves and early summer greenery are both worth the trip.
t.tomioka silk mill@36.3,138.9:
Tomioka Silk Mill is a long, low brick building with a timber frame, and it looks stranger than it is. In 1872, only a few years after the Meiji government opened Japan to the West, the state built this factory to produce silk by modern methods and sold it abroad to pay for the country's modernisation. A French engineer, Paul Brunat, designed it and hired French instructors, and the brick, laid in a pattern known as Flemish bond, was made locally by workers who had never seen a brick building before. The cocoon warehouses, with their sturdy roof frames, are still among the biggest wooden-framed brick buildings in Japan.

Many of the first workers were young women from samurai families, and they brought home what they learned to train others across the country. Silk was Japan's most important export through much of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and the mill remained in operation until 1987. Gunma prefecture was a heartland of silk farming, and you will see old farmhouses with raised roof ventilators designed for raising silkworms. Mulberry trees, the food of the worms, are still grown here, and the hills around the town produce konnyaku and good vegetables.

The ride to Tomioka crosses the Kanto plain toward the Myogi range, a jagged cluster of rock towers and forested ridges that rises behind the town, and the road gets curvier as it climbs. Winter brings a dry, cold wind called the karakkaze that sweeps across the plain from the mountains, and can be bitingly cold. Summer is hot and humid. Roads here are in good condition, though narrow in the older parts, and parking at the mill is straightforward.

Tomioka has nearly fifty thousand people, so petrol stations and restaurants are easy, and you will find soba shops and cafes near the mill. The site opens daily with a ticket, and guides can be booked. The nearby Myogi Shrine, with its dramatic rock setting, and Haruna and Akagi mountains are good for a longer ride. Autumn colour brings crowds to the hills, so choose weekdays if you can.
t.yoshida lava tree molds@35.4,138.8:
Mount Fuji's lava does strange things to trees. When a flow of molten rock surges through a forest, it wraps around trunks and hardens, and when the tree burns away it leaves a hollow cast, a round tube in the rock that looks like a well or a chimney. The lava tree molds at Yoshida are formed in this way, found along the lower slopes in the dense forest known as Aokigahara, where the ground is black, rough and honeycombed with caves. The flows come from eruptions of Fuji in the ninth century and later, and the forest has grown up over the cooling rock ever since.

Underfoot, the ground is a tangle of roots wrapped over lava, covered in moss that muffles every sound. That quiet is unusual, and the forest has an unsettling reputation, in part because of its association with tragedy, but it is also a place of great natural interest, with ice caves and wind caves that stay cold all summer. Visitors should stay on the marked paths and not go off alone, since the lava is rough and the forest disorienting, and a compass does not always behave.

The surrounding country is among the best in Japan for riding. The Fuji Five Lakes are strung around the north side of the mountain, and roads between them run through forest and past water with views of the cone on clear days. The Fuji Subaru Line climbs to the fifth station at over two thousand metres, though access is controlled during the summer climbing season and there is a toll. Winter closes some roads with ice or snow, and the mountain is often hidden in cloud, so the best views come on cold, clear mornings in autumn and winter.

Fujiyoshida, a town of about fifty thousand, has fuel, restaurants and the local speciality, Yoshida udon, a firm, chewy noodle served in a miso and soy soup. Weekends and holidays bring heavy traffic, particularly around Kawaguchiko, so ride on weekdays or at dawn. Bring a warm layer, because even in summer the forest floor is cool, and carry water.
t.ryoan ji@35.0,135.7:
Fifteen stones, a rectangle of raked white gravel, and an earthen wall stained by centuries of oil: that is all of Ryoan-ji's famous garden, and it has kept visitors quiet for five hundred years. The stones sit in five groups, set in beds of moss, and the clever thing, which every guidebook mentions and which is still a pleasure to test, is that from any seat on the temple veranda at least one stone is hidden from view. Nobody knows who made it or what it means. People have read tigers crossing the sea, islands in an ocean, mountains above clouds, or simply an exercise in emptiness. The temple belongs to the Rinzai school of Zen and was founded in the middle of the fifteenth century by a powerful warlord, Hosokawa Katsumoto.

Around the garden, the temple grounds are surprisingly pleasant: a large pond with water lilies, old pines, and a tea house near a stone basin whose inscription reads, roughly, that I learn only to be content. Ryoan-ji is on the north-western edge of Kyoto, at the foot of the hills, and is one of the group of Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto on the World Heritage list. Kinkaku-ji, the Golden Pavilion, is a short ride away, and Ninna-ji is beside it.

Riding in Kyoto is more rewarding at the edges than in the middle. The centre is a grid of one-way streets, dense with buses, taxis and bicycles, and parking for motorbikes is scarce and expensive. But from here the road north into the Kitayama hills, Route 162, called the Shuzan Kaido, climbs through cedar plantations and along the Kiyotaki and Hozu rivers, with long shaded curves and little traffic outside the weekend. In autumn the maples glow along it, and in winter the higher parts may be icy.

Fuel and food are easy in the city, and the temple area has simple restaurants, where you can try yudofu, simmered tofu in a hot broth, which is a Kyoto speciality. Spring and autumn are crowded and lovely. Go early, as the gates open in the morning, and the garden is quietest before the tour groups come.
t.architectonic ensemble of the town of ma:
Mapimí is a silver town that outlived its silver, and the architecture shows it. It sits in the Bolsón de Mapimí, the great desert basin of northern Durango and southern Chihuahua, where the horizon is flat, the air is dry and the sky is mostly empty. The town was founded in the sixteenth century to work mines in the hills nearby, and it grew rich enough to build a church, stone houses and a plaza. Later it was caught up in the fighting of the Mexican Revolution and the town's old buildings still carry the weight of those years.

The historic centre is small and walkable, and the 'architectonic ensemble' listed by UNESCO as part of the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro is the mix of mining-era houses, plaza and parish church. The Camino Real was the silver road, running from Mexico City up to Santa Fe in New Mexico, carrying bullion north to south and supplies, settlers and missionaries the other way for roughly three centuries. Mapimí was one of the stops, and the old road ran through the very landscape you are riding in.

The riding is long, straight and honest. The highways cross creosote bush and mesquite scrub with distant sierras at the edge of vision, and in places the road simply points at the horizon and goes. That makes it easy riding, but there are real hazards: cattle, potholes, trucks, and the wind, which can lean you over on the exposed stretches. Summer is brutally hot, winter nights can be near freezing, and distances between services are large, so keep the tank topped up. Mapimí itself is a town of about five and a half thousand, so you should find fuel and food here, and Bermejillo, further on, is larger.

The Zone of Silence, a patch of desert near here that has a reputation for odd radio behaviour and meteorites, draws a certain kind of visitor. The truth is more mundane, but the empty desert is still strong stuff. Take water, start early, and give yourself time in the plaza, where a cold drink and a bench in the shade do more for you than any monument.
t.chapel of the former hacienda of la limp:
There is something quietly impressive about a chapel standing alone in the Chihuahuan desert. La Limpia was a hacienda in what is now the state of Durango, one of the big estates that organised life across northern Mexico from the seventeenth century onward. Haciendas were farms, ranches, sometimes mines and always small worlds, with owners, workers, a granary, stables and a chapel for religious life. Most have faded, and the chapel is often what survives when the rest has crumbled.

This one is listed as part of the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the old silver road that ran from Mexico City north to Santa Fe. The Camino Real was a route for mule trains, wagons and travellers for three centuries, carrying silver, mercury, cloth, seeds and ideas. The haciendas along it supplied food and fodder and offered shelter. The chapel is a reminder that religion was part of the economic machine, because workers were baptised, married and buried here, and the owner's authority had spiritual cover.

You reach it across big empty country. The roads are long and often almost deserted, with scrub, cactus and low mountains at the edge of the horizon. Surfaces vary from decent asphalt to rough patches with potholes, and cattle drift across the road more often than you would like. Distances are long, so plan your fuel carefully: Rodeo, around thirteen kilometres away, is the nearest town with a few thousand people, and smaller places like Nogales and Coneto de Comonfort are sparser. Carry water, because there is none on the roadside.

Spring and autumn are the best seasons, when the heat is bearable and the light on the hills is clear. Summer afternoons are hot and sometimes end in storms, and winter nights can get cold. The silence at the chapel is genuine. It is the sort of place where the wind is the main sound, and where you can see a very long way. Have a drink, take a photo, and make sure your fuel plan is better than your sense of adventure.
t.chapel of san mateo of the former hacien:
Indé is a small town in northern Durango, and the chapel of San Mateo belonged to a hacienda that supplied the silver road. The Camino Real de Tierra Adentro ran for about 2,600 kilometres from Mexico City to Santa Fe, and this stretch crossed some of the driest country on the way. Around here the landscape is bajada and basin, with mesquite, huisache and prickly pear on the plains and dark mountain ranges in the distance. Rainfall is low, and the wells and springs that haciendas depended on decided where people could live.

The chapel is a modest building, and that is part of its appeal. These haciendas were built with local stone and adobe, and the chapels often had a bell gable instead of a tower, thick walls to keep out the heat, and a plain interior. The settlement around them was part farm, part village. The Camino Real was never a single highway but a network of routes, and its protection by presidios, small garrisons, was important because the north was contested ground.

There is no sizeable town close by, so treat this as remote country. Roads here can be long and quiet, and you may go an hour without seeing another vehicle. That is a pleasure on a motorbike when the surface is good, but it also means that if you break down you may wait. Carry water, a spare tube or repair kit, a charged phone and a paper map or offline map. Fuel stations in northern Mexico are sparse compared to Europe, and it is worth topping up whenever you pass one.

The weather decides the rest. In summer it is very hot, and afternoon storms can come in fast. In winter mornings are cold and the air is clean and clear. The best time to ride is spring or autumn, early in the day. Look for birds of prey on the telegraph poles, and for roadrunners if you are lucky. This is a place for slowing down and looking at the old walls, then getting on with the road.
t.odawara@35.3,139.2:
Odawara is a castle town at the foot of Hakone, and for most riders it is the place where the mountains begin. The castle, which belonged to the Hojo clan until Toyotomi Hideyoshi besieged it in 1590, has a reconstructed keep, built in 1960, with a museum inside. The old town around it is quiet, with a modest shopping street and some traditional shops. It sits on Sagami Bay, with the coast road leading east and west and the Hakone mountains rising behind.

The town is known for food. Odawara is one of Japan's great producers of kamaboko, the white fish paste cakes that appear in noodle soup and on celebration tables, and shops along the coast sell them freshly steamed. The fishing port sells dried horse mackerel, and Odawara also has a long tradition of growing ume plums, which are made into pickles and drinks. It is a pleasant place for a late lunch, with sushi bars close to the station.

For the rider, Odawara is a gateway and a place to refuel. It has a population of about two hundred thousand, so there are petrol stations, convenience stores and restaurants in abundance, and the roads inland lead to the Hakone Turnpike, one of Japan's best-known scenic toll roads. Riding back down into Odawara at the end of a day in the mountains, with the road sloping to the bay and lights in the town below, is a pleasure. The coast road, Route 135, is busy at weekends but good for relaxed riding.

Expect traffic, especially on summer Sundays, and note that speed limits in Japan are low and enforced. Weather on the coast is mild, but Hakone can be wet and foggy when Odawara is dry, so check conditions before you go up. Autumn offers crisp air and good views of Fuji on clear days. Park near the castle, walk up to the keep, then find something warm to eat.
t.funatsu lava tree molds@35.5,138.8:
Seen from above, the forest on the north side of Mount Fuji looks like green felt, and underneath it lies black lava from an eruption in 864 AD. The lava poured through the trees, the wet trunks cooled it around them, and when the timber burned or rotted away it left hollow cylinders in the rock. Those are the tree molds at Funatsu, a short walk of mossy, cool tunnels where you can duck into the lava and look at the exact shape of a tree that stopped existing eleven hundred years ago. Some of the molds are the width of a person's shoulders; a few go deep enough that you want a torch.

The same eruption dammed the old lake and split it into smaller ones, which is why the Fuji Five Lakes exist at all. Aokigahara, the dense forest growing on that lava, is a short ride from here; the ground is porous and the compass needles behave oddly, and the whole thing smells of damp earth and cedar. It is quiet in a very particular way, because the lava soaks up sound like a sponge.

Getting here is half the fun. From Fujiyoshida, a proper town of nearly fifty thousand people with every kind of fuel station, convenience store and ramen counter, you climb through pine woods and the riding turns to long smooth bends that suit a loaded tourer. The Fuji Subaru Line toll road climbs the mountain's flank toward the fifth station, but it is well known that the road is closed to private traffic at times in summer, so check before you plan on it. The better lakeside roads around Kawaguchiko run past thatched farm houses and offer the view that ends up on postcards: Fuji reflected in glassy water, if the cloud allows.

Weather decides everything. Fuji hides behind cloud more often than not, and the best views are in the cold clear mornings of late autumn and winter. The air up here is around a kilometre above sea level, so nights can be sharp even in May. Summers fill the roads with tour buses and rental cars, and the lakes get busy at weekends; a weekday and an early start gets you the quiet version.

Do not skip the local food: houtou, the thick miso noodle stew with pumpkin that Yamanashi keeps in a pot, is exactly what you want after a morning in the damp tunnels.
t.krakow@50.1,19.9:
Kraków has the kind of old town that makes you slow down on foot, and it deserves it. At the centre is the Rynek Główny, the main market square, one of the largest medieval squares in Europe, with the Cloth Hall in the middle and the two uneven towers of St Mary's Basilica at the corner. Each hour a trumpeter plays a bugle call from the taller tower, and the tune stops abruptly in mid-phrase, in memory of a watchman said to have been shot in the throat by a Tatar arrow while sounding the alarm.

South of the square lies Wawel Hill, with its castle and cathedral, where Polish kings were crowned and buried for centuries. The city was Poland's capital until the late sixteenth century, and survived the Second World War with its old centre largely intact. Just across the old town is Kazimierz, the historic Jewish quarter, which has become a district of cafes, synagogues and galleries. Poland's university tradition runs deep here, with the Jagiellonian University dating from 1364, where Copernicus studied.

The ride that begins here is the Eagles' Nests Trail, a chain of medieval castles along the limestone uplands between Kraków and Częstochowa. King Casimir the Great strengthened the border defences in the fourteenth century, building strongholds on the cliffs, and the ruins and restored castles now sit among white rock outcrops, beech woods and farmland. North of Kraków the road enters the Ojców area, with limestone gorges and a small national park. Roads are mostly paved and quiet, rolling rather than steep, with villages every few kilometres. Spring and autumn are lovely, summer can be hot and thundery, and winter can bring ice.

Kraków has all the fuel, workshops and hotels a rider could want, with fuel stations on the ring roads. City traffic is heavy and tram tracks can be slippery when wet. For breakfast, try an obwarzanek, the ring-shaped bread sold from street carts, and for dinner pierogi or żurek soup. Leave the bike in a secure garage and explore the centre on foot.
t.churches of peace in jawor and swidnica@:
After the Thirty Years' War, Silesia belonged to the Catholic Habsburgs, and Lutherans in the region were allowed only the smallest favour. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 allowed them three churches, built outside the town walls, from perishable materials, without towers or bells, and in a single year. The result, in Jawor, Świdnica and a third town that has since lost its church, was one of the most surprising buildings in Europe.

The churches are made of timber, clay and straw, and they are huge. The one at Świdnica, dedicated to the Holy Trinity, is a vast timber-framed barn of a building that could hold thousands of worshippers on balconies and in boxes, with a ceiling painted with scenes from the Bible, and an organ, pulpit and altar of rich Baroque. Jawor's church, on a smaller scale, has the same warmth, with painted galleries and carved decoration. Both are now UNESCO World Heritage sites, and both are still in use for services and concerts.

Jawor is a town of about twenty-four thousand in Lower Silesia, on the road between Legnica and Świdnica, and the landscape around it is gently rolling farmland, with the Sudeten hills a blue line to the south. Roads are generally good and of modest traffic, with long straight stretches between villages and a few pleasant curves through the woods. Cobbled sections do appear in village streets, and level crossings are frequent. Poland enforces speed limits strictly, with cameras in built-up areas, so watch for signs.

Fuel is easy in Jawor, and the town centre has cafés and bakeries around its market square. Silesian food is hearty: dumplings, pork knuckle, żurek, a sour rye soup, and cakes with poppy seeds, and in autumn the markets sell plums and mushrooms. The surrounding hills hold castles and quiet valleys, with Książ castle near Wałbrzych well worth a visit.

Opening hours of the churches are limited, and a visit usually involves buying a ticket from a custodian, so check ahead if you have a tight schedule.
t.mine of ojuela@25.8,-103.8:
The suspension bridge at Ojuela is the first thing most visitors see, and it hangs across a canyon in the desert of Durango like something out of a Western. Built in 1898 by the firm of the Roebling family, the engineers behind the Brooklyn Bridge, it spans about three hundred metres and carries the old mine track across the gorge to the entrance of the Ojuela mine. For years the bridge was in a bad state, and it has been restored for walkers, though you should cross carefully and listen to the guides.

Mapimí, about seven kilometres away, was founded in the late sixteenth century as a silver-mining town in the desert of the north, and the Ojuela mine was the heart of its wealth, producing silver, lead, zinc and later gold and copper. Tunnels run for many kilometres beneath the hill, and visitors can enter a section with a guide, seeing the rough timbers, narrow stairs and low tunnels that miners worked in. The town of Mapimí has been recognised as a Pueblo Mágico, with adobe houses, a pretty plaza and a small museum.

The country around is the Chihuahuan Desert, a land of creosote bush, mesquite, yucca and cactus, with hot summers, cold clear winters and almost no rain. Farther out in the same desert lies the Mapimí Silent Zone, where legend says radio signals fail and meteorites fall, though scientists have not found anything unusual. The Bolsón de Mapimí biosphere reserve, nearby, shelters a rare desert tortoise.

The roads are straight, flat and hot, with long, empty stretches between towns and sudden wind. Summer temperatures often pass forty degrees, and a hat and plenty of water are essential. Watch for livestock, potholes and trucks, and avoid riding at night. Mapimí has a small town centre with a fuel station, and the larger cities of Torreón and Gómez Palacio, about eighty kilometres away, have everything else, so fill up there before heading out.

Visit in spring or autumn, when the mine tunnels are cool and the desert is mild.
t.tokyo kanto rides@35.7,138.9:
The Katsura river runs below, cutting a gorge near Ōtsuki that is crossed by Saruhashi, the Monkey Bridge, one of Japan's three great strange bridges, a wooden cantilever construction that has been rebuilt many times since the Middle Ages. Enzan, to the north-west, is the gateway to the Daibosatsu mountains and the Chichibu-Tama-Kai National Park.

This is a landscape of terraced orchards, with grapes, peaches and persimmons ripening along the slopes. The Kōshū grape, grown here for over a thousand years, makes the white wine of Katsunuma, and the vineyards have given the area a growing reputation among wine lovers, with tasting rooms open to visitors. The old Kōshū Kaidō, the road from Edo to Kōfu, ran through here, and Sasago Pass, a long climb to the east, was one of its steepest sections, with checkpoints and inns that have mostly vanished. Mount Fuji appears on the southern horizon from many viewpoints, a huge white shape above the lower hills.

The roads are a pleasure. From Ōtsuki, routes climb the valleys toward Kosuge and Lake Okutama, with sharp bends, narrow sections and a thick cover of forest, and the Matsuhime road in particular has a fine reputation among riders. The surface is mostly good, but narrow in places, and rockfalls, wet leaves and fallen branches are common. In winter, ice persists in the shade, and snow can close the higher roads. Autumn is the best time, with the orchards and forests in colour, and spring brings blossom in the valleys.

Fuel and food are easy in Ōtsuki, Enzan and the Kōfu basin, with convenience stores and restaurants along the main roads. The local dish is hōtō, a thick noodle soup of flat wheat noodles, pumpkin and vegetables, served in an iron pot and perfect for a cold day. Fresh fruit is for sale at roadside stands in season.

The label mentions Bandai Azuma and Shōsenkyō, but the mountains here have their own appeal, quieter and little known to visitors.
t.hakone@35.2,139.1:
Hakone is where Tokyo goes to get away from itself. The mountain resort sits in the caldera of an old volcano southwest of the capital, about an hour and a half by road without traffic, with Lake Ashi in the middle and Fuji looming to the northwest on a good day. Odawara, on the coast below, is the practical town, with its castle and its fish markets, while the hot-spring villages scattered through the hills have catered to travellers for centuries. The old Tokaido highway crossed these mountains, and you can still walk stretches of its stone-paved surface and see a reconstructed checkpoint beside the lake, where officials of the Tokugawa shogunate once inspected every traveller's papers.

On a bike, the draw is the mountain road. The Hakone Turnpike climbs from the coast in a long run of bends, open and smooth, with good visibility and a toll that keeps heavy trucks away.
