The Skyline and the roads around the crater rim offer views over the lake and the Pacific. Expect weekend crowds of cars and motorcycles, especially on fine autumn days, and be careful in fog, which rolls into the caldera quickly and can drop the temperature several degrees. Winter mornings can bring ice on the higher sections.

Landscape matters here as much as the road. Owakudani, the steaming valley of sulphur vents above the lake, is the remains of a violent eruption roughly three thousand years ago, and the smell of rotten eggs drifts across the road. Locals boil eggs in the hot pools there until the shells turn black, and tell you each one adds seven years to your life. The pampas grass fields of Sengokuhara turn silver in autumn, and the cedar avenue along the old highway is cool and dark even in midsummer.

Fuel is straightforward, with stations in Odawara and along the main road up the valley, but the mountain sections have fewer, so fill at the bottom. Konbini stores at the lakeside and along the turnpike sell hot drinks and snacks. A cup of coffee at a mountain cafe, with the lake and the trees outside, is a decent reward after the climb.

Come on a weekday if you can, and early. By midday the lake road is slow, and by evening the mist often comes back down.
t.kanazawa@36.6,136.7:
Kanazawa escaped the bombs of the Second World War and kept its old quarters, which is a large part of its charm today. The city sits on the Sea of Japan coast of Ishikawa Prefecture, between two rivers and a hill, and for centuries it was ruled by the Maeda clan, the second richest domain in feudal Japan. Their money went into art and craft, and Kanazawa is still known for gold leaf, lacquerware, ceramics and tea ceremony. Kenroku-en, the garden the clan laid out over generations, is counted among the three great gardens of Japan, with its pines held up by rope umbrellas against the heavy winter snow.

Here you can wander the old samurai district, with its mud walls and narrow lanes, and the geisha quarter of Higashi Chaya, where wooden teahouses face each other across stone-paved streets. The fish market near the station, Omicho, sells crab, sweet shrimp and sushi in season, and the sea is close enough that the catch is always fresh. Winter brings snow crab and heavy grey skies, and the city's cuisine has a deep reputation across Japan.

As a place to start a ride, Kanazawa is a city with all the usual urban frictions. The ring road and the main avenues are busy, and traffic lights are frequent, so the early miles are a matter of patience. Once you leave, the Noto Peninsula to the north offers a long, quiet coastal road, with the sea on one side and low hills and rice paddies on the other, small fishing harbours, salt farms and terraced fields. The surface is generally good, speeds are low and drivers are polite. Winter brings snow and ice to the area, and the best months to ride are late spring and autumn.

Fuel is easy around Kanazawa, a city of nearly half a million, with self-service pumps everywhere. Nonoichi and Matsuto, the neighbouring towns, are also well stocked. On the peninsula, stations thin out, especially in the evening, so fill up before heading north. Convenience stores sell a decent coffee and a rice ball at any hour.

Give yourself a morning or an evening in town, if you can. The gardens and the old districts reward slow walking, and Kanazawa is a lot more interesting than most places that serve merely as a start line.
t.lake ashi view@35.2,139.0:
Lake Ashi fills the caldera of the old Hakone volcano, at 720 metres, and it is one of the most visited places in Japan, partly because of the view. On a clear morning, particularly in winter, the cone of Mount Fuji rises above the water in perfect symmetry, and the red torii gate of Hakone Shrine stands in the lake in the foreground.

Hakone has been a travellers' stop for centuries. In the Edo period, the Tokaido, the great road between Edo and Kyoto, crossed the mountains here, and the shogun kept a checkpoint on the shore of the lake to control the passage of weapons and women. The checkpoint has been reconstructed, and a stretch of the old road, lined with huge cedars planted in the seventeenth century, still runs beside the lake. Pirate-style tourist boats cross the water, and the sulphurous steam of Owakudani, the volcanic valley above, drifts in the breeze.

The ride up to the lake is the thing. The roads climb from the coast in a series of tight bends, with hairpins, tunnels and views, and the road around the lake itself is a smooth, winding ribbon. This is a famous place for riders, and on fine weekends the roads are packed with motorbikes, cars and tour buses, so a weekday or an early start is wise. The weather can change in minutes, with fog and rain rolling in from the sea, and in winter ice can form on the upper roads. A few of the scenic roads are toll roads.

Hakone has more than thirteen thousand people, with fuel, restaurants and souvenir shops, and hot-spring baths, onsen, are everywhere. After a day in the saddle, there is nothing better than a hot soak with a view of the mountains. The best time for views of Fuji is early on a cold, clear morning in winter, but spring and autumn are lovely, with cherry blossoms and red maples. The summer is hazy, and the rainy season in June brings hydrangeas but little view.
t.myogi mountain@35.6,139.3:
Hachioji sits where the Tokyo plain finally runs into the hills, a city of well over five hundred thousand people at the foot of the Tama mountains, and the Myogi ride comes back to it as to a front door. In the old days it was a post town on the road to the western provinces, famous for silk, and merchants carried raw silk down the Hachioji road to the ports of Yokohama for export. That trade made the city rich, and the old route is still remembered as the Silk Road of Japan.

The mountain that dominates the skyline is Takao, a modest peak of about six hundred metres with a Buddhist temple, Yakuo-in, on its slopes. The temple is a pilgrimage site and the mountain a favourite weekend hike for Tokyoites, who ride the cable car and eat soba in the shops on the way up. The forest is thick, mixed with cedar, beech and oak, and the Michelin guide once gave Takao three stars, which tells you how many people come.

Hachioji is also a university city and a hub, where the Chuo Expressway, the Ken-O-Do ring route and several national roads meet, so traffic is a feature. Roads out toward Sagamiko and the Kanagawa border climb into forested valleys with decent curves and little commercial traffic, and these are good routes on a weekday morning. Weekend afternoons are crowded with cars heading home, and the evening rush backs up on the main trunk.

The ordinary comforts are all here, with fuel on every main road and cafes, ramen counters and Hachioji's local specialty of ramen with chopped onions on shoyu broth. Spring brings cherry blossom, autumn colours the hills in late November, and summer is humid and loud with cicadas. Winter mornings can bring frost to shaded bends in the mountains, so check conditions. Park and walk the shopping arcades for an hour if there is light left.
t.tokyo west@35.7,139.5:
The reading of forty metres above sea level tells you the geography: the Musashino plateau, a broad terrace of the Tama River's old floodplain, flat as a table and covered in houses, farms and the long green ribbons of watercourses. Kokubunji, the nearest town, is a commuter hub on the Chuo Line, and the route out toward the west starts here, heading for the mountains that appear as a blue line on clear winter days.

What makes this plateau special is its water engineering. In 1653, the Tamagawa Aqueduct was dug to bring drinking water from the Tama River to Edo, about forty kilometres of open channel running along the ridge line, with minimal slope, and it fed the growing city for centuries. Much of it is now a footpath lined with cherry trees, and stretches near Kodaira and Mitaka are a lovely place to cycle. It was engineered by two brothers of the Tamagawa family, whose names are still remembered, and the surname became the canal's own.

As an exit from the city, the route is anything but wild. Roads are straight, the traffic lights are numerous and the speed limits are strictly enforced, so patience is more useful than a throttle. The reward starts further west, past Tachikawa and Ome, where the road tilts upward and the Chichibu-Tama-Kai mountains come into view. Early morning departures avoid the worst traffic, and Sunday dawns are particularly quiet.

Fuel is easy here, and many stations are self-service. Convenience stores sell hot coffee, rice balls and sandwiches. Spring, with the cherry blossoms along the aqueduct, is the most beautiful time to leave, and late autumn adds yellow ginkgo leaves on the pavements. Summer is hot and humid, so carry water and ride early. A few minutes by the old channel, listening to the passing bicycles, is a nice way to remember how much effort went into the city's water.
t.shosenkyo gorge@35.8,139.9:
Matsudo is a city of nearly half a million people on the Chiba side of the Edo River, the border with Tokyo, and nothing about it says Shosenkyo or mountains. It is a commuter place, an hour or so from the gorge's Yamanashi valleys, and so a natural endpoint when the day's riding has taken you back through the whole sprawl of the Kanto plain. Think of it as the dock where the ship comes in.

The Edo River gives the place its character. It was dug and straightened in the seventeenth century to control the Tone river's floods and to carry goods to Edo, and its broad, grassy embankments now hold cycle paths, sports fields and fishermen. Across from Matsudo, in Tokyo's Katsushika ward, lies Shibamata, the setting of the long-running Tora-san film series, and the Yagiri no Watashi, a small ferry that has crossed the river here since the Edo period. It carries foot passengers and cyclists for a small fare, and it is a charming bit of surviving old Japan in a modern suburb.

For a rider, the roads are urban and dull, laced with traffic lights and trucks serving the logistics parks along the Joban line and the Gaikan expressway. The best moments are along the river embankment roads in the early morning, when the light is soft and the air is cool. Rain and typhoons can flood the low ground, and in summer the humidity is something to be endured, with cicadas shouting from every tree.

You will not struggle for services. Petrol stations line every major road, and ramen, curry and sushi shops are around the station. Matsudo also has a pear story: the Nijisseiki variety, still the classic Japanese pear, is said to have been found as a chance seedling here in the 1880s, and Chiba remains famous for its pears and peanuts. Autumn is the most pleasant season, with clear air and dry weather. Park the bike, walk the embankment at sunset, and let the day wind down slowly.
t.tokyo kanto rides@36.3,139.6:
Sano ramen is the first thing to say about this corner of Tochigi. The town is known across Japan for noodles that are flat, springy and kneaded by bamboo poles, served in a clear soy broth that tastes clean and slightly sweet. It also has a famous outlet mall and a temple devoted to warding off bad luck, so the town has a steady flow of visitors.

The terrain is the plain of the Watarase and Tone rivers, marked by drainage channels, levees and rice, with the edge of the Ryōmō hills rising to the north. A few kilometres west, Tatebayashi is known for two things. In spring, the azaleas of Tsutsujigaoka Park bloom in thousands, some of them hundreds of years old, and a festival draws visitors from all over the Kantō. The Morin-ji temple preserves the folk tale of the Bunbuku Chagama, a tanuki that turned into a tea kettle and brought good fortune to a poor priest. It is a cheerful bit of local lore.

South-east of here, the Watarase retention basin is a large wetland where four prefectures meet, built to control flooding and now registered as a Ramsar site, a good place for reeds, herons and migrating birds. In winter, harriers hunt over the reeds and the whole area has a stark beauty. This is not the Japan of mountains and temples but a quiet, productive heartland of vegetables and rice, and the landscape rewards slow looking.

For riders, the roads are flat and straight, which suits an early start from Tokyo before heading to the hills. Fuel is easy, with Sano, Tatebayashi and Fujioka all within a short ride and plenty of stations along the main roads. Ride with attention to crossings, since farm traffic and local drivers do not always look. Pick a hot day and the plain can be oppressive, so take your time and keep water on the bike. In November, when the harvest is done and the air is clear, the views to the mountains are some of the best of the year.
t.tokyo bay@35.6,139.7:
Ten metres above sea level on Tokyo's own shoreline, this stop sits on land that did not exist four centuries ago. Since the Edo period the city has pushed out into the bay, one reclamation at a time, and the districts around Ota, Shinagawa and the Haneda approach are largely built on that fill. From here the waterfront is a quarter hour away, and the water smells of salt, diesel and wet concrete.

The scenery is industrial and strangely beautiful: container cranes, warehouses, canals with moored barges, and the great arch of the Rainbow Bridge a little way north. Planes from Haneda, one of the busiest airports in the world, pass low overhead on approach, and you can watch them from park lawns by the shore. Parks such as the Wild Bird Park at Tokyo Port, a managed wetland of reeds and tidal pools, bring herons and migrating shorebirds to this edge of the megacity, and the contrast with the high-rise skyline across the water is memorable.

On a motorcycle, the bayside is both easy and awkward. The Bayshore Route, a broad road, runs close to the water, with long signals and steady traffic, and the Metropolitan Expressway crosses overhead with its tolls. Weekends are lighter for trucks than weekdays. Strong wind off the water can be tiring, and fog on winter mornings is not unusual. The joy comes in the evening, when the lights come on across the water and ships slide out of the harbour.

Services are plentiful, with fuel stations along every major road and countless restaurants. The nearby fish market district and old Shinagawa post town have places for sushi or a simple grilled-fish lunch. Parking for motorcycles is available in coin lots, though prices vary. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, when the air is clear and the wind quieter. Take a short walk along a pier before you leave, and watch the city show its working side.
t.utsunomiya@36.6,139.9:
Say gyoza in Japan and most people will say Utsunomiya. The capital of Tochigi has made the dumpling its civic emblem, with dozens of specialist shops, statues of dumplings in the station area and a popular rivalry with Hamamatsu over which city eats more of them. It is a cheerful, big-city sort of town, home to four hundred and fifty thousand people, and for riders it is the gateway to Nikkō, thirty-odd kilometres to the north-west.

The city is also built on stone. Ōya, a soft, greenish volcanic tuff quarried nearby since ancient times, forms the walls of old warehouses and churches, and Frank Lloyd Wright used it in his Imperial Hotel in Tokyo. The quarries have left enormous underground chambers, now used as an eerie, cool museum and event space. Utsunomiya was a castle town and a key stop on the Nikkō Kaidō, the road that pilgrims and lords took to the shrines of Nikkō.

The road to Nikkō is one of Japan's great avenues. A long line of cedar trees, planted in the seventeenth century by a feudal lord as an offering to the shrine, still runs along the old highway, forming a corridor of dark trunks that is among the longest tree-lined roads in the world. Riding under them in the early morning, with dappled light and the smell of resin, is a gentle pleasure. The modern Nikkō-Utsunomiya road is faster but less memorable, so choose the old way if time allows.

Fuel is no problem here. Utsunomiya is full of stations, and there are plenty more along the route. For food, gyoza is the obvious choice, served pan-fried, boiled or in soup, usually in a set with rice, and a plate is cheap and quick. Check the weather in Nikkō before you go, since the mountains can be cold and foggy while the city is warm. If you reach the avenue in the evening on your way back, the light through the trees is worth the wait.
t.irohazaka ascent@36.7,139.5:
The Irohazaka climbs from Nikkō, at about six hundred metres, to Lake Chūzenji at roughly twelve hundred and seventy, and each bend is labelled with one of the forty-eight characters of the old Japanese iroha syllable poem, so you can tick them off in order like a very steep alphabet. The road is actually two roads, a one-way uphill route built in 1954 and a one-way downhill route added in 1965, so you meet the bends in one direction only and never face oncoming traffic on them.

The ride is superb and slightly nerve-racking in equal parts. The corners are tight, with a rhythm of braking, leaning and accelerating that never quite lets you settle, and the surface is usually good, though damp, with a layer of fallen leaves. In autumn, the maples and birches turn the whole slope red and gold, and the traffic grows heavy, particularly at weekends in mid to late October, when queues can stretch for hours. Japanese macaques sit on the guardrails and are happy to inspect a parked bike. Winter brings snow and ice, and chains or studded tyres are needed.

At the top, the road delivers you to Chūzenji, a deep lake formed when a lava flow from Mount Nantai blocked the Daiya river. The lake sits at a cold, clear altitude, ringed by wooded hills, and the outflow drops over Kegon Falls, a ninety-seven metre ribbon of white water that is one of Japan's most famous cascades. In the Meiji period, foreign diplomats built summer villas along the shore, and some of the buildings are still preserved.

Fuel is not available on the climb, so fill in Nikkō or Imaichi before you start. The town of Nikkō, below, has plenty of stations and many restaurants, and its yuba, a delicate tofu skin dish, is the local speciality. Allow extra time on autumn weekends and check road conditions in winter, as the pass can close or require chains. Early morning is the best moment for the climb. A cloud-capped Nantai at sunrise is one of the sights of the Japanese mountains.
t.hachioji@35.7,139.3:
Mount Takao stands at the edge of Hachiōji like a patient dog, a green hill of about six hundred metres that Tokyoites climb in their hundreds of thousands. For a rider, it is a start and finish point, a convenient place for fuel, parking and a good bowl of ramen before the mountains begin. The city sits at the foot of the Tama hills, and the climate here is a few degrees cooler than central Tokyo.

Hachiōji has a clear identity. The local ramen is a shoyu broth with chopped onions floating on top, a simple, comforting bowl that sells at counters across the city. The city was an important silk centre, and its merchants traded in bales of silk that travelled to Yokohama along a road still called the Silk Road. In the sixteenth century, the Hōjō clan of Odawara held a castle on a hill here, which fell to Toyotomi Hideyoshi's army in 1590, and the remains of its walls can still be walked. In late November, the avenue of ginkgo trees along the road to Mount Takao turns a brilliant yellow, and the city holds a festival beneath them.

The riding that starts here goes west. Route 20, the old Kōshū Kaidō, climbs past the foot of Mount Takao and through the long Kobotoke tunnel, then continues toward Sagamiko, Ōtsuki and the Chūō corridor. Other roads lead north-west to Ōme and the Okutama valley, or south-west to the Tanzawa foothills. The early morning is the best time, when the city is quiet and the mountains are cool. Sunday traffic is heavy on the way out.

Fuel and food are everywhere. The city has hundreds of stations and restaurants, and the area around Hachiōji station is lively with cafés and small bars. If you finish here at the end of the day, plan to arrive before the evening rush, when the roads back into central Tokyo are slow. A bowl of ramen after a long ride is hard to beat, and the soy broth, rich and salty, is just what a tired rider needs.
t.ome exit roads@35.8,139.3:
At the end of a day in the mountains, the Tama valley delivers you back to Ōme like a conveyor belt. For a rider coming down from Okutama, it is the place where the road widens, the traffic thickens and the first petrol stations appear, a signal that the mountains are done for the day. Fuel here is no problem, with stations on every main road, and Fussa and Hannō are close.

Before you reach town, the valley has some good things to stop for. Mitake, a gorge of the Tama river, offers canoeing, riverside walks and small restaurants with terraces over the water. Mount Mitake, which rises above, has a shrine reached by cable car where wolves were once worshipped as protectors of the harvest, and wolf talismans are still sold. In Sawai, a famous sake brewery draws its water from the mountains, and visitors can taste the product in a beautiful setting.

In Ōme itself, the old centre keeps hand-painted film billboards and a museum devoted to retro culture, a charming reminder of the days when the town was a weaving centre. Ōme was also on the old route that carried lime to Edo. The streets are quiet on weekday evenings, and a short walk with a cup of coffee suits the end of a long ride. If you are in the mood, a bowl of hearty noodles in a little family restaurant completes the day.

The way back to central Tokyo is the main challenge. Route 16 and the Ōme Kaidō fill with returning traffic on Sunday afternoons, and tailbacks are common. If you can, leave the mountains early or stay for a late dinner and ride when the roads have emptied. The Chūō expressway offers a quicker way back, though it also jams. Keep your concentration up, as tired riders are most at risk in the last few kilometres, and enjoy the warm lights as you return to the city.
t.nikko@36.8,139.6:
Nikko is where Tokugawa Ieyasu was laid to rest, and the town lives with the weight of that. Ieyasu, who founded the shogunate that ruled Japan for two and a half centuries, died in 1616 and was enshrined here in the mountains north of Tokyo, and the Toshogu shrine, completed a year later and enlarged by his grandson, is a riot of gold leaf, carving and colour, quite unlike the restraint most people associate with Japanese temples. The famous carving of the three monkeys, hear no evil, see no evil, speak no evil, is here.

The setting matters as much as the buildings. Huge cedars, planted over decades as a gift by a loyal lord, line the approaches, and the mist often clings among them. The town sits at the foot of the mountains of Nikko National Park, and above it rise volcanic peaks, a high lake and waterfalls. Autumn colour is spectacular, usually in mid to late October, and brings crowds.

For a rider, the climb is the event. The Irohazaka road, with its forty-eight hairpins named after the letters of the old Japanese alphabet, climbs the steep slope toward Lake Chuzenji in two one-way sections, one for each direction. The curves are tight and the surface is good, but the road is busy in autumn and misty in the mornings. At the top, the lake and the Kegon Falls drop in a single plume of nearly a hundred metres, and beyond lies the Senjogahara marsh, an open plain of grass and birch beside a ridge of volcanic hills.

Nikko itself is a small town with fuel, restaurants and plenty of hotels. A local speciality is yuba, thin sheets of tofu skin, served in various forms. Summer is cool by Tokyo standards, which is why imperial families built holiday villas here. Snow can close the high road from late autumn, so check ahead if you ride in November. Arrive early or late to avoid the tour buses, and give the temple a proper morning.
t.nagoya@35.2,136.9:
Nagoya is the city that builds cars, and it carries that practical, slightly modest air in everything. It is the fourth-largest city in Japan, with about two million people, and the home of Toyota, whose factories and museums lie in the surrounding plain. It sits between Tokyo and Osaka on the old Tokaido road, and although it lacks their fame, locals are proud of its food, its castle and its quiet confidence.

The castle, built by Tokugawa Ieyasu in the early seventeenth century for his ninth son, is the symbol, with two golden shachihoko, mythical fish with tigers' heads, perched on the roof. The main keep was destroyed in the bombing of 1945 and rebuilt in concrete, but the palace buildings are being restored with fine painted screens. Atsuta Shrine, one of the most important Shinto shrines, shelters among old camphor trees, and it is said to hold the sacred sword Kusanagi, one of the imperial regalia.

Nagoya cuisine is bold. Miso katsu is a pork cutlet in rich red miso sauce, hitsumabushi is grilled eel served three ways over rice, and tebasaki are fried chicken wings seasoned with pepper. Kishimen are flat wheat noodles, and the breakfast habit of a cheap morning set with toast and egg in coffee shops is a local custom.

On a motorbike, the city is easy to navigate, with a regular grid, but traffic is heavy, and the expressways carry tolls. Fuel is plentiful. The mountains to the east and north, toward Okazaki, Gifu and the Kiso valley, offer good riding, with twisty roads and old post towns. Summer is hot and humid, with typhoons in autumn. Spring is a nice time to visit, with cherry trees along the castle moat. Park outside the centre and use the subway to visit sights, since one-way streets and expressway ramps around the station can trap a rider who has not planned the exit.
t.takayama@36.2,137.3:
Takayama sits in the Hida mountains in the centre of Honshu, a small city of about sixty-five thousand surrounded by peaks of the Northern Alps. For centuries it was cut off by snow, and its carpenters became famous across Japan, so skilled that they were sent to build temples and palaces in Kyoto and Edo. That heritage is visible in the old town, where dark wooden merchants' houses with latticed fronts line the narrow streets of Sanmachi Suji, and sake breweries mark themselves with cedar balls hanging over the doors.

Takayama is best known for its festivals, held in spring and autumn, when ornate floats with mechanical puppets are pulled through the streets. Hida beef, marbled and tender, is served as steak, on skewers or on a magnolia leaf over a small charcoal burner, and the morning markets by the Miyagawa river sell pickles, apples and handicrafts. The city is a rewarding place for a night, with hot-spring inns and quiet evenings.

The roads from Takayama are among the best in the Japanese Alps. Route 158 leads west toward Shirakawa-go through long tunnels and valleys, and the mountain roads toward Norikura and the Hida high country are twisty and steep, with fine views. The Hida region receives heavy snow, so many high roads close from late autumn until spring, and even in summer fog and showers can arrive suddenly. Autumn colours are marvellous.

You will find fuel in the town, and it is wise to fill up before heading into the valleys, where stations are sparse. Takayama's pace is slow, with plenty of cafes and noodle shops, and a stroll along the river takes you past old bridges and quiet lanes. Tourists crowd the old town in the middle of the day, so go early or late for the best light. After a day of mountain riding, the smell of woodsmoke and miso soup makes it a perfect place to rest.
t.ogimachi village@36.3,136.9:
Ogimachi is the largest village in Shirakawa-go, a deep valley in the mountains of Gifu where the houses wear steep thatched roofs like hands pressed together in prayer. The style is called gassho-zukuri, praying hands, and the angle of about sixty degrees is a response to heavy snow, which can pile up for months. The roofs are made of thatch more than a metre thick, and the villagers once re-thatched them together in a communal effort, a custom still observed.

Many of the houses are large, three or four storeys, and the upper floors were used for raising silkworms, as well as for saltpetre production in the past, which was an industry of the Hida mountains and supplied gunpowder to feudal lords. Families lived together in big households, and the buildings were framed with wooden beams lashed with rope, without nails. UNESCO listed the village together with Gokayama in Toyama in 1995, and some of the houses are now museums, while others remain family homes, shops and inns.

The valley is spectacular in every season. Spring brings water to the rice paddies, and green hills around the houses. Summer is warm and lush, autumn burns red and gold, and in winter the village sits under deep snow, with special evening illuminations on a few weekends that attract large crowds by reservation. Visiting on a weekday in early morning gives you the village almost to yourself, with mist along the river Sho.

For riders, the approach is good, along Route 156 from the south or 158 from Takayama, through tunnels and gorges, and the roads are well surfaced. Parking for motorbikes is available at the edge of the village, and a small fee may be charged. Fuel stations are scarce in the valley, so fill up in Takayama or along the way. A bowl of soba or a dish of local river fish is a pleasant lunch. Please remember that people live and work here, so be quiet, and do not wander into private houses or fields.
t.nagano@36.7,138.2:
Nagano is a city organised around a temple. Zenko-ji, which is over thirteen centuries old by tradition, has drawn pilgrims for so long that the city grew up on its approach, and the main avenue, lined with shops selling sweets, incense and crafts, leads gently uphill to the great wooden hall. The temple belongs to no single Buddhist sect, and its principal image, a hidden Buddha said to have come from Korea in the sixth or seventh century, is never shown to the public. A copy is displayed every few years.

In a dark corridor beneath the main altar, visitors can walk in total blackness and feel along the wall for a key to paradise, a small ritual that people enjoy. Nagano hosted the Winter Olympics in 1998, and the surrounding mountains hold ski resorts, hot springs and the famous Jigokudani snow monkeys, who bathe in a steaming pool in winter. The region is known as Shinshu, and its apples, soba noodles and pickled vegetables, oyaki dumplings and sake are well loved.

The riding around Nagano is superb. To the east, the road toward Utsukushigahara and the Venus Line climbs through highland meadows with wide views, and to the north, the roads toward Togakushi pass cedar forests and shrines. The mountain roads close for winter, typically from about December until April, and mornings in spring can be icy, so check the conditions before setting out. Autumn colours around late October are splendid.

Nagano city is large enough to offer fuel and food in plenty, and it makes a convenient base. Soba from Togakushi is a good lunch, served cold on bamboo trays. Parking for bikes is available near the temple, though weekends and festivals are crowded. Get up early to hear the monks chant at the morning service, a moving experience even for visitors who know little about Buddhism. The mountain air is cool and fresh.
t.kanazawa@36.6,136.6:
Kanazawa is one of the few Japanese cities of its size to have come through the Second World War untouched, and the old quarters show it. It sits on the Sea of Japan coast, with the Sai and Asano rivers running through it, and was for nearly three hundred years the seat of the Maeda family, the richest feudal lords in Japan after the shogun, who ruled the Kaga domain and spent their wealth on arts and crafts. That legacy survives in gold leaf, silk dyeing, lacquer and ceramics, and in a taste for refined things.

The best known sight is Kenrokuen, a garden begun in the seventeenth century and counted among the three great gardens of Japan. Its ponds, bridges, pines supported by ropes in winter and a famous two-legged stone lantern make it lovely in every season, especially under snow. Kanazawa Castle stands next door. In the Higashi Chaya district, wooden teahouses with lattice fronts still host geisha performances, and shops sell gold leaf in almost everything, including ice cream. The fish market at Omicho is the place to try the local crab and sushi.

North of the city lies the Noto Peninsula, which juts into the Sea of Japan, with rocky coasts, rice terraces, fishing villages and quiet roads. The Noto Satoyama Kaido and the coast roads offer long, easy riding with sea views. In January 2024, a powerful earthquake badly damaged parts of the peninsula, with road collapses and damage to towns, so riders should check the current state of the roads and open sections before setting out, since repairs have been ongoing. At Chirihama, a long beach of firm sand is open to vehicles, a rarity in Japan.

Kanazawa has fuel and food at every turn, with Nonoichi and Matto adding more. Winters are grey and snowy, and the best seasons are spring and autumn. Expect tolls on the expressways.
t.boso@35.2,139.7:
The Tokyo Bay ferry is the secret of this point. It carries motorcycles, and it is the pleasant way to link the two peninsulas, since the alternative is a long drive around the head of the bay or the tunnel and bridge of the Aqua-Line.

Riding the ferry is a break in the middle of the day. The boat is large and slow, with a deck where you can stand and watch the container ships, the fishing boats and the hills of both shores. On a clear day, Mount Fuji is visible to the west, and the sea air is fresh. The road at each end is typical of the Japanese coast, with narrow lanes, tunnels and bends, and a surface that is well kept but with steep gradients. Check the timetable before you go, as sailings can be cancelled in bad weather, and queue early on weekends.

The bay has strategic importance. Commodore Perry's black ships entered it in 1853 to demand that Japan open to trade, and the Uraga channel here was the gateway to Edo. Yokosuka, to the north, is still home to a major naval base, both American and Japanese, and its harbour has historic warships on display. On the Kanaya side, Nokogiri-yama, the Saw Mountain, a ridge of jagged stone, has a quarry, a huge carved Buddha and a lookout called Jigoku Nozoki, or Hell Peek, that overhangs a cliff.

Fuel and food are easy at both ends. Yokosuka has big stations, and the Kanaya port has fish restaurants and a small market, where the local catch, including horse mackerel, is served fried or as sashimi. Convenience stores can supply snacks.

Stand on the deck and watch the shore slide by. It is a calm interlude between two roads.
t.mount haruna@35.5,139.4:
Minamirinkan, in Yamato city, is a little to the south, and the road that connects them is Route 16, the great ring road around Tokyo, which carries enormous traffic.

The ride that ends here began in the mountains of Gunma, around Mount Haruna and Ikaho, so the last section is an urban one. The roads are busy, with lights and lanes, and the surface is good but dull. Do not expect to be alone: bikers of every kind use this ring road, and on a dry Sunday morning you will see groups of riders on big tourers and small commuters sharing the same lanes. Route 16 has a reputation in Japan for car culture and late-night drivers, and its big roadside stores, restaurants and car dealerships are all around. Keep your distance and watch for lane changes. A weekday evening is the busiest, so a weekend morning is better.

Despite the sprawl, the area has green pockets. The Tama Hills are crossed by narrow lanes between woods and bamboo, and a few old farmhouses and small shrines survive. Machida has a long history as a market town, and its main street, near the station, has a lively, crowded character. The nearby Tsurukawa Kaido, an old road, was once used to carry silk and other goods to the port of Yokohama.

Fuel is no trouble. Stations are frequent along Route 16, and family restaurants, ramen shops and convenience stores are everywhere. A bowl of ramen and a plate of gyoza at a roadside restaurant is the usual rider's meal. The Odakyu and JR lines run through Machida, which makes the final leg home easy.

Take your time on the last stretch. The mountains are far behind, but the evening light on the hills can still be pleasant.
t.hanno@35.9,139.3:
Hanno is where Saitama's flat suburbs run out and the green ridges begin, at about 100 metres above the sea, on the Iruma river at the mouth of the valley that leads up toward Okutama and Chichibu. It is a city of about eighty-six thousand people, so a fuel stop is easy, and it has a long history as a timber town. For centuries the cedar and cypress felled in the mountains upstream were floated or hauled down here to supply the building boom of Edo, and the old lumber trade gave the place much of its wealth.

Today Hanno is better known for something gentler. Moomin Valley Park, beside Lake Miyazawa, is a Finnish-inspired village with a theme dedicated to the beloved trolls of Tove Jansson, and it is a favourite family outing. The lake itself is a quiet reservoir surrounded by woods, with a path around its shore, and it is often the starting point for walking and cycling trips into the hills. Cherry blossom in early April and the autumn colours bring crowds.

The Hanno riding starts the moment you leave the town. Routes 299 and 70 climb into the valley through cedar forest and small hamlets, with tight bends, shade and occasional mossy patches, and it is known among riders as the gateway to the best roads west of Tokyo. The Shomaru and Tokigawa areas have cheerful, winding roads, and the Chichibu basin lies just over the hills. At weekends, the road is thick with bikes and cars, so a weekday or a very early start is a good idea.

Convenience stores and petrol stations are plentiful in town, but they become sparse as you climb, and some mountain stations close early in the evening, so fill up before you head into the hills. Many riders gather at a few popular stops near the foothills, particularly on Sunday mornings, and the atmosphere can be quite sociable.

Check your tyre pressures, warm up the engine gently and enjoy the long, shaded climb. After the grey suburbs, the green of the mountains feels like a reward.
t.ashinoko skyline@36.0,139.4:
The Kawagoe streets, with their dark warehouses of tiled roofs, a bell tower called Toki no Kane and rows of sweet shops selling sweet potato treats, are the best place to feel the atmosphere of old Tokyo, and it is worth the detour on any ride that ends in this area.

The ride that ended here began far to the west, on the Ashinoko skyline road, so this is the plains end. The roads are flat and fast, running between fields of vegetables, tea bushes and rice, with a surface that is generally good and bends that are slight. The Iruma and Koma rivers cross the area, and the Chichibu mountains stand on the horizon, white with snow in winter. Traffic is moderate, though heavy around Kawagoe, and the best time to ride is early in the day. Bamboo groves and low shrines break up the farmland, and in early summer the fields glow green with young tea and vegetables.

The area is known for its sweet potato, and the Kawagoe variety is among the best in Japan, with a creamy, sweet flesh. Further west, near Hidaka, the Kinchakuda park has a vast field of red spider lilies that bloom in September, a remarkable sight that draws large crowds. The Koma district, once settled by immigrants from the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo, has a shrine that preserves the memory.

Fuel is easy, since Sakado and Kawagoe have stations and supermarkets, and the area has many small restaurants. Sweet potato ice cream, roasted sweet potatoes and sweet potato beer are sold in Kawagoe, and a bowl of udon is a local specialty. The Tobu Tojo line runs from Sakado to Ikebukuro in about fifty minutes.

Look at the horizon in the evening. The line of the Chichibu mountains is a reminder of the road you have ridden.
t.tomiura to@35.3,139.9:
Futtsu, with its long cape reaching towards the Miura peninsula, is a few kilometres to the south. The coast here is industrial, with the huge Nippon Steel plant at Kimitsu, but the hills behind are green, wooded and full of small valleys.

This is the midpoint of the Tomiura and Nojimazaki loop, and it is the part that pulls you into the countryside. The roads climb from the coast into the Bōsō hills, with narrow lanes, tunnels and bends through bamboo and cedar woods. The surface is mostly good, though some of the smaller roads have patches of loose gravel and fallen leaves. Traffic is light, apart from weekends, and the roads around Kururi, a small castle town inland, are some of the best in the region. Summer is hot and humid, and typhoons can bring heavy rain in September, so the clearest and best riding comes in November and spring.

The Bōsō hills are low, not much over three hundred metres, but they have a quiet, old feel. Nokogiri-yama, near Futtsu, is a ridge of jagged stone that was quarried for centuries, with a giant Buddha carved into the cliff in the eighteenth century and a viewing platform that juts out over a drop. Kururi has a small castle ruin and a lake, and in spring cherry and plum blossoms make the area colourful.

Fuel is easy in Kimitsu, a city of ninety thousand, with stations on the main road and supermarkets and restaurants. The Aqua-Line expressway, with its rest area in the middle of the bay, the Umihotaru, is not far, and it has a food court with views over the water. Local fish and seaweed are served in the small restaurants of the coast.

Take a moment at the viewpoint on Nokogiri-yama if you can. On a clear day the bay, the ships and Mount Fuji make a sweeping panorama.
t.gunma@35.6,139.4:
Zama is home to an American army base, Camp Zama, which has been there since the 1940s and is the headquarters of the US Army in Japan. The Sagami river runs a few kilometres to the west, and Mount Oyama, a sacred peak, rises on the horizon on a clear day.

For a ride on three mountains in Gunma, this is the long way home. The roads are busy and wide, with bus lanes and lights, but there are also narrow lanes through the hills, with bends and short climbs. The surface is good, with few potholes, and traffic moves steadily. In summer, the Zama Sunflower Festival fills the fields along the river with huge yellow flowers, and in autumn, the area is quiet and clear. Keep to the limits, as police and cameras are frequent.

The Tama Hills have been farmed for centuries, with chestnuts, persimmons and vegetables as the main crops, and small shrines and Buddhist halls stand among the trees. Sagamihara, the big city to the west, was an army town before the war, and the old military roads and tunnels are still used. Machida, to the east, is a hub for the whole area, with a lively market and department stores.

Fuel and food are no problem, with stations on every main road and a large variety of eating places. The Odakyu and Sotetsu lines connect the area to Shinjuku and Yokohama, and the expressway is only a few minutes away. A bowl of ramen at a roadside shop is a rider's reward, and the bakeries near the stations are good.

Stop where the hills open a view of Mount Fuji, which is visible on winter days. The snow cone above the haze is a good end to the day.
t.venus line@35.8,139.3:
Ōme is a town of old movie billboards. Along its main street, hand-painted signs advertise classic films from the 1950s and 1960s, part of an effort to revive the town as a retro attraction, and the old shops and cafes are full of Showa-era atmosphere.

This is the gateway to the hills, and the road west from Ōme, Route 411, follows the river up to Okutama Lake. The Venus Line, as the ride is called, climbs gently, with bends and tunnels, and the surface is good. The lower part of the valley is busy, with cars and cyclists on sunny weekends, but the upper reaches are quiet and green. The Mitake gorge, with its rocky cliffs and rafting spots, is a short ride away, and the Mitake shrine on its mountain draws walkers. Autumn leaves, from late October, are spectacular.

Hannō, across the prefecture border in Saitama, has a surprising claim. The Moomin Valley Park and Metsä Village, near Lake Miyazawa, are modelled on the stories of Tove Jansson, and the area has Nordic-style buildings and forest walks. The foothills here are covered in cedar and cypress plantations, and tea fields spread across the lower slopes. The Ōme Marathon, a thirty-kilometre race held each February, is one of the oldest in Japan.

Fuel is available in Ōme, a city of nearly a hundred and fifty thousand, with stations on the main road, and it is wise to fill up before heading into the hills. The old town has soba and udon restaurants, and the local sake breweries, like the one at Sawanoi in the Mitake gorge, offer tastings. A small bakery by the station sells good bread.

Spend a few minutes reading the film posters. They are a charming reminder of a Japan that has largely vanished.
t.izu skyline@35.8,139.9:
Sōka is famous for its rice crackers. The senbei makers of the city, just north of Tokyo, have produced the crisp, soy-flavoured snacks for generations, and the shops by the station sell them fresh, grilled over charcoal.

For a ride on the Izu skyline and the Jōgasaki coast, this is a plain finish. The roads are straight and busy, with lights and lanes, and the surface is good. The area is crossed by expressways and railway lines, and the landscape is low, with the horizon marked only by apartment blocks. But there is a quiet charm in the canals and fields that survive between the housing estates, and the roads along the river banks are pleasant at dusk.

Sōka has a famous avenue. Matsubara, a long walk beside the old Nikkō highway, is lined with pine trees, and it was a stage on the road that the poet Bashō walked at the start of his great journey to the north in 1689. It is a gentle, shaded route, now a park, with a bridge and tea houses. Yashio, to the south, is a newer town, built mostly in the second half of the twentieth century to house commuters, and it has a large park with a lake.

Fuel is easy, with stations along the main roads and supermarkets close by. The restaurants of Sōka are modest, and the senbei shops are the most interesting stop. A tea house on the Matsubara avenue serves green tea and sweets in the traditional way. The Tobu Skytree line runs from Sōka to central Tokyo, and the stations are modern.

Walk the pine avenue if you have time. The shade and the stones underfoot are a reminder of how old this road is.
t.irohazaka hairpins@36.7,139.5:
The Irohazaka is the most famous road in Nikko, and one of the best known in Japan. It climbs from the town at about 640 metres to Lake Chuzenji at roughly 1,270 metres, in a series of forty-eight hairpin bends, each marked with a sign bearing one of the characters of the old Japanese alphabet, called iroha, which has forty-eight letters. The road is split into two one-way sections, with the original, built in the 1950s, carrying traffic down and a second, with twenty-eight bends, carrying traffic up, so you never meet oncoming vehicles on the corners.

The hairpins are tight, but the surface is good and the camber is generous, which makes the climb a joy on a bike. Rhythm matters, because the bends come fast, and the gradient requires you to use engine braking on the descent. Wet leaves and fog can make things slippery, and you should watch for monkeys, Japanese macaques, which sit by the road and sometimes wander into the lanes. Do not feed them, because they can be aggressive.

The best time to come is in October and early November, when the maples and birches turn red and gold, and the whole mountainside seems to be on fire. It is also the busiest, and traffic can crawl for hours, with queues stretching back toward town, so start at dawn. In winter, snow and ice often close the road to vehicles without chains, so check before travelling.

At the top, the Kegon Falls drop nearly a hundred metres into a gorge, one of Japan's three great waterfalls, and an elevator takes you down to a viewing platform at its base. There is also a ropeway at Akechidaira, which gives a panoramic view of the hairpins, the lake and the mountains.

Nikko itself has about sixteen thousand people, with fuel and plenty of food.
t.lake chuzenji@36.7,139.5:
Lake Chuzenji lies at about 1,270 metres in the mountains above Nikko, and it was made by a volcano. Some twenty thousand years ago, Mount Nantai, a steep cone that now rises to nearly 2,500 metres on the north shore, erupted and its lava dammed the Daiya River, forming this long, clear, deep lake. The water is cold, even in summer, and it is stocked with trout and salmon, and the lake is surrounded by forest. Seen at dawn, with mist rising from the surface, it is a calm and lovely sight.

In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, foreign diplomats posted to Tokyo escaped the summer heat by building holiday villas on the shore, and two of them, the former British and Italian embassy villas, have been restored and can be visited. The sailing and rowing boats on the lake, and the old wooden hotels, recall those times. Utagahama, on the eastern shore, is a pleasant beach for a stroll, though the water is chilly for swimming, so the label's swim is optimistic unless you are brave.

Nikko has its great shrines and temples, particularly the Toshogu, the elaborate mausoleum of the first Tokugawa shogun, set among old cedars. The plateau of Senjogahara, to the north-west, is a wide marsh with walking paths and clear views of the surrounding mountains, and is worth exploring if you have time. The Kegon Falls drain the lake dramatically at its eastern end.

The ride up is by the Irohazaka hairpins, and the road along the shore is easy and scenic, with views over the water and the mountains. In autumn, traffic is heavy, with long queues, so plan for a very early start. Summer is cooler than the lowlands, and winter brings snow and ice, which can close the roads.

As a finishing point it is hard to beat: a mountain lake, a hot meal and a bath.
t.wajima@37.4,136.9:
Wajima sits on the northern coast of the Noto Peninsula, in Ishikawa prefecture, a long finger of land pushing out into the Sea of Japan, and for a long time it was best known for two things: lacquerware and its morning market. Wajima-nuri lacquer, made with layers of lacquer over a base mixed with local diatomaceous earth, is among the finest in Japan, with a deep gloss that lasts for generations. The market, held every morning along a street near the harbour, sold fish, vegetables and crafts, with elderly women calling out to passers-by.

On New Year's Day 2024, a powerful earthquake struck the Noto Peninsula, causing major damage in Wajima, including a large fire that destroyed much of the market district, and the effects were felt throughout the region. Recovery has been slow, and rebuilding is continuing. Roads that were damaged have been reopened in stages, but you should check the current state of the road and local conditions before travelling, and bear in mind that some businesses are still closed. Visitors should be respectful, and spending money in local shops and restaurants is a useful way to help.

Close by, the Senmaida at Shiroyone, a hillside of about a thousand tiny terraced rice paddies falling toward the sea, is one of the most photographed sights on the peninsula, a patchwork of green in summer and gold in autumn. The coastal road itself, along the rocky shore, was among the best in Japan for riding, with long views and smooth curves, and the sunset over the sea is often superb.

Wajima is a long way from the nearest big city, Nanao, some thirty-eight kilometres to the south, so fuel is something to plan for. Wajima has its own petrol stations, but it is wise to arrive with a full tank, and to check opening hours. Seafood in the area, particularly crab in winter, is renowned.

Winters are cold and snowy, with strong winds off the sea, and summers are warm and humid. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with comfortable temperatures and clear air. It is a place that rewards slow travel and a patient, respectful approach.
t.nagatoro river@36.1,139.1:
Nagatoro is a small town on the Arakawa River, at the point where the water leaves the Chichibu mountains and cuts through a long stretch of flat, banded rock. The riverbed here is made of crystalline schist, a pale green stone laid down in broad stepped terraces, known as Iwadatami, or rock tatami, because it looks like a floor of giant mats. Geologists have studied the formation for well over a century, and it is among the most celebrated rock exposures in Japan.

The best way to see it is by water. Open wooden boats, steered by boatmen with long poles, carry passengers through the rapids in a trip that lasts about half an hour, and it is a fun and slightly wet experience in summer. In winter the boats run with covers and heaters. A footbridge and a path along the bank give good views, and the autumn colours of the surrounding hills are lovely. The town has a number of shops selling shaved ice, noodles and souvenirs, and the main street has an old-fashioned atmosphere.

At about 140 metres above sea level, the town sits in a gentle valley, and the roads leading out of it climb into the hills in all directions. They are mostly narrow and winding, with some tight bends and occasional rough patches, and they are popular with riders on weekends. Traffic can build up in the town at peak times, especially on sunny Sundays, so early morning is the best time. Near the river you will find parking for motorcycles at several spots.

The nearest large town is Yorii, about seven kilometres away, with petrol and supermarkets, and there are petrol stations in Nagatoro itself. A bowl of soba or a plate of the local miso potato dumplings makes an easy lunch. Shaved ice with syrup, made from natural ice, is also a local speciality in summer.

Walk down to the rocks, take off your gloves and watch the water. It is a lovely, quiet place to stop.
t.d707 north junction@-26.0,16.0:
This is a point on the map rather than a town, in the dry country of southern Namibia where the Tiras Mountains lift out of the Namib's gravel plains. There is no village here, no shade and nothing with a name beyond the number of the road, and nobody lives close enough to appear on a list of nearby places. That is exactly the point. The D707 is a gravel road that runs through some of the emptiest and most beautiful terrain in the country, and the start of it feels like the moment the real trip begins.

The road is a graded gravel track, usually in decent condition but with patches of corrugation, soft sand in the dry riverbeds and the occasional loose stretch after rain. Drop your tyre pressures a little if you are on a loaded adventure bike, and keep your speed to something you can stop from. Flash floods are rare but can cut the crossings. The landscape is huge: red dunes in the distance, granite hills, camelthorn trees and wide yellow grass after rain, with mountain ranges folding away on the horizon. You will probably see oryx, springbok and ostriches, and in the evening the light on the rocks turns copper and then pink.

Carry extra fuel and water, fill up at the last real town before you turn on to it, and tell someone where you are headed. Other travellers are few, so if something goes wrong you may wait a long time. Make sure the bike is ready, with a spare tube, a pump and tools, because the nearest mechanic is a very long way away.

The best months are the cool, dry ones from May to September, when days are warm and nights are cold enough to see your breath. Summers are very hot and afternoon temperatures climb fast. Start early, stop for lunch under a tree, and let the quiet work on you, because few places offer this much open space.
t.namtib reserve@-25.8,16.2:
The Namtib Biosphere Reserve lies in the southern Tiras Mountains of Namibia, on private farmland that has been set aside as a reserve for wildlife and desert landscape. There is no town nearby and no population to list, only red sand, rocky slopes and wide grass plains that run up against the mountains, with the Namib Desert lying to the west. The nearest place with real supplies is a long way off, which gives you an idea of the scale.

The road here is the D707, a gravel route that winds between hills and across dry riverbeds. The surface is graded, so most bikes manage it with care, but corrugations shake everything loose, so check your luggage straps at every stop. In the wet season short storms can leave water across the road, and sand gathers in the lowest points. Between those obstacles you get the best of the ride, with mountain walls on one side, plains on the other and views that stretch to the horizon. Speed is the enemy, because animals and sudden bends appear without warning.

The landscape is the real subject. The Tiras Mountains are ancient, made of folded rock that has weathered into jagged ridges and boulder slopes, and the plains below hold quiver trees in places and low scrub that turns green with rain. Look for oryx, springbok and the occasional mountain zebra, and birds of prey riding thermals. At night the sky is among the darkest on the continent, and the stars are astonishing, so if you can sleep in a lodge or camp nearby, you will remember it for years.

Fuel is not available here, so carry what you need, and bring water, since none is guaranteed. Tell your hosts when you expect to arrive, because a breakdown out here can take hours to solve. The cool season from May to September is the most comfortable, with warm days and clear nights. In summer the heat is fierce, so ride in the early morning and rest in the afternoon.
t.czestochowa@50.8,19.1:
For Poles, Częstochowa means one thing, the Jasna Góra monastery, and about a quarter of a million people live around it in a city that exists largely to serve that fact. The monastery stands on a limestone ridge, a fortified complex of walls, bastions and a tall baroque tower, and within it hangs the icon of the Black Madonna, a dark painted image of the Virgin and Child, with two scars across her cheek. Several million pilgrims arrive every year, many on foot, in groups that walk for days from every corner of the country.

The monastery was founded by Paulite monks in 1382, and the icon's history is wrapped in legend. In 1655, during the Swedish invasion known as the Deluge, a small garrison here held out against a much larger army, and the defence became a turning point in national morale, the proof, for Poles, of divine protection. Pope John Paul II visited several times, and the place became a symbol of resistance during the communist years. The treasury and military museum, with votive offerings from soldiers and pilgrims, are worth a visit, and the long avenue leading up to the monastery is always busy.

For a rider the real draw lies in the surroundings. The Kraków-Częstochowa Upland, also known as the Jura, is a limestone country of white cliffs, caves and the ruins of small medieval castles, the Eagles' Nests, built in the fourteenth century by King Casimir the Great to guard the border. The route follows lanes through forests and farmland, with gentle bends, short climbs and views of pale rock towers rising above the trees. Roads are usually good, though sometimes narrow, and traffic is heavy in the city and around holidays.

Services in Częstochowa are comprehensive, with stations, workshops, supermarkets and plenty of cafes serving soup, dumplings and cake.

If you can, arrive in the late afternoon, when the crowds are thinner and the sun lights the tower. Walk along the ramparts, and be respectful, since this is a living place of worship and not only a monument.
t.medieval town of torun@53.0,18.6:
Toruń is a Gothic brick town that survived the twentieth century almost untouched, which is rare for Poland, and that makes it the best place in the country to see what a medieval trading city looked like. The Teutonic Knights founded it in 1231 on the Vistula, and it grew rich as a member of the Hanseatic League, with merchants shipping grain, timber and goods down the river towards the Baltic. UNESCO listed the old town in 1997, and the red-brick churches, granaries, town hall and city walls are still there.

The most famous son is Nicolaus Copernicus, born here in 1473, the astronomer who argued that the Earth goes around the sun. His house, a narrow Gothic building on a cobbled street, is now a museum, and a statue of him sits in the market square. The town hall, a massive Gothic building with a tall tower, anchors the square, and the Leaning Tower, a medieval defence tower that tilts alarmingly, is a popular landmark. Churches such as St John's, with its enormous bell, are worth entering for their painted vaults.

Toruń is also the capital of gingerbread. The tradition goes back to the Middle Ages, when the local honey and imported spices made it possible, and the pierniki are sold in shops across the old town, in shapes from hearts to little Copernicus figures. Some are hard as a brick, and some soft and rich. A small museum shows how they are made, and you can bake your own.

For riding, the city is an easy stop on the long run from Gdańsk to the south. The roads here are flat and fast, through farmland and forest, with long, straight stretches and not much else. The surface is generally good, but trucks are heavy on the main roads and the cobbled streets of the old town are slippery when wet. Parking for motorbikes is possible just outside the walls, and the old town is best seen on foot. A bridge across the Vistula offers a fine view of the skyline, especially in the evening.

Fuel and services are plentiful in a city of around two hundred thousand, and Wielka Nieszawka, just downriver, is a quieter place for a break. Eat a bowl of soup and buy a bag of gingerbread, then ride on.

Stay for the golden hour on the river bank, when the walls glow.
t.lutheran church of peace under the invoc:
Jawor's Church of Peace is a miracle built out of necessity. After the Thirty Years' War, the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 left Silesia under the Catholic Habsburgs, who allowed their Protestant subjects to build only three churches, under strict conditions. They had to be outside the town walls, built of perishable materials, with no tower, no bells and no brick or stone, and they had to be finished within a year. The Lutherans of Jawor responded by building a church of timber, clay and straw, with a roof of thatch, beginning in 1654, and completing it in 1655.

The result is astonishing. It is one of the largest timber-framed churches in Europe, with room for several thousand worshippers on benches and in galleries, all inside a modest-looking building that hides its immense interior behind plain walls. The inside is richly painted, with biblical scenes and decorated galleries piled one above the other, in a way that lifts the spirit and makes you wonder how such a thing was achieved. Because the wood and clay are perishable, the church has required constant care, and UNESCO listed it in 2001, along with the Church of Peace in Świdnica.

The setting is quiet. Jawor, a small town of about twenty-four thousand people, lies in Lower Silesia, in a gently rolling farmland landscape with the Sudetes visible on the horizon. The old town has a market square and a Gothic church, and the area was once part of the Piast duchy of Jawor. The ride's second stop, the Centennial Hall in Wrocław, is a very different building, a vast reinforced-concrete dome designed by Max Berg and completed in 1913, which UNESCO listed in 2006.

Riding here is easy, over flat or lightly rolling roads through fields of wheat, rapeseed and sugar beet, with many small villages and orchards. The surface is good in general, but the local roads can be narrow and patched. Traffic is light, except on the main roads, which carry heavy trucks. In summer, the heat can be fierce, and in winter the roads can ice up.

Fuel and food are no problem in Jawor, with stations on the main roads and cafes near the market square. Fill up there before heading to Wrocław.

Visit the church with an hour to spare, and remember that it is a working place of worship. Silence is the right response.
t.medora@46.9,-103.5:
Medora is a western town that exists partly as a theatre set and partly as a gateway, and both roles work. It lies on the edge of the North Dakota Badlands, beside the Little Missouri River, and it was founded in the 1880s by the Marquis de Morès, a French aristocrat who planned a meatpacking empire and named the town for his wife, Medora. The scheme failed within a few years, but a young Theodore Roosevelt arrived about the same time, hunting bison and later ranching nearby, and he later said that his time in the Dakotas shaped everything that followed. Today the main street has boardwalks, saloons and a summer musical staged in an amphitheatre.

The South Unit of Theodore Roosevelt National Park starts at the edge of town, with a scenic loop of about thirty-six miles. It is a gentle, well-paved road that rolls over buttes and down into river bottoms, with banded layers of clay, sandstone and coal in orange, grey and pink. Bison walk along and across the road, prairie dogs pop out of burrows, and wild horses graze on the hillsides. Speed limits are low for good reason, because a bison on the tarmac is a roadblock, and you give it space and time. Pronghorn and mule deer are common, and elk are sometimes seen.

Evening is the best time for the loop, when long light turns the badlands gold and the heat fades. In the wind, sagebrush and juniper scent the air. Thunderstorms can roll across the prairie in summer afternoons, so keep an eye on the sky, and in winter the roads can be icy or closed. A park entry fee applies, and the visitor centre in Medora has maps and information about road conditions.

Practical details matter in this empty country. Medora has fuel, food and places to stay, but the next towns, Belfield and Beach, are twenty-five to thirty-five miles away, and Dickinson is the nearest larger place. Fill the tank before you head out, and bring water on hot days. Late spring and early autumn are the most comfortable seasons, with fewer people than in July and August.
t.nanao@37.1,137.0:
Nanao sits on the sheltered inner coast of the Noto Peninsula, on a bay of the same name, where the Sea of Japan is calmer than on the exposed western shore. It was once the capital of the old Noto province, and a castle of the Hatakeyama family stood on the hills above the town, until it fell to the warlord Uesugi Kenshin in 1577. The castle is now a ruin of stone walls and a pleasant park. The town is a working port, with a fish market and an old street of merchants' houses.

Nanao has a famous festival. The Seihaku-sai in May features enormous wooden floats called Dekayama, up to twelve meters tall, painted in bright colors and pulled through the streets by crowds, a spectacle that is among the festivals inscribed by UNESCO in 2016. Nearby Wakura Onsen is one of Japan's famous hot-spring resorts, with seaside baths, and the bay is known for oysters and sweet shrimp. Noto's cuisine, with its fresh seafood and sake, is well regarded across the country.

The peninsula suffered badly in the earthquake on New Year's Day 2024, which caused deep damage in the north and west, and some roads and communities were hit hard. Recovery has been under way for some time, but conditions along parts of the coast may still be uneven, so check road status before you ride. Where the roads are open, the coastal route around the peninsula is a joy: it follows the shoreline through fishing villages, past rice terraces, rocky headlands and long beaches, with sea views and gentle curves. Surfaces are generally good.

Nanao has fuel, supermarkets, convenience stores and restaurants, and it is the largest town on the peninsula's east side, so it is a good place to stock up. The best months are May, with fresh green and the festival, and October, when the air is crisp and the sea glitters. Summer is hot and humid, and winter brings snow and strong winds off the Sea of Japan, which can close the roads. The light on the water in the evening, with fishing boats going out, is memorable.
t.gdansk@54.4,18.6:
Gdańsk is a port that has been rich, ruined and rebuilt more than once, and the city wears all three eras at once. The old Hanseatic merchants of the Middle Ages grew fat on grain, timber and amber, and their tall, narrow merchant houses still line the Long Market, where the Neptune fountain gazes at the Gothic town hall. Almost everything in the old centre was flattened in 1945 and rebuilt with such care, from old paintings and plans, that the facades look centuries old. Along the Motława river the great wooden medieval crane still straddles the quay.

The city is also a place where modern history started. On 1 September 1939 the first shots of the Second World War were fired at Westerplatte, on the harbour mouth. Four decades later the Lenin Shipyard became the birthplace of Solidarity, the independent trade union led by Lech Wałęsa, and the strikes of August 1980 set in motion the peaceful unravelling of the Eastern Bloc. A museum in the old shipyard halls tells that story with unusual power.

For a rider the city itself is something to be ridden through carefully, with trams, cobbles on the old lanes and heavy traffic on the ring roads. The pleasure lies beyond. North of Gdańsk, the road follows the coast through Sopot and Gdynia, then out along the thin spit of the Hel Peninsula, with the Baltic on one side and the Bay of Puck on the other. It is flat and often windy, with sand, pines and wide skies. South-west, the Kashubian Lakes country rises into forested hills with winding lanes and small villages, a good place to find twisty roads in a region that is otherwise level.

Fuel is plentiful everywhere around the Tricity. Local food leans on fish, with smoked herring and fresh cod, and amber jewellery appears in every stall on Mariacka street. Come from May to September, but know that July weekends on the coast are packed and traffic crawls.
t.kurumayama@36.1,138.2:
Kurumayama is a smooth, grassy mountain on the Kirigamine plateau in central Nagano, at nearly two thousand metres, and it stands above one of the loveliest high-altitude roads in Japan. The plateau is a broad volcanic upland, a pale green tilted table of grass and wildflowers lifted high above the lakes and valleys, and the road that crosses it, known as the Venus Line, was built to show it off. On a clear day the view from the top is huge: the Northern Alps to the west, the Yatsugatake range to the south, and, if you are lucky, the distant cone of Mount Fuji.

The mountain is part of a high plateau whose name, Kirigamine, means the peak of mist, and the name is earned. Fog rolls across the grass with little warning and wipes out the view, then lifts and reveals the lot. The meadows here are famous for their flowers in summer, and the grazing cattle, the open skies and the cool air make a fine contrast to the heat of the lowlands. In winter the hills are covered in snow, and sections of the road close from late autumn through spring, so check before you set out.

For a rider, the Venus Line is a gem. It is a smooth, well-kept scenic road with wide, flowing bends, long straights and sweeping views over the plateau, and almost no commercial traffic. Speed limits are low and strictly watched, as they are across Japan, but the real pleasure here is the pace: gliding across open grassland at an easy speed with the mountains in the background. It is popular with riders at weekends and in autumn, and there are often groups of motorcyclists stopping at the roadside car parks. Early mornings and weekdays are quieter.

The area has a small number of mountain restaurants and shops near the viewpoints, and the local food is simple: soba noodles, a speciality of Nagano, served hot or cold, with mountain vegetables and tempura. Japanese stations are generally full service, and the attendants will guide you to the pump.

Bring a light jacket even in summer, since the air at this height can be cold when the sun goes in. The best seasons are early summer, for the flowers, and October, when the grass turns to gold and the larches on the lower slopes are bright yellow.
t.kirigamine@36.1,138.2:
Kirigamine is a highland plateau in central Nagano, and the Venus Line passes across it like a ribbon laid over a green blanket. The name means the peak of mist, and in the summer months, when warm air from the valleys meets the cool air above, the fog moves across the grass in slow rolling banks. The plateau is a volcanic shelf at roughly fifteen to nineteen hundred metres, with gentle slopes, a few small peaks and wide open spaces where cattle graze. It is a gentle contrast to the sharp Alps that rise on the horizon.

The views are the main attraction, and they are well earned. To the west lie the Northern Alps and the Chūō range, to the south the long volcanic ridge of the Yatsugatake, and to the north the broad shoulder of the Asama volcano. Far below, Lake Suwa glints in its basin. The city of Suwa, on the lakeshore, is famous for its hot springs and for the Suwa shrines, some of the oldest in Japan, which hold a remarkable festival every six years, the Onbashira, when huge tree trunks are hauled down the hillside and raised at the shrine corners. It is a spectacular event, and Suwa is worth a stop on a day off.

The riding on the plateau is gentle and enjoyable. The Venus Line runs smoothly across the open grassland, with easy bends and a good surface, and is among the nicest roads in the region for a relaxed ride. There is no heavy traffic, but you will find tourists, cyclists and the occasional tractor, and the speed limits are low. The road is closed for part of the winter, when snow lies deep, and fog can cut visibility to a few metres, so use lights and keep to a sensible pace. Autumn colours here are superb, and the air is crisp and clear.

At various points along the road there are car parks and small restaurants, and some of them sell local products, including dairy goods, apples and soba. For fuel, Suwa, about nine kilometres away, is the nearest sizeable town, and Okaya and Chino have more stations and supermarkets. Fill the tank there, since there is none on the plateau.

If you have time, the hot springs of Kamisuwa and the town's lakeside promenade make a pleasant stop after the climb. Japanese hot springs are a wonderful way to ease a stiff back, and many have public baths for a small fee.
t.utsukushigahara@36.2,138.1:
Utsukushigahara is a high plateau in the Japanese Alps, at about two thousand metres, and the Venus Line is the road that carries riders up to it. The name means Beautiful Highland, and the open grassland on top is used as summer pasture, with cattle grazing among the wildflowers. Matsumoto, about thirteen kilometres away, is the large city below, with a famous black castle and plenty of fuel and food. Up on the plateau there is little more than a couple of rest houses, an open-air museum of sculptures and a few car parks, so supplies belong in your tank before you climb.

The Venus Line is a classic Japanese touring road, with long, smooth, sweeping bends through forest and then open highland, and spectacular views of the Northern Alps on a clear day. The surface is excellent, and the speed limits are low and enforced, so a relaxed pace is best. In the cooler parts, fog can fall quickly, and in autumn the colours are brilliant. The road is closed in winter because of snow, and usually reopens in spring. Weekends see crowds of motorcyclists and cars, and in Japan there is a polite culture of waving to fellow riders.

The nature on the plateau is distinct. Alpine flowers bloom in short bursts in summer, and the grass turns golden in autumn. Skylarks sing over the pasture, and the wind is cool even in July. The Utsukushigahara Open-Air Museum, with sculptures by Japanese and international artists scattered among the meadows, is a quirky and pleasant stop. The air smells of grass and cattle, and the quiet when engines stop is striking.

In Japan, mountain rest houses serve simple but satisfying food: curry rice, soba noodles, and soft-serve ice cream, which in the highlands is often made with local milk. Take cash, as small places may not accept cards. Coming here on a weekday morning in June or late September is ideal, when the traffic is light and the sky is clear. The Venus Line ends at a high point, but the ride down the other side, back toward Matsumoto, is a good reward.
t.daikanzan@35.2,139.0:
Daikanzan is where Hakone's motorcycles go to gather. It is a high lookout on the rim of the great volcanic caldera at about a thousand metres, and in the car park at the summit of the Hakone Turnpike on a fine weekend you will find a few hundred bikes lined up, from vintage Hondas to the latest superbikes, with their riders drinking canned coffee and talking in low voices about the road. The view is the other half of the story. Below the car park, Lake Ashi lies in the old crater, and beyond it, when the sky is clear, Mount Fuji rises in a perfect cone, framed by clouds and mountains.

The road is the Hakone Turnpike, a toll route that climbs from the coast near Yugawara to the caldera rim in a series of bends that has made it one of the most famous riding roads in the Kanto region. It is a smooth, wide road, with long, flowing curves and tight hairpins, and the surface is generally excellent. It has also been a favourite for car enthusiasts and for the Japanese street-racing scene, which means police, speed cameras and noise controls are part of the picture, and you should ride with that in mind. Limits are low and enforced, and weekends see a visible police presence. Ride it with respect, and you will enjoy it far more.

The weather at the top is a lottery. Cloud often covers the mountain when the coast is bright, and Fuji hides for days at a time, usually showing itself in the cold, dry air of winter or early in the morning. A clear dawn in autumn or winter can reward you with a view that justifies the early start. In wet weather the road is slippery and fog reduces visibility. In winter, snow and ice are possible, and the road may be closed or require chains.

At the summit there is a rest area with a restaurant, a shop and a toilet, and vending machines that serve hot and cold drinks, which is the Japanese solution to every problem. The food is simple, noodles and curry rice, and the portions are generous. Odawara, on the coast, has a famous castle and is easy to reach.

If you are lucky enough to catch Fuji at dawn, you will see why so many riders come. Arrive early on a weekday if you want space to park and a view without the crowd.
t.lake ashi@35.2,139.0:
Lake Ashi fills the old crater of Hakone volcano, a long, narrow sheet of blue water ringed by forested mountains and watched over, on clear days, by the cone of Mount Fuji.
