The lake was formed when the volcano collapsed and a river was dammed, a few thousand years ago, and the surrounding hills still steam and bubble with volcanic heat. The whole area is a popular getaway from Tokyo, about a hundred kilometres to the east, and has been since the days of the shoguns, when travellers on the Tokaido road between Edo and Kyoto passed through on foot and horseback.

That history is still visible. At the southern end of the lake, near Moto-Hakone, stands a reconstruction of the Hakone checkpoint, the barrier where travellers had to show their papers during the Edo period, when the government kept tight control of people moving between the capital and the west. Close by, an avenue of ancient cedar trees, planted along the old road in the seventeenth century, still shades a stretch of the original paving stones. On the shore itself is the Hakone Shrine, with a red torii gate standing in the water, which is the most photographed spot on the lake. Sightseeing boats shaped like pirate ships cross the water, which adds a note of the absurd to the scene.

For riders, the lake is a stopping point rather than a destination, since the roads around it are busy and slow, and the crowds in summer and autumn can be heavy. The best riding is on the roads that climb away from it, the Hakone Turnpike and the Skyline, which lead to the viewpoints and the ridges above. The roads around the lake are narrow, winding and often shaded by trees, and the surface is generally good. Early morning is the best time, when mist floats on the water and the crowds are not yet awake. In the cooler months, the air is clear and Fuji is more likely to show herself.

There are restaurants, cafes and souvenir shops around the main landing stages, and the local specialty is black eggs, boiled in the sulphurous waters of Owakudani, the volcanic valley nearby, and said to add years to your life. Fuel is available in Hakone and in the lowland towns of Odawara and Yugawara, so it is best to fill before you climb, and parking can be tight in the high season.

Walk a little way along the shore at the end of the day. The light on the water and the quiet of the cedar trees are the best of Hakone.
t.chirihama nagisa driveway@36.9,136.8:
Most beaches ask you to leave the vehicle in the car park. Chirihama asks you to bring it along. On the west coast of the Noto Peninsula, facing the Sea of Japan, a strip of sand some eight kilometres long is packed so hard by the waves and the fine grain that ordinary cars and buses can drive along it, which is claimed to be unique in Japan. The sand squeaks underfoot, the surf thunders in from the left, and a line of tyre tracks runs away ahead of you along the waterline. It is a surreal experience even if you are only watching it from the dunes.

Whether a motorcycle should go on it is another matter. The packed sand near the water is firm, but higher up it is soft and loose, and a wet day, a rising tide or a single drift of dry grains can put a heavy bike on its side. Many riders keep to the paved road along the dunes and walk down to the beach instead, which is perfectly satisfying. The Noto Peninsula was struck by a severe earthquake in January 2024, and parts of the coast and its roads were damaged and changed, so check current conditions before you plan a route here, and respect any closures.

The coast around Hakui and Chirihama is a gentler, flatter section of the peninsula, with pine windbreaks, rice fields and small fishing villages. The roads are generally smooth and easy, with long straights and gentle bends, and traffic is light outside holidays. In winter the Sea of Japan brings grey skies, snow and hard winds, and the sunsets over the water in clear weather are celebrated. In summer, the beach has swimmers and sandcastles, and the whole place has a relaxed seaside mood.

The town of Hakui, only two kilometres away, has some claim to be the odd one of the peninsula, since it has marketed itself as a town of UFOs, with a small space science museum and a flying saucer motif. The local story involves an old legend and a modern sense of humour. It is a fun place to wander, and a good place to find a meal. Fuel stations, convenience stores and restaurants are easy to find in Hakui, and the seafood of Noto, fresh fish, crab in winter and rich oysters, is worth a try.

The best time is a calm, clear evening, when the sun goes down over the sea and the tracks in the sand turn gold. Bring a windproof layer, since the Japan Sea can be cold even in summer.
t.nikko@36.7,139.7:
Nikkō is the town beneath a World Heritage shrine complex, and for centuries it has been a place of pilgrimage. Toshogu, the great shrine of the first Tokugawa shogun, Ieyasu, stands in a cedar forest, covered in gold leaf and intricate carvings, including the famous sleeping cat and the three wise monkeys. The Rinnoji temple and Futarasan shrine complete the group, and together with the nearby red Shinkyo bridge they draw visitors from across Japan and abroad. Nikkō has fewer than sixteen thousand people, while Imaichi, only a short way down the valley, is larger and has more fuel and shops.

The saying goes, Never say magnificent until you have seen Nikkō, and it is a fair summary of the effect the place has. The shrines were built in the seventeenth century and are marvels of woodwork, lacquer and painted detail. The town lies at the foot of the mountains, with the Daiya river flowing through, and the forests around are thick with cedar and beech.

For riders, Nikkō is the start of the Irohazaka roads, two one-way winding routes that climb about 500 metres to Lake Chuzenji with a total of 48 hairpin bends, each marked with a letter of the old Japanese alphabet, the iroha. The roads were built in the 1950s, and the upward and downward routes are separate, so you climb one and descend the other. The tarmac is smooth, the hairpins are tight and well signed, and the road is usually busy with tourists, buses and other bikes. In autumn the foliage here is among the most celebrated in Japan, and traffic can be heavy.

Fuel is available in town and in Imaichi. In Nikkō, you can eat yuba, tofu skin, a local speciality that comes from the temple-food tradition, or soba noodles and grilled fish. The weather changes quickly in the mountains: mist, rain and cooler air often arrive on the plateau above. In winter, snow and ice can close the roads or require tyre chains. The best times are May to early June and mid-October, with fresh green or red leaves, and an early start to beat the buses.
t.akechidaira@36.7,139.5:
Akechidaira is a viewing platform above Nikko that exists mostly to show off a road. The road is the Irohazaka, a set of forty-eight hairpin bends that climb the steep slope from the town toward Lake Chuzenji and Oku-Nikko, and the name comes from the old Japanese alphabet, the iroha, which has forty-eight characters, one for each bend. The upper terminus of the climb is Akechidaira, a lookout at about 1,370 metres, reached by a short cable car, from which you see the zigzags below and, across the gulf of the valley, the whole of Lake Chuzenji with the great Mount Nantai standing guard behind. Kegon Falls, nearly a hundred metres high, drops into a gorge to one side.

The Irohazaka is actually two roads, since the climb and descent are on separate one-way carriageways. The older one, opened in the 1950s, carries the downhill traffic, and the second, which came a decade later, carries the climb. It means that you will meet no oncoming traffic on the bends, which makes it one of the more relaxed hairpin sequences to ride, though the bends are tight and the gradient steady, and the surface can be wet and covered in leaves in autumn. Speed limits are low and the police are present. Wild monkeys, Japanese macaques, sit by the roadside on the upper sections and should be left strictly alone, since they are used to being fed by tourists and can be aggressive when they think a bag has food in it.

Autumn is the main season, when the whole slope turns red, orange and yellow, usually in mid-October at the top and later lower down. It is spectacular but traffic can be extremely heavy on weekends and holidays, with queues stretching back through Nikko, so go on a weekday and start early. Fog is common, and in winter the road can be icy and snow tyres or chains are required.

Nikko itself, about eight kilometres below, is the other great draw, with the Toshogu shrine, the lavishly decorated mausoleum of Tokugawa Ieyasu, founder of the shogunate that ruled Japan for two and a half centuries. The complex and its neighbours are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and worth a day on their own. Fuel stations and restaurants are plentiful in Nikko, and local specialities include yuba, the delicate skin from soy milk, and soba noodles.

Fill the tank in town before the climb, since the road has no stations. The cafe at the viewpoint is a good place to get a hot drink and look out over the valley while you recover your nerve.
t.seeheim@-26.8,17.8:
Seeheim is a railway halt turned crossroads, a handful of buildings in the south of Namibia where the road from the coast and the road from Keetmanshoop converge near the Fish River. It is not much to look at, but the scale of the country around it is a reason to stop. The land is dry, rocky and enormous, with granite hills, dark dolerite outcrops, and gravel plains that run out to a horizon that never quite arrives. Rain is rare and fierce when it comes, and the riverbeds are dry for most of the year, but after a good storm the Fish River can flood the lowlands.

The name is German, and so is the history. The area was part of German South West Africa from the 1880s until the First World War, and the railway that ran from the port of Lüderitz to Keetmanshoop made places like this possible. A famous old hotel here, with a stone-built look and a terrace over the valley, has been serving travellers for generations, and it is the kind of place where you can sit under a ceiling fan with a cold drink and listen to the wind. Quiver trees, the tree-sized aloes that are one of the symbols of the south, grow on dolerite hills nearby.

The riding in this part of the country is long, straight, empty and deeply satisfying, if you like space. The tarmac is generally fine, with occasional potholes, and the gravel roads off it vary from smooth to corrugated and loose. Wind can be a problem, particularly crosswinds on exposed straights, and the sun is strong. Few vehicles share the road, and distances between services are long, so a full tank and a decent water supply are the first rules of the region. Watch for livestock and wildlife on the road, especially at dawn and dusk.

Keetmanshoop, the regional town, is the place for fuel, a proper supermarket and repairs, and you should fill the tank there or at Grünau rather than count on a pump at the crossroads. Meat is the mainstay of local cooking, from braai to biltong, and a cold Windhoek lager tastes very good here. Nights can be chilly, so a warm layer is worth carrying even in a hot season.
t.hobas@-27.6,17.7:
Hobas is the gateway to the Fish River Canyon, the second-largest canyon in the world, and it is a small camp with a gate, a campsite shaded by trees and a swimming pool that seems miraculous in this landscape. The canyon itself is a huge scar in the earth, about 160 kilometres long, up to twenty-seven kilometres wide in places, and around 550 metres deep at its lowest point. It was carved by the Fish River over hundreds of millions of years, and by tectonic movement that cracked the plateau. From the rim, the river winds in great horseshoe bends at the bottom, a green-brown thread among the pale rock walls.

The roads that lead here are mostly gravel in the final stretch, and conditions vary. A well-graded stretch can be a pleasure, with wide bends and good visibility, while a corrugated, loose one takes concentration and a lighter hand on the throttle. Dust is part of the day, and so is the heat, which can pass forty degrees in summer. Ride early, and do not push your luck on loose gravel with a loaded bike. The view at the main lookout is a short ride beyond the gate, and it is worth more than any photograph.

To the south, in the canyon's lower reaches, lies Ai-Ais, a hot spring resort where the water rises at a temperature that was long considered healing. The Nama people knew of it long before the Germans arrived, and the name means something like burning water. The famous hiking trail along the canyon floor is open only in the cooler months, roughly May to September, and it is a serious undertaking that requires a permit and fitness.

The sure places to fill up are Grünau and Keetmanshoop on the main road, so arrive with a full tank and a small reserve. The campsite and the shop offer basic supplies and cold drinks, but check what is open before you rely on it. Baboons and rock hyraxes watch you from the rocks, and at sunset the canyon walls glow in layers of orange and red, with a silence that you have to experience to believe.
t.fish river canyon viewpoint@-27.6,17.6:
The Fish River Canyon in southern Namibia is the second largest canyon in the world after the Grand Canyon, about 160 kilometres long, up to 27 kilometres wide and about 550 metres deep at its deepest. The Fish River winds along the bottom in great loops, and the viewpoint at Hobas looks down on the most famous bend, called Hell's Bend. The canyon formed over hundreds of millions of years, partly by faulting and partly by river erosion, and the rock walls show the layers of history in grey, brown and red. In the dry season, the river shrinks to a series of pools, and after rain it can flood.

The surrounding country is empty. Ai-Ais, a hot spring resort at the southern end of the canyon, and Hobas, with its campsite and park office, are the only services nearby, and fuel is a real concern. The nearest town with reliable supplies is Keetmanshoop, about 160 kilometres north, and Noordoewer, at the South African border, is also a long way off. Fill the tank in a town, carry spare fuel and plenty of water, and do not count on remote pumps being open.

The ride here crosses a large, open plain of gravel and sand, with distant mountains and a wide sky. Gravel roads are usually good but corrugated in places, and loose sand and sharp stones can puncture tyres. Speeds should be modest, especially on corners, and oncoming dust from vehicles can hide hazards. The summers are extremely hot, with temperatures that can exceed forty degrees, so the best season is the cooler winter, from May to September, when days are warm and nights cold.

San people lived in the area for thousands of years, and later the Nama herded their livestock across the plains. The canyon is also the site of a famous five-day hiking trail, open only in the cooler months and requiring a medical certificate. At sunset, the walls of the canyon glow orange and purple, and the sky fills with stars after dark. It is a landscape that makes you feel small, and a ride that rewards patience.
t.panther junction@29.3,-103.2:
Panther Junction is the headquarters of Big Bend National Park, a modest cluster of buildings, a visitor centre, a post office and a fuel station in the middle of the Chihuahuan Desert, on the road that connects the park's entrance with the Chisos Mountains. It sits at a little under four thousand feet, in a broad basin of creosote and yucca, with the jagged Chisos range to the south and a vast sky overhead. The park is one of the most remote in the lower forty-eight, and the nearest sizeable towns are a long way off.

Big Bend takes its name from the great curve in the Rio Grande, which swings south and then north again along the Mexican border, and the park contains deep canyons, desert plains and a mountain range with forests of pine and oak, all in a single protected area. It has more species of birds than any other national park, and mountain lions, black bears, javelinas and roadrunners live there. At night, the sky is among the darkest in the country, and the Milky Way is spectacular.

The Ross Maxwell Scenic Drive begins nearby and runs thirty miles south-west across the desert to the river at Santa Elena Canyon. It is named after the park's first superintendent, and it passes the volcanic spires of Mule Ears, the colourful rocks of Tuff Canyon, and the Castolon ruins, an old border trading post. The road is paved, with gentle curves and good views, and it crosses open desert, dropping toward the river. Heat is intense in summer, with temperatures often above forty degrees, so ride early or in the cooler months.

Fuel is available here, and it is wise to fill up before heading into the park's remote areas, since stations are few and far apart. Supplies at the store are limited, and the nearest towns are far, so bring water and food. Weather can be extreme, with summer heat, sudden thunderstorms, flash floods in the arroyos and winter cold snaps. Mobile phones do not work in most of the park. The best time is from November to March, when days are warm and the nights are cold and clear. Watch for wildlife crossing the road at dusk.
t.sotol vista@29.2,-103.4:
Sotol Vista is where Big Bend National Park shows you how much of it there is. The overlook sits on a rise beside the Ross Maxwell Scenic Drive, named for the park's first superintendent, and the view runs south and west across a basin of pale desert with the Chisos Mountains standing behind you and the far-off notch of Santa Elena Canyon on the horizon. The land is open Chihuahuan Desert, and in every direction you see more of it. There is nothing between you and the Rio Grande but space, heat and the occasional hawk.

The plant that gives the place its name is the sotol, a tough, spiky rosette with long, narrow leaves, rather like a yucca with a grudge. It covers the slopes beside the road, and in spring it throws up tall flower stalks, which locals once used to make a strong drink. Lechuguilla, ocotillo and prickly pear fill in the gaps, and after a good rain the desert turns greener than you would believe. The geology is volcanic, with old lava flows and tuff laid down in the Tertiary period, and in the distance you can pick out the layered bluffs of Mesa de Anguila.

The drive itself is thirty miles of smooth, well-graded tarmac, running from the high country near the Chisos down to the river at Castolon, with a lovely, slow rhythm of curves, dips and sudden views. The speed limit is low, and the drive is closer to a gentle ride than a thrill. Heat is the main issue. From May to September, afternoon temperatures can climb past forty degrees, and a motorcycle jacket becomes an oven, so ride early and carry more water than seems sensible. In winter the days are mild and the nights cold.

This is remote country, and services are few. The store at Castolon is limited, and the nearest towns of any size are far away. Fill up before you set out, carry water, and let someone know your plans, since mobile signal is patchy. The sunsets over the desert, with the Chisos turning purple behind you, are among the best in Texas.
t.mule ears@29.2,-103.4:
Two rock horns stand up from the desert floor beside the road, close together and slightly tilted, and anybody who has ever seen a mule will recognise them instantly. The Mule Ears are the remains of volcanic dikes, sheets of molten rock that forced their way into cracks in the earth millions of years ago, hardened, and were then exposed as the softer rock around them wore away. They rise roughly a thousand feet above the surrounding plain and dominate this section of Big Bend National Park's Ross Maxwell Scenic Drive.

The viewpoint is an easy stop, with a parking area and a short trail that leads out across the desert toward the peaks and a small spring tucked into a fold in the hills. In the right season you will find a patch of green and a trickle of water that seems almost miraculous after the dry miles. The trail is a few miles round trip, with little shade, so it is best in the cool of the morning. Lizards scuttle, roadrunners cross the road and, at dawn and dusk, coyotes and javelinas are about.

Riding here is a gentle, flowing joy. The Ross Maxwell Scenic Drive curves between volcanic hills with long straight sections, short climbs and the occasional dip where a desert wash crosses. The tarmac is generally good, and the traffic is light. Wind can be strong, and flash floods in the summer rains can leave mud and debris on the road. In midday sun the heat is intense, so take your breaks in the morning or evening, and carry plenty of water. Winter mornings can be cold enough for gloves, but by noon the sun has warmed the rock.

The area has a long human history. Native peoples lived and travelled along the Rio Grande for thousands of years, and in the early twentieth century ranchers and farmers settled here, with a small community at Castolon, a short way further on. The old trading post there is now a seasonal store, and border raids during the Mexican Revolution brought US cavalry to Castolon around 1916. Today the river is quiet and shallow, and the Mexican hills on the far side are as empty as the Texas ones.

Fuel and food are not available at Mule Ears. The park fuel station at Panther Junction and the town of Study Butte, outside the west entrance, are the sources, and Terlingua nearby has a few more services, including a ghost town with a famous porch. Fill up, because the drive is long.
t.rio grande village@29.2,-103.0:
The east side of Big Bend National Park drops into a green seam, and Rio Grande Village is the tiny settlement on the river where the Chihuahuan Desert finally gets a drink. Cottonwoods, reed beds and a campground sit in the floodplain, a store sells ice and groceries, and a few hundred metres away the Rio Grande slides past with Mexico on the far bank. The air smells of river mud and creosote, and in the evening there is a lot of birdsong. Southwest of here the Chisos Mountains hold the sunset, and to the east the Sierra del Carmen stands in the haze like a stage backdrop.

For a ride that follows the river road, this is a good place to set off from and a poor place to be unprepared. Treat the surrounding country as remote. The park has very few services, summer afternoons are brutal, and a breakdown on the unpaved track can mean waiting for a long time. Carry more water than seems necessary, tell someone your plan, and check the current condition of the road at a ranger station, because rain turns the clay washes to something unrideable. The track is gravel and dirt, with sandy patches, rock steps and creek crossings, so the right bike is a dual-sport and the right pace is slow.

There is a small hot spring a short walk from the road, where J.O. Langford, an early settler, built a bathhouse early in the twentieth century after moving here from Mississippi for his health; the stone ruins are still there beside the river and the water is warm year round. The old Boquillas Canyon overlook is nearby, where the walls close in and the river bends out of sight, and the road continues to the border crossing at Boquillas, which is a short rowboat ride and a legitimate way to have lunch in Mexico if you carry a passport.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Panther Junction, the park headquarters, is the reliable place for fuel, and you should top up there before heading out into the park interior.

October to March is the sensible season, with warm days and cold nights. The border country is wild and honest, and the quiet here is real.
t.mariscal mine@29.1,-103.2:
The Mariscal Mine is a ruin on the edge of nothing, which is exactly why it is worth the long dirt ride. In the southern part of Big Bend National Park the River Road runs west from the eastern side toward the Rio Grande, and in this corner of the desert you come across old adobe and stone buildings, rusted equipment, and the scarred slopes of Mariscal Mountain, where for decades people dug for mercury.

The ore was cinnabar, the red mineral from which quicksilver is refined, and mining here went on in the first half of the twentieth century. It was hard work in a harsh place: the heat is extreme, the water scarce, and the closest town was a long, rough journey away. The remains of the furnace and the workers' houses are still standing, and the whole site has a stillness that is difficult to explain until you stand in it. Mexico lies just across the river, and the Sierra del Carmen runs along the horizon on that side, pale and sharp in the afternoon light.

The riding is not for every bike. The River Road is a graded but rough dirt track, with sand, washboard, and stretches of rocky wash that become hard going when wet. An adventure bike with good tyres and a rider comfortable on gravel will manage, but a heavy tourer or road bike will suffer and possibly stop. Allow plenty of time, tell someone your route, and carry more water than seems sensible. Phone signal is poor to nonexistent. Check at a ranger station for road conditions before you set out, because summer storms can wash sections out for days.

Panther Junction, in the middle of the park, and the communities of Study Butte and Terlingua outside it, are where to fill the tank. Winter and early spring are the best seasons; summer is brutal, with temperatures that can top forty degrees. Look for roadrunners, javelinas, and the occasional coyote, and keep an eye on the sky in the evening, when the colours over the Chihuahuan Desert are remarkable.
t.talley@29.1,-103.4:
Talley is not much more than a name on a map, but the name tells you something about the rider's experience of Big Bend. It lies in the southern part of the national park, near the Rio Grande where the river carves its way through a deep limestone canyon, and the River Road passes through country that feels very far from anywhere. For a motorcyclist who has made it this far along the dirt, it is the sort of place that tells you what you have just ridden.

The geology is the main attraction. The Rio Grande here has cut into ancient limestone, and the canyon walls rise in steps and cliffs, grey and cream against the blue sky. Paddlers know the stretch for its river trips, and they come out of the water near this part of the park, so you may see people with rafts and canoes. The desert around is the Chihuahuan, a landscape of lechuguilla, creosote, ocotillo, and prickly pear that takes on a pale glow at sunrise and a long red light in the evening. In spring, after a wet winter, it can bloom beautifully.

The road is the River Road, a gravel and dirt track that demands attention. Sand patches can catch a front wheel, washes can hide soft spots, and the washboard shakes everything loose. Pace yourself and stop often. This is adventure-bike territory, and even then it is best to carry a repair kit, a pump, and plenty of water. Cell coverage is not to be trusted. Tell the ranger station where you are going and when you expect to be back. The park authorities publish current road conditions, and it is wise to read them.

Fuel and supplies are far away. Panther Junction, the park headquarters, has a station, and the settlements of Study Butte and Terlingua just outside the western boundary have more choice, including cafes and a small museum in a ghost town. Plan the day so that you reach the gravel with a full tank and enough hours of light. Night comes quickly and the desert gets cold fast outside the summer months. The reward is silence, space, and the feeling of having crossed a real frontier.
t.castolon@29.1,-103.5:
Castolon is an old army outpost that turned into a cotton-farming village and then into a quiet park service stop, with a few adobe buildings and a trading post clustered near the river. It sits in the southwestern part of Big Bend National Park, where the Rio Grande draws a long green line through the pale desert, and across the water lies Mexico, with only a rowing boat's width of difference. The place is small enough to see in ten minutes and interesting enough to spend an hour.

The history is blunt. In the years around the Mexican Revolution, the border was a dangerous place, and the US cavalry kept a camp here to protect settlers from raiders. Afterwards farmers planted cotton on the river flats, and the store, known as La Harmonia, served workers on both sides of the river. The company went away and the farming faded, but the store survives, selling cold drinks, snacks and supplies in a long, shaded building.

The ride to get here is the whole point. Coming from the east on the river track, you pass through creosote flats, along dry washes, with the Chisos Mountains bulging to the north and the Mexican range sitting low and blue to the south. The surface is dirt and gravel, sometimes rocky and sometimes silty, and rain can make a mess of it. The paved route on the west side is the Ross Maxwell Scenic Drive, which comes down from the mountains and passes some of the best views in the park, including a long view toward Santa Elena Canyon, where the river has cut a slot more than three hundred metres deep through the limestone.

A short drive from Castolon is the trailhead for that canyon, and it is worth a walk in the late afternoon when the cliffs glow. Watch the heat, and carry plenty of water, because there is little shade.

Services are thin. The night sky is among the darkest in the lower forty-eight, and a clear night out here is a quiet reminder of how big the country is.
t.baltiysk@54.7,19.9:
Baltiysk is Russia's westernmost port and the country's gate onto the open Baltic, a naval town of about thirty-four thousand people at the tip of the Sambian Peninsula, where a narrow channel connects the Vistula Lagoon to the sea. Until 1945 it was Pillau, in East Prussia, and the grid of tidy streets, the old brick buildings near the harbour and the lighthouse on the waterfront all date from that earlier life. The Baltic Fleet is based here, so the harbour is full of grey ships, and you should treat anything with a gun on it as a subject for your eyes only, not your camera.

The road from Kaliningrad runs west through a mix of farmland, pine woods and small towns, and it is among the flattest rides in Russia. The asphalt is mostly good, curves are gentle, and the interest comes from the landscape rather than the gradient: wide skies, sandy forest, and glimpses of the lagoon on one side and the sea on the other. Traffic is heavier on summer weekends, when Kaliningrad families head for the beaches, and on a hot Saturday the road can be slow. An early start or an autumn day makes it far more pleasant. The wind off the Baltic is a constant, and it can be cold even in July.

With a town of this size, practicalities are easy. There are petrol stations, shops, cafes and a few hotels, and you will not need to plan around supplies. Svetlyy, with twenty-two thousand people, lies fifteen kilometres back toward the city, while Primorsk, a smaller place of about two thousand, lies eleven kilometres away along the coast, with the dunes and the old German streets of a seaside resort. Both are worth a quick look if you have time. In summer, smoked fish and cold beer are the staples at roadside stalls.

The coast around Baltiysk belongs to the amber country. The Sambian Peninsula holds most of the world's known amber, and pieces still wash up on the beaches after storms, so if you have a patient eye and a cold morning, there is a chance to find some. The sea is grey and cold, the sand is pale and wide, and the pine forest behind smells of resin. Walk to the end of the mole at the harbour mouth if it is open, and watch ships pass through the channel. It is the end of one of Europe's long coastal roads.
t.suyama sengen jinja shrine@35.3,138.8:
On the southern flank of Mount Fuji, above the town of Susono, a quiet shrine stands among tall cedar trees at the start of one of the oldest climbing routes on the mountain. The Suyama Sengen-jinja is dedicated to the goddess of Fuji and marks the beginning of the Suyama trail, used by pilgrims for centuries before falling into disuse in the twentieth century and being partly revived in recent years. It is one of the component sites of Fujisan, Sacred Place and Source of Artistic Inspiration, listed by UNESCO in 2013.

The shrine is small and peaceful, with moss-covered stone lanterns and the scent of cedar and incense in the air. Unlike the busy shrines and trails on the more popular routes, it sees few visitors, and you can often have it almost to yourself. On a clear day, the summit of Fuji, at 3,776 metres, rises above the trees, and the view of its perfect cone across the fields and forests is one of the classic images of Japan. Mount Fuji has been worshipped for centuries as a sacred mountain, and pilgrims would purify themselves at shrines like this before beginning the climb.

The roads around Fuji are excellent for riding, with smooth surfaces, careful drivers and stunning views. The Fuji Skyline and other roads that climb the mountain's flanks lead to car parks and trailheads at the fifth stations, with hairpins and changing landscapes from forest to volcanic rock, though some may be subject to closures or restrictions in winter and during the climbing season. The Hakone area, a short ride east, has more curvy mountain roads and lakes with views of Fuji. Traffic can be heavy on weekends and holidays.

Gotemba, a city of over eighty thousand, has fuel, shops and restaurants, as well as a large outlet mall. Local specialities include Fujinomiya yakisoba, fried noodles with a chewy texture, and fresh trout from mountain streams. The best views of Fuji come in the colder months, when the air is clear, while summer is often hazy and humid. Bring warm layers if you plan to ride high on the mountain.
t.auschwitz birkenau german nazi concentra:
There is no right way to arrive at Auschwitz-Birkenau, and no ride passes through it casually. This was the largest of the German Nazi concentration and extermination camps, built during the occupation of Poland near the town of Oświęcim, which the Germans called Auschwitz. Between 1940 and January 1945, at least 1.1 million people were murdered here, the vast majority of them Jews deported from across Europe, along with Poles, Roma, Soviet prisoners of war and many others. On 27 January 1945, Soviet soldiers liberated the camp, and that date is now International Holocaust Remembrance Day. UNESCO listed the site in 1979 as a memorial to the victims and a warning to humanity.

The memorial has two main parts. Auschwitz I, the original camp, with its brick barracks and the gate bearing the cynical slogan Arbeit macht frei, houses exhibitions on the history of the camp and the lives of the prisoners. Birkenau, about three kilometres away near the village of Brzezinka, is vast: rows of wooden and brick barracks stretching into the distance, the railway line and ramp where trains arrived and selections took place, and the ruins of the gas chambers and crematoria, blown up by the SS as they fled. Walking there is overwhelming.

Practical matters deserve respect too. Entry to the memorial is free but requires a reserved time slot, and during the busiest hours, especially in the warmer months, visits are only possible with a guide. Book well in advance. Allow at least three or four hours, and dress and behave with dignity; this is a cemetery. Large bags are not allowed inside, so plan where to leave your riding gear; there are facilities at the visitor centre.

Oświęcim, a town of about forty thousand, has all the ordinary services; it also has a Jewish centre and a restored synagogue that tells the story of the town's Jewish community before the war. The surrounding roads are flat and busy, linking Kraków, about an hour to the east, with Silesia and the Czech border. After a visit, many people need time to sit in silence before they can ride again. Take that time.
t.lake yamanakako@35.4,138.9:
Yamanakako is the largest and highest of the Fuji Five Lakes, lying at nearly a thousand metres at the eastern foot of Mount Fuji, and on a clear winter morning, with the snow cone of the mountain mirrored in still water, it delivers the view that sells a million postcards. The lake was formed when lava flows from Fuji dammed the valley, and it is shallow, with reed beds, swans and boating piers along the shore. In summer it is a cool escape from the heat of Tokyo, busy with families, rowing boats and lakeside cafés; in winter the crowds thin and the mountain is at its most impressive.

The whole area around Fuji is volcanic: black lava fields covered in forest, lava caves, springs that bubble up through the porous rock. Fujiyoshida, the town at the foot of the traditional climbing route, has the Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen shrine, set among giant cedars, where pilgrims began their ascent for centuries. The local food is hoto, thick flat noodles stewed with pumpkin and vegetables in miso, and Fujiyoshida's udon is famously chewy.

For motorcyclists, this is a major destination. Route 138 climbs out of the Gotemba side over the Kagosaka Pass and down to the lake, and Route 413, the old Doshi road, runs east through the mountains towards Sagamihara along a river valley, with a long run of corners that draws riders from Tokyo every weekend. The roads around the lake are gentle and scenic, and to the south-west Route 139 runs past the other lakes and the Aokigahara forest. Traffic is heavy on holidays and in the summer, and the roads can ice up in winter, especially in the early morning. Speed limits in Japan are low, and police are particularly active on popular weekend routes.

Yamanakako village has fuel, convenience stores and restaurants along the lake road, and Fujiyoshida and Gotemba are both large towns with full services. There are onsen hot springs in the area, perfect after a cold ride, and plenty of campsites and lodges. If you want the classic view, go to the northern shore at sunrise between November and February, when the air is clearest; in the summer, Fuji often hides behind cloud for days.
t.hitoana fuji ko iseki@35.4,138.6:
Deep in the lava forests on the western foot of Mount Fuji there is a cave formed when molten rock flowed down the slopes and its crust cooled while the interior drained away. The Hitoana lava tube is small and low, but in the sixteenth century an ascetic called Hasegawa Kakugyo is said to have practised extreme austerities inside it, and he became the founder figure of the Fuji-ko, the popular confraternities whose members climbed Fuji as an act of worship. Around the cave entrance stand hundreds of stone memorials erected by Fuji-ko groups over the centuries, mossy and leaning among the trees. The site is one of the components of the World Heritage listing Fujisan, Sacred Place and Source of Artistic Inspiration.

The cave sits on the Asagiri plateau, a high grassland and dairy region between Fuji and the mountains to the west, where cows graze on open pasture and the volcano fills the sky on clear days. Fresh milk and ice cream are sold at farm shops along the roads, and the light in the early morning, when Fuji turns pink, is magical. Clouds often hide the summit by midday.

Riding here is a joy. Route 139, the main road running north from Fujinomiya around the west side of the mountain toward Lake Motosu and the Fuji Five Lakes, is wide, smooth and flowing, with gentle curves and constant views of the volcano. Smaller roads wander across the plateau through farmland and forest. Japanese traffic is orderly, but speed limits are low and enforcement strict. Weekends can be busy with tourists. Winter brings snow and ice at this altitude, around seven to nine hundred metres, so spring and autumn are best.

Fujinomiya, sixteen kilometres away, is the main town, with fuel, shops and the Fujisan Hongu Sengen Taisha shrine, the head of the Sengen shrines dedicated to the mountain's goddess. The town is known for Fujinomiya yakisoba, fried noodles with a chewy texture, sold everywhere. Fujikawaguchiko, on the north side of the mountain, is another base.

The cave itself is accessed via a small park, and entry into the tube may be restricted; the memorials and the forest are worth the stop regardless.
t.shiraito no taki waterfalls@35.3,138.6:
The water that falls at Shiraito has spent a long time underground. Rain and snowmelt seep into the porous volcanic rock of Mount Fuji, travel through the layers for years, and emerge from a cliff face southwest of the mountain as hundreds of thin streams, pouring over a curved wall about twenty metres high and some one hundred and fifty metres wide. The name means white threads, and the effect is just that: a curtain of silvery strands falling into a clear pool, with the Fuji-ko pilgrims once performing purification rituals here. The falls are part of the Fujisan World Heritage Site, and the neighbouring Otodome falls, a single powerful cascade, roar a short walk away.

The setting is lush and green, with moss, ferns and trees around the falls, and the water is cold and clear even in summer. A stairway leads down to the basin, where viewing platforms give the best perspective. On clear days, Fuji is visible above the falls as you walk down toward them. The surrounding area is part of the Asagiri plateau, with pasture, farms and forest.

The roads around Shiraito are pleasant and gentle, with Route 139 and Route 414 linking the falls to Fujinomiya and the Fuji Five Lakes. The riding is relaxed rather than exciting, with smooth surfaces, light traffic and views of the volcano. On weekends and holidays, parking at the falls can be busy, but there is space for bikes. The Tanuki lake, a short ride away, reflects Fuji on still mornings, and around certain dates in spring and late summer the sun rises exactly over the summit, known as Diamond Fuji, attracting crowds of photographers.

Fujinomiya, eleven kilometres away, is the sensible place to refuel, and Fuji city, further south, is a larger industrial town. Near the falls, small shops sell grilled trout, local sweets and souvenirs. The climate is mild, with hot summers and cool winters, and snow is possible on the plateau. Early morning is the best time to visit, before the crowds and while Fuji is still clear of clouds.
t.daigo ji@35.0,135.8:
The oldest building in Kyoto does not stand in the city centre but in the southeastern hills, at the temple of Daigo-ji: a five storey pagoda completed in 951, which has survived fires, earthquakes and wars that destroyed almost everything else of its age in the city. The temple was founded in the ninth century on Mount Daigo, and its grounds spread from the foot of the mountain to the summit, linked by a steep path, with halls, gardens and sub temples along the way. It is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto World Heritage Site.

Daigo-ji is famous for cherry blossoms. In 1598, the warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi held a grand cherry blossom viewing party here for some thirteen hundred guests, and the temple still holds a procession in his memory each spring. The Sanbo-in garden, laid out under Hideyoshi's direction, is a masterpiece of rocks, ponds and pines. In autumn, the maples around the pond of the Bentendo hall turn brilliant red.

The temple lies in the Yamashina basin, between Kyoto and Lake Biwa, in a district that is more suburban than historic. Uji, to the south, is the home of Japanese green tea and of the Byodo-in temple, whose Phoenix Hall appears on the ten yen coin. Otsu, on Lake Biwa, is a short ride east over the hills.

Riding in Kyoto is challenging, with heavy traffic, narrow streets and crowds of tourists, and parking a bike in the centre requires finding designated motorcycle parking. The roads in the hills around the city are more pleasant, including the routes over the mountains toward Lake Biwa and the roads into the tea country of Uji and Wazuka, where terraced tea fields cover the hillsides.

Uji and Otsu have fuel and services, and Kyoto has everything. Try matcha in Uji, whether as tea, ice cream or soba noodles. Daigo-ji is busy in cherry blossom season and autumn, and quieter at other times. Allow time for the climb to the upper temple, which takes an hour or more on foot.
t.kawaguchi asama jinja shrine@35.5,138.8:
Mount Fuji was never meant to be seen only from a distance, and the shrines at its foot are where the older idea of the mountain as a god survives. The Kawaguchi Asama-jinja sits among tall old cedars on the north side, near Lake Kawaguchi, one of the five lakes that ring the mountain's northern foot, and it is one of the shrines that were used by pilgrims before they began the climb. The deity honoured at the Asama shrines is Konohanasakuya-hime, the princess of the blossoming trees, who is linked with the mountain and its volcanic fire.

The cedars at the shrine are some of the largest in the area, and walking in under them feels like stepping out of the tourist crowds. The shrine is part of the Mount Fuji World Heritage property, listed as a cultural landscape in 2013, which includes the climbing routes, lakes, shrines and the old pilgrim lodgings. Between them they show how the mountain became sacred, with believers walking in white clothing and ringing bells, and the old Fuji-ko confraternities still exist.

For a rider, this corner of Japan is a classic. The road round the lakes is a pleasure, with open stretches, lake views and, if the weather allows, the cone of Fuji above you. The Fuji Subaru Line climbs to the fifth station at around 2,300 metres, but it is closed in winter and may be restricted in the peak climbing season, so check before you go. Cloud often covers the summit by mid-morning, so early starts reward you with the best views, and autumn and winter mornings are the clearest. Weekends and holidays are busy, with tour buses, and the temperature at the lake is cooler than in Tokyo.

Fujikawaguchiko is the nearest town and has several fuel stations, while Fujiyoshida, a bit farther, has more shops and the old pilgrim street. Try hōtō, the thick noodle stew of Yamanashi, which is warming on a cool day, and if you can, take a short walk in the nearby forest of Aokigahara, where moss covers the lava and the ground is quiet.
t.hongan ji@35.0,135.8:
Kyoto's Hongan-ji, in the middle of the city a short walk from the main railway station, is a temple of the Jodo Shinshu school of Buddhism, the largest branch of Buddhism in Japan, and one of the most important buildings in the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto inscribed by UNESCO in 1994. The city of one and a half million people spreads in every direction, and it is no place for fast riding, but the temple is one of the quietest and most human of the great monuments.

The school was founded on the teachings of Shinran, a thirteenth-century monk who taught that faith in Amida Buddha, rather than hard discipline, could save anyone, from peasants to nobles. After his death in 1262 a small mausoleum was built in Kyoto, which grew into the Hongan-ji, and the school became a powerful religious and political force. In the sixteenth century, the warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi granted it land on the present site, and the temple later split into two branches, the Nishi, or west, and Higashi, or east, Hongan-ji, which stand a few minutes apart. The west temple's halls are remarkable for their size and for the way the great wooden pillars and beams, the huge gilded interior, and the carved gate with its intricate decoration show the wealth of the order. Worship goes on all day, and visitors are welcome in the main halls, but it is polite to be quiet and to take off your shoes.

Kyoto is a challenge for a rider. The grid of streets is easy to follow, but traffic is slow, bicycles weave through, parking is scarce and expensive, and the narrow lanes of the old districts are best explored on foot. A scooter or a bicycle is the sensible way to see the city, and a motorcycle is best left at your hotel. The reward is the mountains around the city, such as Mount Hiei to the north-east, and the roads over the northern hills towards Lake Biwa and the Japan Sea coast, which are excellent.

There is fuel, food and coffee in abundance. Kyoto's cuisine is subtle, with tofu, pickles, seasonal vegetables and kaiseki, but there are also cheap noodle bars all around the station. Spring, with the cherry blossom, and November, with the maple leaves, are the busiest seasons, and summer is hot and sticky.
t.tarnowskie gory lead silver zinc mine an:
Upper Silesia is Poland's industrial heart, a densely built region of coal mines, steelworks, spoil heaps and tidy brick housing, and at its northern edge lies Tarnowskie Gory, a town of about sixty thousand people that grew up around silver, lead and zinc. The mine and its underground water system were inscribed by UNESCO in 2017, and the town's historic centre is about a kilometre from the entrance. Katowice, the regional capital, is some thirty kilometres to the south-east.

Ore was dug here from the Middle Ages, and the town received its charter in the sixteenth century, when silver mining boomed. By the eighteenth century the shafts had reached the water table, and the real problem was how to keep the mines dry. The solution was a steam engine, one of the earliest used on the European continent, installed in 1788 on the advice of the Prussian mining administration, and a network of drainage tunnels, or adits, that carried the water away. The most famous, the Black Trout Adit, is a long, narrow tunnel that visitors can travel along in a small boat, pushed by guides, in near darkness with dripping stone walls close on either side. The old silver mine can also be toured on foot, with a tight descent underground and low passages. Wear sturdy shoes and expect a chilly, damp environment all year, at about ten degrees.

The surrounding region is a mix of towns and woodland. Riding in Silesia means a lot of urban motorway and heavy traffic, with trams, roundabouts and roadworks, and the better roads lie to the north, in the pine forests and farm country to the north, or to the south, where the Beskid mountains rise. Cobbles remain on a few older streets, and in winter salt and ice make the roads treacherous. Spring and autumn are best. Winters are cold and grey.

Tarnowskie Gory has all the services, with petrol stations on the main roads, supermarkets and a pleasant old market square with cafes. Silesian cooking is hearty, with kluski slaskie, soft potato dumplings with a dimple, served with roulade of beef and red cabbage, and the region has its own dialect, which locals speak with pride. Book mine tours in advance in summer, since groups are limited.
t.birkenau@50.0,19.2:
Birkenau is the second and largest part of the Auschwitz camp complex, built by the Nazi regime from 1941 on the flat land near Brzezinka, just outside Oświęcim in southern Poland. It is where most of the million or so people murdered at Auschwitz were killed, the great majority of them Jews. The camp was meant to be seen from the entrance, with the brick gatehouse and the railway line running straight through it, and that scale is the first thing that silences visitors. There is no softening it, and nobody who goes should expect to.

The ground here is flat, damp, birch-fringed farmland by the Soła river, and in the main season the car parks fill early and queues form at the entrance. Free entry passes are offered, but timed tickets or guided tours are common in busy months, and it is wise to check the current arrangements before you ride out. Motorcycle parking is normally available nearby, though gear is a problem: you will be walking for a long time in jackets and boots, in weather that is often cold and wet. Take layers. Take water. Plan for at least a couple of hours, and give yourself time afterwards to sit and gather yourself before getting back on the road.

Oświęcim itself is a normal small Polish city of forty thousand with petrol stations, cafés and a chemical works that has shaped its economy since the war. It is a place where people live, which is part of why the memory is difficult. Some riders plan this stop alone as a quiet day. Others find that it fits better at the start or end of a longer journey, where they are not trying to cross a mountain pass in the afternoon. The nearby Auschwitz I main camp, a few kilometres away, has its own museum, and many visitors see both.

The roads that lead here from Ostrava and the Beskids are unremarkable and fast, flat plain after rolling foothills. This is a place that asks for attention more than a good line through a bend, and the ride is best remembered as the part that gets you here.
t.jisho ji@35.0,135.8:
Jisho-ji, known to most of the world as Ginkaku-ji, the Silver Pavilion, sits at the foot of the Higashiyama hills in the northeast of Kyoto. It began in the 1480s as the retirement villa of the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa, a man who lost interest in governing during a period of civil collapse and devoted himself to art, tea and gardens instead. After his death it became a Zen temple. The pavilion was never actually covered in silver, despite the name, and visitors still argue about whether the plan was dropped for lack of money or for taste.

What makes the place special is the garden. There is a raked sand platform and a sand cone shaped like Mount Fuji, a moss garden under maples, and a little pond reflecting the small wooden pavilion. The sense of quiet restraint is what we mean when we talk about the Higashiyama culture: the tea ceremony, flower arranging, ink painting and the idea of beauty in simplicity all developed from this circle. Just outside, the Philosopher's Path follows a canal lined with cherry trees south toward Nanzen-ji, and it is lovely whatever the season.

Kyoto is not a city to ride through for pleasure. Streets are narrow and busy, the grid is confusing, and parking close to temples is awkward, so many riders arrive early, leave the bike in a paid lot and walk. Fuel stations are plentiful in the suburbs, but fewer in the very centre. The wards of Kamigyo and Sakyo, as well as Kyoto itself, supply all the food and coffee you could want, and the area around the temple has tea houses and small shops selling sweets and pickles.

The real riding begins as you leave the city. North towards Kurama and Kibune, the forested lanes climb and twist through cedar, and in the other direction the road to Nara runs through low hills and tea country. In autumn the maples in the hills turn red and gold and the temple grounds are packed; in early morning even then it can be peaceful. Winter brings a thin cold light and the rare dusting of snow on the roofs, which is perhaps the best moment of all.
t.mihonomatsubara pine tree grove@35.0,138:
Miho is a thin hook of land curling out into Suruga Bay, and Mihonomatsubara is the pine grove that covers it: tens of thousands of dark pines behind a long beach of grey, pebbly sand. People come for the view. On a clear day Mount Fuji sits on the other side of the bay, framed by the trees and the curve of the shore, and that image has been painted, printed and photographed for centuries. It is why the grove was included in the UNESCO listing for Fuji in 2013, as an artistic setting for the mountain rather than as a piece of nature in itself.

The place also has a legend, the one behind the Noh play Hagoromo. A fisherman finds a heavenly feather robe hanging on a pine, a celestial maiden begs him to return it, and in exchange she performs a dance for him. One particular pine near the shrine is still called the pine of the feather robe. Whether or not you believe in angels, the story suits the soft light on the water.

Suruga Bay is the deepest bay in Japan, dropping steeply to well over two thousand metres, which is why the sea here turns such a sharp dark blue and why the port at nearby Shimizu can handle big ships. Behind the grove the Tokai region's famous tea fields climb the slopes, and Shizuoka is where much of Japan's green tea comes from. In spring, look for the little pink sakura shrimp from Yui, a few kilometres up the coast, served fried or on rice.

For riding, the approach is a flat coastal road, busy near the port and quiet along the grove itself. There is a long walk through the pines to the beach, so plan to leave the bike in the car park and spend half an hour on foot. Shizuoka city, thirteen kilometres away, has everything in fuel, food and accommodation, and further up the coast Fuji and Yaizu offer alternatives. The best time is a cold, clear winter morning, when the snowcapped peak stands sharp over the bay; in summer the mountain tends to vanish in haze by mid-morning. The rides from here run on to the great art museums of Tokyo, taking the coastal Tomei corridor and the hills around Hakone on the way.
t.ninna ji@35.0,135.7:
Ninna-ji lies on the north-western side of Kyoto, in the district of Omuro, and it is one of those temples that tell you a great deal about how Japanese politics once worked. It was founded in 888 by the emperor Uda, who after abdicating became a Buddhist priest and lived here as head of the temple, and for generations afterwards its abbots were members of the imperial family. The complex is known for its Niomon gate, its five-storey pagoda from the seventeenth century, and its garden with a view of the hills. UNESCO included it among the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto in 1994.

The cherry trees of Omuro are the temple's special feature. They are a late-blooming type, short and thick, with trunks that grow low to the ground, and they flower in mid to late April, some weeks after the famous trees in the rest of Kyoto have dropped their petals. That makes Ninna-ji a quiet place to visit in the season when the rest of the city is crowded. The blossom, set against the dark roofs and the pagoda, is spectacular.

Kyoto is a challenging city for riders. The grid is easy to follow, but the streets are narrow, the traffic is dense and slow, and parking for motorcycles is limited, so look for a designated space near the temple. Much of the centre is slow going, and the bicycle is the real king of the road. West of the temple, the Arashiyama district has a bamboo grove and a river, and the road beyond, along the Hozu gorge and up into the northern hills, is far more enjoyable on a bike. The Kitayama cedar forests and the road to Shuzan bring a feel of deep country within thirty minutes of the city.

Fuel is plentiful on the main avenues, and a few convenience stores near the temple offer coffee. For a proper meal, the temple area has noodle shops and tofu restaurants, and Kyoto's famous vegetarian cooking is worth sampling. Make time for the tea house at the temple.

Autumn colours come in November and December, and the light is soft. If you arrive early, the temple is often empty and the gravel paths are raked clean.
t.kamomioya jinja@35.0,135.8:
The shrine that people call Shimogamo, or properly Kamomioya-jinja, stands at the point where the Kamo and Takano rivers meet in northern Kyoto, and in front of it spreads an old forest that is a rare thing in a city of one and a half million. The Tadasu no Mori, the Forest of Correction, is a stand of ancient trees, elms, zelkova and oaks, which survives from the primeval woods that once covered the Kyoto basin, and a gravel path runs for several hundred metres from the entrance through the trees to the main gate. The sound of the stream beside you and the dim light under the canopy make it easy to forget the traffic nearby.

The Kamo shrines predate Kyoto itself. They were the guardian shrines of the Kamo clan, powerful before the court moved here in 794, and after the capital was founded they became important protectors of the city. In mid-May, the Aoi Matsuri, the Hollyhock Festival, sends a procession of courtiers in Heian-period costume from the Imperial Palace to Shimogamo and on to the upper Kamo shrine, with hollyhock leaves pinned to their hats, and it is one of the three great festivals of Kyoto. The shrine was listed by UNESCO in 1994.

It makes a lovely place for a rider to start a day, because the forest is shady and cool, and the neighbourhood lies north of the centre, a short way from the road along the Kamo river that leads out into the hills. Parking for bikes is possible nearby, but check signs. The streets around the shrine are narrow, with bicycles and buses, and the pace should be slow. In summer the air is humid, and the cicadas are loud, while in autumn the leaves in the forest turn gold.

Fuel is easy in Kyoto, with stations on the main roads in the Kita and Kamigyo wards. The little teahouses near the shrine sell mitarashi dango, a skewer of rice dumplings in sweet soy glaze that is said to have originated here, and which makes a good mid-morning snack.

The road that follows this ride list continues to Nara, to the site of the ancient Heijo Palace, and the way south passes through Uji, the home of Japan's best green tea.
t.nijo jo@35.0,135.7:
Nijo Castle is not really a castle, in the sense of a stronghold, but a palace dressed up as one. The first shogun of the Tokugawa dynasty, Tokugawa Ieyasu, built it in 1603 as his residence in Kyoto, to show the emperor and the nobles who held real power in Japan, and his grandson Iemitsu added to it in the 1620s. The Ninomaru Palace, the main building, has long corridors with floors that squeak like nightingales when walked on, a feature meant to warn of intruders, and rooms covered in gold-leaf screens painted with tigers, pines and eagles by the Kano school. The style was intended to impress and intimidate visiting lords.

It was here, in 1867, that the last shogun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, announced the return of power to the emperor, which ended more than two and a half centuries of Tokugawa rule and opened the way to modern Japan. The castle later became an imperial villa, and then was given to the city. UNESCO listed it in 1994.

Kyoto is a grid, and Nijo stands in the centre of it, on Horikawa Street, a few kilometres from the main station. The moat and stone walls are very impressive in cherry blossom season in early April, when the evening illuminations draw crowds. Traffic around the castle is heavy, with buses and taxis, and the best way to approach on a bike is early in the morning or on a weekday. Parking for motorcycles is available at some car parks nearby, though you should check the prices and be prepared to walk.

Fuel is easy in Kyoto, a city with stations on every major road, although they are fewer in the central part. Cafes and noodle shops are everywhere. The roads out of Kyoto north and west lead to mountain country, and the ride list continues to Yoshino and Omine, in Nara's mountains, and the Kimpu-jinja shrine, a shrine tied to Shugendo, the mountain religion of Japan's ascetic priests, reached by a road that climbs through cedar forest.

Visit in the quiet of morning, listen to the floors, and then leave the city behind with the engine warm and a cup of green tea in your pocket.
t.lutheran church of peace under the invoc:
The Church of Peace at Świdnica is one of the most unusual churches in Europe, because the law demanded it be built cheaply and fast. After the Thirty Years' War, the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 gave Silesia's Lutherans, who lived under Catholic Habsburg rule, permission to build three churches, and only three, in the whole province, at Jawor, Głogów and Świdnica. They were not allowed to use stone or brick, nor to build a tower or a spire, and they had to be outside the town walls and finished within a year. The builders responded with timber, clay and straw, and with astonishing ingenuity. The church at Świdnica, completed in 1657, is a vast half-timbered building that can hold around seven thousand people, and its interior is a baroque wonder of galleries, painted panels and a gilded pulpit, more like a theatre than a church. UNESCO listed the churches of Świdnica and Jawor in 2001.

The wooden walls have a warm, honeyed tone, and the sound inside is soft. The galleries rise in tiers to a painted ceiling with scenes from the Bible, and the vault is held up by bare oak beams. A great organ stands at one end, and the whole structure feels like the hull of an upturned ship. The story of how a minority community with few resources built something so big in so short a time is a part of the fascination.

Świdnica is a calm old town, laid out around a market square, and its Catholic cathedral has the highest tower in Lower Silesia. The roads around it lead south to the Sowie mountains, the Owl Mountains, and the castle of Książ, a great palace on a rock above a gorge, a short ride away. The country is gentle, with rolling fields, wooded hills and small villages, and the roads are generally in good shape, though the surface can be patchy in the villages and cobbles are common in old town centres. Autumn colours in the Sowie hills are very fine, and winter can be snowy.

Świdnica, with sixty thousand people, has fuel on the ring road, and Jaworzyna Śląska, a smaller town nearby, has some too. The market square has cafes with cake and Polish pierogi.

The church is a modest walk from the square and sits in a park, and it is a good place to slow down.
t.shrines and temples of nikko@36.7,139.6:
Cedar trees line the road into Nikko as if it were a cathedral nave. The Nikko Kaido avenue, planted over many years in the seventeenth century, runs for about thirty-seven kilometres and is counted among the longest tree-lined avenues in the world, and the trees are huge now, thick and dark, with a floor of moss. It makes a quiet start, and it sets the tone for the town, which is as much a forest as a religious site.

The shrines and temples that give the ride its name are the reason Nikko appears in every guidebook. Toshogu, the mausoleum of the first Tokugawa shogun, Ieyasu, was founded after his death in 1616, and the dazzling buildings you see today were mostly rebuilt on a grand scale in the 1630s under his grandson Iemitsu. Gold leaf, carved beasts, and the famous three monkeys cover every surface. Nearby are Futarasan Shrine, much older and much calmer, and Rinnoji, the temple that drew pilgrims to these mountains long before the Tokugawa arrived. The red Shinkyo bridge over the Daiya river is the traditional gate. It takes a couple of hours to see properly, and the car park and the gift shops fill by mid-morning, so arrive early or at the end of the afternoon.

For a rider the real prize is what lies above. The Irohazaka, with its forty-eight hairpins, climbs from the town to the lake at Chuzenji, one road for the ascent and another for the descent, and it is among the best-known mountain roads in Japan. The turns are numbered with the characters of the old iroha alphabet. The climb is steady and technical but not unfriendly, the surface is generally good, and the views over the valley get wide quickly. Kegon Falls, nearly a hundred metres high, drops from the lake just beyond. In autumn the entire slope turns red and orange, and every car in Tochigi seems to be on it that weekend, so aim for a weekday. In winter the upper sections can ice over and the road may require chains or be closed outright.

Nikko is a proper town of some sixteen thousand people, so there are fuel stations, restaurants and places to rest. Try yuba, the skin of heated soy milk, which is a local speciality served in many forms. This ride also touches the Arafune cold storage, a reminder that the clear mountain water here once made Nikko a centre for natural ice, cut in winter and kept for the summer, long before refrigerators existed.
t.kyo o gokoku ji@35.0,135.7:
Kyoto has dozens of temples that could stand in for the city, but the five-storey pagoda of To-ji does the job better than any, because you can see it from the Shinkansen. Kyo-o-gokoku-ji is its formal name, and the temple was founded at the very beginning of the Heian capital, in the 790s, as one of two guardian temples placed on either side of the southern gate. Its pagoda, at about fifty-five metres, is the tallest wooden pagoda in Japan, and the version that stands today dates to the middle of the seventeenth century, rebuilt after fire by the third Tokugawa shogun, Iemitsu. Earlier ones were struck by lightning with some regularity, which shows the risk of building high in a thunderstorm country.

Emperor Saga gave the temple to the monk Kukai, known after death as Kobo Daishi, in 823, and it became a centre of esoteric Shingon Buddhism, with a lecture hall full of carved Buddhist figures arranged as a three-dimensional mandala. The founder is still honoured on the twenty-first of every month with a big flea market, one of the best in Japan, where you can buy antiques, plants, pickles and old kimonos. If the date works for your schedule, it is worth bending your trip around it.

For a rider, Kyoto is a place to park the bike and walk, and that means the stop here is about patience. The grid streets are narrow and one-way in places, the bicycles and buses are everywhere, and you must follow the signs for motorcycle parking, which can be hard to find. Aim for early morning, before the tour groups arrive, and enjoy the temple with only the sound of gravel. The route then goes west towards Yakushi-ji in Nara, another of the old temples, with twin pagodas, and it can cross the hills by one of the minor roads away from the heavy traffic.

Fuel is easy within the city, but stations tend to be in the outer ring, so top up on the way in. The neighbourhood has plenty of small places for noodles and sweets, and the nearby Kyoto Station area is full of choice. April and November are lovely but crowded, July is steamy and August swelters, while January mornings can be crisp, empty and silver, in many ways the best light for photographs.
t.lake kawaguchiko@35.5,138.7:
You can ride around Kawaguchiko in a morning and spend the next three days waiting for Mount Fuji to come out of the cloud. That is the local joke, and it holds a grain of truth: the volcano, at 3,776 metres, makes its own weather, and the summit often hides until the cold, clear hours just after dawn, especially in winter. Lake Kawaguchiko is the most visited of the Fuji Five Lakes, sitting at about 830 metres on the north side of the mountain, in the town of Fujikawaguchiko, and the classic view is from the northern shore with the cone reflected in still water.

The lake is a place for easy-going riding more than adventure. A road runs right around it, with views across the water to the mountain and along the shore to hotels, bakeries and small museums. The traffic is thick at weekends and public holidays, when the car parks fill and tour buses crowd the corners. If you would like it calm, come on a weekday, or start before eight. Lavender flowers around the lakeside in late June and early July, and in November the maples along the shore turn red, a famous display that draws crowds of photographers with long lenses.

For a proper road, the Fuji Subaru Line climbs from the lake to the fifth station at about 2,300 metres, where the trees stop and the cinder starts. It is a toll road, and it is closed to traffic for part of the year when snow arrives and during the climbing season it is often restricted for private vehicles, so check before you set off. Higher up, the air is thin and cold even in July, and a jacket makes a lot of sense. The volcanic landscape up there is stark and strange: black scoria, stunted larch, and a view far over the plain.

Down at the lake, try houtou, the thick miso-based noodle stew that Yamanashi prefecture is known for, ladled out with pumpkin and vegetables. It is a hearty way to end a day. Fujikawaguchiko is a town of more than twenty thousand people, so fuel stations, shops and hotels are no problem. Fuji's slopes were designated a World Heritage cultural site in 2013, and the old pilgrimage routes of the mountain confraternities still leave their mark in the shrines and guest houses on the edge of the forest. The nearby Aokigahara woodland, growing over a lava flow, is a hushed and tangled place with a reputation, and best seen on a respectful visit.
t.kamowakeikazuchi jinja@35.1,135.8:
Thunder gave this shrine its name. Kamowakeikazuchi, the god worshipped at Kamigamo, is a deity of lightning, and the compound beside the Kamo river in northern Kyoto is thought to be one of the oldest Shinto sites in Japan, with a founding that tradition dates to the seventh century. In the compound, two neat cones of white sand stand in front of the main sanctuary, symbols of purity, imitating the sacred hill where the god is said to have come down. Beyond them, a small stream runs under a bridge in a grove of old trees, and the whole place has a quiet, swept look, like a stage before the performance.

The performances come in May. The Aoi Festival, which links Kamigamo with its sister shrine downriver at Shimogamo, is one of Kyoto's three great festivals, a procession of nobles, ox carts and horses dressed in the style of the Heian court, all wearing leaves of hollyhock, aoi, as emblems. Just before it, in early May, a horse race called Kurabeuma is run on the grass at the shrine, a tradition that runs back more than nine hundred years. The shrine was included in the World Heritage listing of the historic monuments of ancient Kyoto in 1994.

The ride from here goes south to the Nara palace site, which links two capitals, the Heian one at Kyoto and the earlier Heijo one, the first great planned city on the island, founded in 710. The route cuts through Kyoto's outskirts and then southwards through the hills and valleys around Uji, a town famous for green tea, along the Kizu river and over the low ridges that separate the two basins. It is not demanding riding, more a pleasant, rural pace through tea fields and bamboo, with villages in between. North of Kamigamo, by contrast, the Kitayama hills rise quickly into forested valleys, and a short ride up the road toward Kurama and Kibune shows another side of Kyoto, steep, shady and cool even in summer.

Kamigamo is a neighbourhood of the city, so petrol stations, bakeries and noodle counters surround it. The shrine itself is open to walk around freely, though some inner areas have restrictions, and early morning is the best time, when the gravel is raked and the temple priests are sweeping. Parking for motorbikes is limited, so use a nearby lot and walk.
t.tenryu ji@35.0,135.7:
People come to Arashiyama for the bamboo, and they leave with the memory of a garden. Tenryu-ji, the great Zen temple at the foot of the hills on the west side of Kyoto, was founded in 1339 by the shogun Ashikaga Takauji, who built it to console the spirit of the emperor Go-Daigo, his former rival. The garden, designed by the Zen master Muso Soseki, is older than almost every other thing you will see in the area: a pond with rocks arranged like a mountain landscape, with the hills of Arashiyama pulled into the view as borrowed scenery. It has survived fire after fire, though most of the halls themselves are later rebuilds.

Beside the temple's north gate you step directly into the famous bamboo grove, a cool, green corridor where the stems rise far overhead and clatter softly in the wind. It is busy from mid-morning, so the best time to see it is before eight. Beyond, the Katsura river runs wide and slow below the Togetsukyo bridge, and old boatmen still take visitors on the rapids upstream at Hozu. In November the hills around turn red and gold.

For a rider, the interest here lies in the roads that lead out of Arashiyama. Behind the temple, the Kyoto hills rise into forest, and the Shuzan Kaido, now Route 162, climbs north toward Takao and Keihoku, a road that follows a river valley through cedar plantations and tiny villages, with a pleasant mix of bends and gentle gradients. On weekdays it is quiet, and on warm weekends it fills with cyclists and groups of riders heading for the mountain restaurants. This ride, though, heads south to the Fujiwara palace site near Kashihara, crossing the whole of Kyoto and then the border into Nara.

In Arashiyama itself, the main street is lined with cafes, sweet shops, and stands selling tofu, matcha ice cream and pickles. Petrol stations are on the main roads around the district, but within the tourist area, parking for bikes can be hard to find, so try the car parks at the edge. It is a ride best savoured slowly, with a good coffee, because the temple repays attention. Spring and autumn are the most beautiful seasons, but also the busiest, while winter brings a rare quiet and the occasional dusting of snow.
t.historic monuments of ancient kyoto@35.0:
Kyoto sits in a basin with mountains on three sides, a grid of streets laid out in the late eighth century on the model of the Chinese capital, and it remained the imperial seat until 1868. That long continuity explains why the World Heritage list includes seventeen separate places under the name of the historic monuments of ancient Kyoto: temples, shrines and one castle, dotted around the city and across the border into Otsu. The city was spared the worst of the bombing in the Second World War, which is a large part of why so much survives.

For a rider, the city is easier than its reputation suggests, if you leave your expectations at the edge. The grid helps, the avenues run straight, and the big roads around the outer ring let you cross town fast. But the central streets are narrow, one-way and crowded with bicycles, taxis and buses, and parking for motorbikes is limited. A good plan is to leave the machine at the hotel and walk, or to find a dedicated bike park and base yourself there. In the evening, the lanes of Gion and Pontocho glow with paper lanterns, and the smell of grilled fish and charcoal drifts through the alleys.

The ride that begins in Kyoto heads for Yakushi-ji in Nara, an old Buddhist temple founded at the end of the seventh century whose twin pagodas hold some of the finest early architecture in Japan. The route takes you south through the Uji district, where the best Japanese green tea is grown and where you can find a cup of matcha served alongside sweet bean paste in an old tea house. It is also the home of Byodo-in, the Phoenix Hall, an eleventh-century building familiar from the ten-yen coin. From there you follow the Kizu river valley and cross low hills into the Nara basin, a quiet and mildly rolling ride past rice fields, tea terraces and bamboo thickets.

You can fuel in nearly any part of the city, but the busiest areas near Kyoto Station or Gion have fewer stations than the outer districts, so top up when you see one. Food is an art here: tofu cooked in a dozen ways, vegetables pickled in rice bran, and the multi-course meals known as kaiseki. In the hot, damp summer, a cold bowl of noodles by the river is just the thing, and in winter the hills are clean and cold, with bare maples against a pale sky.
t.saiho ji@35.0,135.7:
Saiho-ji has a nickname that tells the whole story: Kokedera, the moss temple. The garden is carpeted by well over a hundred varieties of moss, in shades from emerald to near yellow, spreading between the trees and around the pond in a soft, damp quilt, and a day of rain makes it glow. The effect is accidental in origin, since the moss spread after the temple was neglected in the nineteenth century, but it fits the garden's older bones, which were laid out in the fourteenth century by the Zen master Muso Soseki.
