From the N7, the road runs west across the flat, gravelly plain of Namaqualand, with horizons that go on forever, past small farms and the occasional donkey cart, and in spring the verges may be covered in daisies. There is almost no traffic, so you can settle into a rhythm, though wind and blowing sand can be a nuisance, and a cold sea mist can drop the temperature by ten degrees within minutes. Dress in layers, and keep your visor clean.

Beyond town, roads continue north toward the Richtersveld, a wild landscape of rock and succulents that is part of a transfrontier park, mostly on gravel tracks that need preparation and a capable bike. Port Nolloth has fuel, a couple of guesthouses and restaurants serving fresh fish and crayfish, and a hardware shop, but the nearest large town is far off, so fill up at every chance and carry water. The sunsets over the cold, grey ocean are memorable, and the smell of kelp and salt stays with you.
t.helmeringhausen@-25.9,16.8:
Helmeringhausen is hardly a village at all: a hotel, a farm, a few outbuildings and a lot of sky, set on the gravel road that runs along the edge of the Namib in southern Namibia. It was founded as a farm in the early twentieth century by German settlers who named it after their home village in Germany, and it has changed little since. A small farm museum beside the hotel displays old wagons, ploughs and household objects, giving a picture of what life was like for early settlers in this dry land.

The area is rugged and full of distances. Red dunes and open plains give way to rocky hills and the occasional stand of quiver trees, strange aloes that look like something drawn by Dr Seuss. Not far away stands Duwisib Castle, a fortress-like mansion built in 1909 by a German officer, Hansheinrich von Wolf, with stones hauled from far off and furnishings brought by ox wagon, and now a quirky museum in the middle of nowhere. Distances here are larger than they look on the map, and a stop at the hotel for a cold drink and a slice of cake can be a lifeline.

The D707 is one of the great gravel roads of Namibia, running through a country of grassy plains, rocky outcrops and dune fields at the foot of the Namib-Naukluft. Surfaces are generally graded but can be corrugated or sandy, and loose gravel on bends requires a steady hand. Wildlife is plentiful, with oryx, springbok and ostrich often seen near the road. Sunrise and sunset paint the landscape in warm tones, and the wind can be strong in the afternoon.

Fuel is the thing to plan. There may be a pump at Helmeringhausen, but supplies in remote places are not guaranteed, so do not rely on it, and carry enough to reach the next sure stop. Aus, a long way south, and Solitaire, to the north, are the places with regular supplies. The hotel has a restaurant, bar and basic rooms, as well as a campsite, and it is a popular overnight stop for travellers on the route. Book in advance in the busy season, bring water, and keep a spare tube and tools.
t.aus namibia@-26.7,16.3:
Aus is a village in the stony hills of southern Namibia, at about 1,400 metres, and its job is to watch over the road to the coast. Beyond it, the land drops toward the Atlantic and the old diamond town of Lüderitz, and the desert grows harsher with every kilometre. In the First World War, the South African forces who took the colony from Germany built an internment camp here, where thousands of German prisoners were held, and traces of the camp, including stone foundations, can still be seen among the rocks on the hillside.

The surprise lies a short way west, near the railway halt of Garub: a herd of wild desert horses that live in the Namib without any permanent water other than a trough pumped for them. How they got here is debated, with stories that they descended from horses abandoned by German cavalry or from a farm stud, but they have survived on sparse grass in this dry country for a century. A viewing platform near the trough lets you watch them drink, especially in the morning and evening.

Riding in the region is a pleasure for those who like open space. The B4 highway runs from Aus to Lüderitz in a long, gently dipping line across plains of stone and sand, with ghostly dunes drifting over the road in places, and the wind can blow hard, sometimes carrying sand across the tarmac. The D707 and other gravel roads lead north through the dramatic scenery of the Tsau Khaeb region. Nights are cold at this altitude, with frost in winter, while days can be hot, so layers are a good idea.

Aus has a petrol station, a couple of guesthouses and a small shop, and it is the last reliable stop before the coast, so fill the tank and your water bottles before heading west. Lüderitz, about a hundred and twenty kilometres away, is a quirky town of colonial architecture and cold sea breezes, and Kolmanskop, a ghost town buried in sand, lies on the way. Obey the signs in the diamond restricted area, and do not leave the road. The stars here are superb, and a night in Aus is a good place to see them.
t.fish river canyon@-27.6,17.6:
The Fish River Canyon is one of those places where the map and the eye disagree. On paper it is a crack in the far south of Namibia, in the Karas region, a long way from anything. In person the ground simply stops, and a gorge on the order of 160 kilometres long and well over 500 metres deep drops away in a series of giant hairpin bends carved by a river that only runs properly after the summer rains. It is regularly named as the second-largest canyon on earth, which is a claim worth a shrug, because standing at the rim you are not comparing it with anything.

Getting there is half the point. You come in on gravel, mostly graded and fast enough, across a flat and stony plain of dry grass, dolerite boulders and the odd quiver tree, with the horizon so far off that a bakkie's dust plume is visible for ten minutes before it reaches you. Corrugations are the real enemy. Let some air out, keep your speed honest, and give oncoming trucks the whole road, because they will not give you any of it. Wind can be fierce on the plateau and sand blows across the track in thin snakes.

Time your arrival for the end of the day. The rock turns from grey to rust to something close to purple, and the baboons and rock hyrax come out of the cracks as the heat drops. Midday is harsh, flat and hot enough to make the viewpoints a quick-look affair. The Nama people lived and grazed this country long before German colonial maps put names on it, and the canyon's famous five-day hiking trail is closed through the hottest months, for good reason.

Practicalities are thin, so plan them. Fill up before you leave the tar, in towns such as Keetmanshoop or Grünau, and carry water. Camping and basic accommodation exist near the canyon, and the hot springs at Ai-Ais lie further south at the end of the gorge, a lovely place to soak sore shoulders if you have time. Without a spare tyre and a patched-up sense of patience this is a bad road to ride; with both, it is one of the best silences in Africa.
t.kameoka food@35.0,135.6:
Kameoka is a city in the hills west of Kyoto, in the basin where the Hozu river leaves its mountain gorge and spreads out into the plain. Most visitors know it only as the place where the river boats start, wooden flat-bottomed craft that carry passengers down the Hozu gorge to Arashiyama, steered by boatmen with long poles, and a ride in one is still among the pleasures of the Kyoto area. With about ninety-seven thousand people, it is larger than it first seems, and it makes a very practical place to eat.

History has a dramatic cameo here. Kameyama castle, now long gone, was the base of Akechi Mitsuhide, the general who in 1582 marched his army out of Kameoka toward Kyoto and turned on his lord, Oda Nobunaga, at Honno-ji temple. The remains of the castle site lie within the grounds of a religious organisation, and the memory of the betrayal still colours the town's story. The surrounding hills are quiet, with bamboo and cedar and terraced fields.

For a rider, Kameoka is the gateway to some of the best country roads in the Kyoto region. Heading north-west, the road climbs through forested hills to the thatched-roof villages of Miyama, and west toward the wooded valleys of Tamba, with mostly good surfaces, medium bends and few cars. Along the way there are small farm shops, tea houses and noodle restaurants. The rainy season, in June and early July, brings humidity and mist, summer is hot, and the best months are April, May, October and November, with cherry blossom in spring and autumn leaves in the hills.

As a food stop, the city has a good range: noodle shops, family restaurants, bakeries, convenience stores that are better than they have any right to be, and local specialities such as Tamba chestnuts, black beans and sweet potatoes, depending on the season. Fuel stations are easy to find, and the town centre is compact. Parking is straightforward, with free bike spaces at some restaurants. Have a hot bowl of something, and refill the tank before the hills, where stations are sparser and close early.
t.fuji@35.2,138.7:
Fuji is the city at the foot of the mountain, and the mountain dominates everything. On a clear winter morning, the great snow-capped cone rises straight up behind factory chimneys, rooftops and rice fields, so close and so huge that it seems painted on the sky. The city itself spreads across the coastal plain on Suruga Bay, where the fast, wide Fuji River meets the sea, and it is an industrial place, long known for its paper mills fed by the abundant water that flows from the mountain.

The water is the key to the region. Snow and rain soak into the porous volcanic rock of Mount Fuji and re-emerge years later as cold, clear springs that feed the rivers and the factories. Next door, in Fujinomiya, the Fujisan Hongū Sengen Taisha, the head shrine of the mountain's sacred tradition, sits beside a spring pool that fills with this water, and pilgrims once began their climb there. Fujinomiya is also famous for its own chewy style of yakisoba, and the fishing port at Tagonoura is known for shirasu, tiny whitebait served raw or boiled over rice.

The riding begins once you leave the plain. Route 139 climbs north from Fujinomiya across the Asagiri plateau, through dairy farms and grasslands with the mountain looming over them, past the Shiraito Falls, where water pours from the rock in a curtain of white threads. The road continues to Lake Motosu and the Fuji Five Lakes, where routes around the lakes lead to the Misaka Pass and the view-filled roads above Lake Yamanaka. The climb is gentle and well surfaced, with long sweepers and good sightlines.

Timing is everything for the view. Fuji is often hidden in cloud or haze, especially in summer, and the best chances are in the early morning and from late autumn to early spring, when the air is cold and clear. Winter brings frost and occasional snow on higher roads, so check conditions. The coastal plain is busy with lorries, and the Tomei and Shin-Tomei expressways run through the city, convenient but tolled.

Fuji has fuel, convenience stores and restaurants everywhere, though petrol stations in the mountains are fewer and some close early in the evening, so fill up in the city before you climb. Remember that Japan drives on the left, and that the mountain roads can be busy with tourists on weekends and holidays.
t.near kokubunji@35.7,139.5:
Western Tokyo does not look like much from the train, a continuous sprawl of houses and stations, but walk a little and the old landscape shows through. Springs emerge at its foot, feeding small streams like the Nogawa, and some of the paths along them feel almost rural, with bamboo groves, old trees and the sound of running water.

History runs deep here. In the eighth century, Emperor Shōmu ordered a provincial temple, a kokubun-ji, to be built in every province of Japan, and the one for Musashi province stood here, giving the area its name. The foundations of the great temple can still be seen in a park, and a smaller temple continues the tradition nearby. A spring-fed path known as Otakanomichi, meaning the falcon's road because the shoguns once hunted here, leads past a pond and through gardens.

Koganei Park is one of Tokyo's largest, famous for its cherry blossoms in spring and home to the Edo-Tokyo Open Air Architectural Museum, a collection of historic buildings moved from across the city, including farmhouses, shops and a bathhouse. It offers a rare glimpse of the Tokyo that has largely disappeared.

The riding starts once you escape the city. The Okutama ride follows the Tama River west past Ōme into the mountains, where the road winds along gorges to Lake Okutama, a reservoir surrounded by forested peaks. The Myōgi, Karuizawa and Haruna rides go northwest into Gunma, with Mount Myōgi's jagged rocks, the highland resort of Karuizawa and the hairpins up Mount Haruna, made famous by the street-racing manga and anime Initial D. Expect traffic and lights through the suburbs, and use the tolled expressways if time is short.

Fuel, convenience stores and restaurants are everywhere in the area, from ramen shops to family restaurants near the stations. Riding in Tokyo means keeping left, watching for bicycles on the pavements and finding parking, which can be scarce and strictly enforced. In summer the heat and humidity are oppressive, and typhoons can bring heavy rain in late summer and autumn, so spring and late autumn are the most comfortable seasons for riding.
t.kawaguchi@35.8,139.7:
First, a confusion worth clearing up: this Kawaguchi is not the lake town at the foot of Mount Fuji, which is spelled Kawaguchiko and lies far to the west. This is Kawaguchi city in Saitama, a big, busy place of nearly half a million people just across the Arakawa river from northern Tokyo. On a ride to Shosenkyo and the Fuji lakes, it is where you leave the capital behind, or where you come back into it, and it is a sensible place to eat before or after.

Kawaguchi has an honest working past. For much of the twentieth century it was Japan's great cast-iron town, full of small foundries with tall cupola furnaces, and it was famous enough for a 1962 film, Foundry Town, starring the young Sayuri Yoshinaga, which showed the life of working families among the chimneys. Most of the foundries have gone, replaced by apartment towers, but the city still has a certain no-nonsense character. In the Angyo district, to the east, nurseries have grown garden trees and bonsai for centuries, supplying the gardens of Tokyo, and the area is still full of greenhouses and plant markets.

As a food stop, it offers everything Japanese towns do well: ramen shops with counters and ticket machines, family restaurants, gyudon chains, curry shops, and convenience stores where you can grab onigiri, cold tea and coffee in a can. Look for places near the stations, especially Kawaguchi station, where there is a lot of choice. Parking for motorcycles can be tricky in central areas, so look for designated bike parking rather than leaving it on the pavement.

The riding here is urban and slow. Traffic in Saitama is heavy, with lots of lights, trucks and delivery scooters, and the main roads, like Route 122, are wide but crowded. The Shuto expressway and the Tokyo Gaikan ring road cross the area and are quicker, though they charge tolls and have rules for two-up riding. Once you head west towards the mountains, things change completely, and the roads into Yamanashi climb through forests and valleys toward the granite cliffs of Shosenkyo and the lakes under Fuji.

Fuel is easy to find, and many stations in Japan are staffed and will fill the tank for you. A good meal and a full tank here, and you are set for the long day west.
t.near tanashicho@35.8,139.6:
The western suburbs of Tokyo go on and on, and Nishitokyo, Kiyose and the old town of Tanashi sit in the middle of them: a quiet, flat, residential belt of low houses, apartment blocks, train stations and shopping streets, about twenty kilometres from the centre. Nishitokyo was formed in 2001 when Tanashi and Hoya merged, and its tallest landmark is a slim tower that carries broadcasting and observation equipment, visible from far away.

Kiyose, just to the north, has an unusual history. In the early twentieth century its clean air and woods made it a centre for tuberculosis sanatoria, and the town became one of Japan's main hospital areas. Many medical institutions remain today, and the woods that once healed the sick still survive in patches, along with the Yanase river valley, where you can walk along the water among fields and groves. Elsewhere, the suburbs are a mix of new houses and old farm plots, where vegetables are still grown in small fields between homes.

It is a logical end to a Tanzawa and Doshi Road day. The Doshi Road, Route 413, runs from Sagamihara through a beautiful forested valley to Lake Yamanaka at the foot of Mount Fuji, with river crossings, tight curves and steep climbs, and it is a favourite with Tokyo riders, though it gets crowded at weekends and police are often present. The ride back usually comes in on the Chuo expressway or along the roads through Hachioji and Tachikawa, and then into the long suburbs. Expect heavy traffic, lots of lights, and slow progress in the late afternoon.

There are plenty of convenience stores, family restaurants, ramen shops and fuel stations around, and many train lines into central Tokyo, which helps if someone is collecting you. It is not a beautiful place, but it is calm, safe and practical, and after a long day in the mountains, a hot bath at a local sento, the public bath that many Tokyo neighbourhoods still have, may be the best end you could wish for.
t.miura@35.1,139.6:
At the very tip of the Miura Peninsula, south of Yokosuka, the land ends in low cliffs, rocky shelves, cabbage fields and a fishing harbour that has supplied Tokyo with tuna for generations. Misaki port is the heart of Miura, and that is where you go to eat. The city has around fifty thousand people, but it feels like a coastal country town, with the sea always close and the smell of salt and fish on the wind.

Misaki maguro is the dish. The harbour is lined with restaurants serving tuna in every form, raw on rice in a big bowl, grilled, fried, as sashimi or as rich slices of fatty toro, and the long queues at lunchtime on weekends tell you how famous it is. Miura is also known for its vegetables, especially its big white radishes, the daikon, and its cabbages, grown in fields that stretch right to the edge of the cliffs, with the sea glittering behind them. In winter you will see daikon hanging to dry on frames by farmhouses.

Just across a bridge from the harbour lies Jogashima, a small island with a lighthouse, a park and rocky shores carved into strange shapes by the waves. The walk along the southern cliffs is lovely, with views across the mouth of Tokyo Bay to the Boso peninsula and, on clear days, Mount Fuji to the west and the island of Oshima to the south. Kites, hawks and cormorants ride the wind. The poet Hakushu Kitahara lived here and wrote a famous song about the rain on Jogashima, and there is a monument to him on the island.

The ride down the peninsula follows Route 134 and the coast roads past Hayama, where the imperial family has a seaside villa, and then through hills, tunnels and farmland. Expect traffic on weekends, especially in summer, when beaches like Miura Kaigan fill with Tokyo families. Early morning is the best time, when the light is soft and the roads are quiet, and the wind off the sea can be strong in winter and spring.

Fuel, convenience stores and food are easy to find in Miura and in Yokosuka on the way back. If you only do one thing here, eat a tuna bowl by the harbour, then sit on the rocks on Jogashima and watch the waves come in from the Pacific.
t.nagatoro@36.1,139.1:
Nagatoro is a small town in the hills of western Saitama where the Arakawa river squeezes through a gorge of layered grey-green rock, and that rock is the reason the place is famous. Along the riverbank lies the Iwadatami, a broad flat terrace of crystalline schist, worn smooth by the water and split into slabs like stepping stones, and it is a national natural monument. Japanese geologists have studied it since the late nineteenth century, and Nagatoro calls itself the birthplace of Japanese geology, with the Saitama Museum of Natural History right in town.

The river is the show. Flat-bottomed wooden boats, steered by boatmen with long poles, carry visitors down the rapids between the rock walls, and in summer there is rafting and canoeing. The water is clear and green, and on hot days families sit on the rocks with their feet in it. In autumn, the maples along the gorge turn red, and in spring cherry blossoms line the river and the road. Above the town, a ropeway climbs Mount Hodo, where wintersweet flowers bloom in January and February, and the Hodosan shrine sits among old trees at its foot.

As a food stop, Nagatoro and the Chichibu area have their own specialities. Kakigori, shaved ice, is a summer ritual here, made from natural ice harvested in winter from ponds in the mountains, light and fluffy and topped with syrups. Chichibu is also known for miso potatoes, fried and coated in sweet miso sauce, and for waraji katsu, huge breaded pork cutlets shaped like straw sandals. Soba noodles made from local buckwheat are another good choice, cold on a hot day or hot in winter.

The riding to and from Nagatoro is a pleasure. Route 140 follows the Arakawa valley from Yorii, with gentle bends, good surfaces and views of the river, and the roads up into the Chichibu mountains climb through forests to passes and lookout points, with tight corners and very little traffic on weekdays. Chichibu Muse Park, on a ridge above the city of Chichibu, has wide views over the basin and the mountains. On weekends, the main roads can be busy with day-trippers from Tokyo.

Nagatoro has fuel, convenience stores and many small restaurants and cafés along the main street near the station. Arrive early, before the tour buses, and watch the boats glide through the gorge in the morning light.
t.near medora@47.0,-103.5:
The badlands of western North Dakota are where a young Theodore Roosevelt came to recover from grief, and where, he later said, he became the man who could be president. In 1884, after his wife and mother died on the same day, he retreated to his ranches in these rugged hills along the Little Missouri River and spent several years living the life of a cattle rancher.

Roosevelt's Maltese Cross Cabin, which he lived in during his first years in the badlands, has been moved to the visitor centre in Medora, and you can walk through its small rooms. The site of his second home, the Elkhorn Ranch, is further north and much harder to reach. Medora itself is a tiny town of old wooden buildings, revived as a tourist destination, with a summer musical show in an outdoor amphitheatre.

The South Unit scenic loop is one of the best wildlife rides in the West. Bison wander across the road, wild horses graze on the plateaus, and prairie dog towns spread across the flats, with their residents barking at passing traffic. Elk, pronghorn and mule deer are also common. The bison are huge and unpredictable, and you should keep a respectful distance and never approach them, especially on a motorcycle.

The road itself is narrow and winding, with steep gradients and sharp curves, and it climbs to several viewpoints with sweeping views over the badlands. Parts of the loop have been closed in recent years because of landslides and road damage, so check the current situation before you set out. The Painted Canyon Overlook, just off Interstate 94 to the east, offers a stunning view over the colourful badlands.

Medora has fuel, food and lodging in summer, but services are limited in winter. Belfield, about twenty-five kilometres to the east, and Beach, about forty kilometres to the west, have basic services. The nearest larger town is Dickinson, about sixty kilometres east. Early morning and late evening are the hours to be here, when the wildlife is most active and the light is warm.
t.imaichi@36.7,139.7:
Imaichi is the low-key gateway to Nikkō, a town on the plain where three old roads meet before the mountains begin. Officially it has been part of Nikkō city since a municipal merger in the 2000s, but locally it keeps its own name and character: a railway town, a market town, lots of ordinary streets and convenience stores, with the Nikkō mountains rising to the north-west and the Kinugawa river running nearby. For riders heading to the Irohazaka hairpins, it is where you sort out fuel, lunch and the last coffee before the climb.

The great sight here is the Nikkō cedar avenue. In the seventeenth century a feudal lord planted Japanese cedars along the roads converging on Nikkō, reportedly as an offering to the shrine of Tokugawa Ieyasu, because he could not afford a grander gift such as the stone lanterns offered by other lords. Some twelve thousand trees still survive along roughly thirty-five kilometres of road, many of them enormous, and the avenue is listed as the longest tree-lined road in the world. Riding beneath them is a strange, cool experience, the light dimmed and the air smelling of resin and damp bark, even on a hot day.

Steam trains run on a line out of Imaichi towards Kinugawa Onsen, and on weekends you can see the old locomotive puffing past the rice fields. The area is also known for its water: springs from the Nikkō mountains feed sake breweries and soba shops, and yuba, the delicate skin skimmed from soy milk, is a regional speciality you will find on menus all around Nikkō.

The riding beyond is the main event. From Nikkō the road climbs steeply along the river, and the Irohazaka is actually two one-way roads, one up and one down, with forty-eight hairpins between them, one for each syllable of the old Japanese iroha poem. At the top is Lake Chūzenji and the Kegon Falls. In autumn the maples make the climb famous and the traffic dreadful, so go early on a weekday. Expect speed limits that feel very low, polite but strict policing, and drivers who stop to admire the view in surprising places. Imaichi is the place to fill up, because services thin out on the way up and become tourist-priced at the lake.
t.near hakone@35.2,139.0:
The southern end of Lake Ashi lies in the bowl of the Hakone volcano, a caldera ringed by grassy ridges, and the roads that run around its rim are some of the most ridden in Japan. Hakone town itself is a scattered place of hot-spring inns, shrines and lakeside piers, and on clear days, which come mostly in winter and early spring, Mount Fuji stands over the far end of the lake, perfectly symmetrical and white-topped. The rest of the year it hides in haze and cloud more often than the posters admit.

History left a clear mark here. The old Tōkaidō highway between Edo and Kyoto crossed these mountains, and the Tokugawa shogunate placed a checkpoint on the lakeshore at Hakone to control traffic, especially women leaving Edo and guns coming in. The checkpoint has been reconstructed and you can walk through it, and nearby sections of the old road are still paved with uneven stones beneath tall cedars. Across the lake, the red torii gate of Hakone Shrine stands in the water and draws a queue of photographers all day.

The volcano is still alive. At Ōwakudani steam and sulphur pour out of a raw yellow slope, and eggs boiled in the hot springs turn black and are sold by the bag with the promise that each adds seven years to your life. Activity there sometimes closes the area for safety, so check before you count on it. The hot springs are the other reason people come: onsen baths in Hakone are a long tradition, and a soak after a cold ride is about as good as it gets.

For riding, the Hakone Skyline runs along the western ridge with wide views and fast, open curves, while the Turnpike climbs from the Odawara side in long, steep sweeps. Both are toll roads. Fog can roll in from nowhere and reduce visibility to a few metres, and weekend traffic, including other riders and sports cars, can be heavy, so the best time is early on a weekday. Hakone has fuel, though prices are a little higher than on the coast, and Odawara has everything if you are low. Food is everywhere, from soba to elaborate inn dinners.
t.near odawara@35.2,139.1:
Odawara is where Sagami Bay meets the mountains, a city on the coast at the foot of the Hakone range, and for most riders heading up to the Turnpike it is the jumping-off point: a big station town with fuel on every arterial road, fish restaurants near the harbour and the last flat kilometres before the climb. The Hayakawa river runs out of the mountains here, and on its southern side the road begins to rise almost immediately.

The town's centrepiece is Odawara Castle, home of the Later Hōjō clan, who ruled much of the Kantō region from here in the sixteenth century. In 1590 Toyotomi Hideyoshi besieged the castle with an enormous army, built a fortress on a hill overlooking it, and starved the Hōjō into surrender, completing his unification of Japan. The present keep is a modern reconstruction, but the moat, the walls and the cherry trees in spring make it a good place to walk for an hour, and the view from the top takes in the bay and the coast towards the Izu Peninsula.

Odawara is also a food town. Kamaboko, the steamed fish cake that appears in so many Japanese dishes, has been made here for generations, and shops near the coast road sell it fresh, along with dried fish and pickled ume plums. The fishing port at Hayakawa has simple restaurants serving whatever came in that morning, often aji, horse mackerel, as sashimi or fried.

The Turnpike leaves from near Hayakawa and climbs for roughly fourteen kilometres to the ridge at Daikanzan, about a thousand metres up, in long, flowing curves through forest with a smooth, well-kept surface. It is a toll road, popular with motorcycle clubs and car enthusiasts, and on weekend mornings you will find a car park at the top full of machines and people talking about them. The views back over the bay are wonderful in clear weather, but fog often sits on the upper section, so ride to the conditions. Fill up in Odawara before you start, because the mountain roads have few stations and the ones in Hakone charge for the privilege.
t.near nonoichi@36.6,136.7:
Nonoichi is a quiet residential city on the flat plain just south of Kanazawa, the kind of place most visitors pass through without noticing. That is no criticism. It is a good place to start a ride towards the Noto Peninsula, with easy fuel, convenience stores and fast arterial roads, and Kanazawa is only a few kilometres away. The Tedori river comes down from the Hakusan mountains to the south and spreads its alluvial plain to the sea, and on a clear day the snow on Hakusan, one of Japan's three holy mountains, hangs over the rice fields.

Kanazawa is the reason to linger. It was the seat of the Maeda clan, the richest domain in Edo-period Japan after the shogun's own, and it was spared heavy bombing in the Second World War, so the old districts survive. Kenroku-en, laid out by the Maeda lords over generations, is counted among the three great gardens of Japan, and the Higashi Chaya district has wooden teahouses where geisha still perform. The city produces almost all of Japan's gold leaf, and you can buy ice cream with a sheet of it on top if you want to be silly about it.

The food is serious. Ōmichō market has fish from the Sea of Japan piled on ice, and in winter the snow crab season is a regional obsession. Kaga cooking, with dishes like jibuni, duck stewed with wheat gluten and vegetables, is quite different from Tokyo fare, and the sake from the Hakusan breweries is excellent.

The ride north to Noto runs along the coast, flat at first and then rolling, and one stretch, the Chirihama beach driveway, lets you ride along firm sand at the water's edge. A word of caution: the Noto Peninsula was struck by a severe earthquake on New Year's Day 2024, with heavy damage to towns and roads, and repairs have taken a long time, so check current conditions and closures before planning the full loop. Nonoichi itself is calm and practical, with plenty of fuel and food, and the weather on this coast can turn quickly, with grey skies and rain coming off the sea even in summer.
t.near kawasaki@35.6,139.6:
It is not a famous place, but it is a sensible base for rides south-west to the Izu Peninsula, because it lies on the right side of the metropolis.

Kawasaki is mostly an industrial city, stretching from the factories and refineries of Tokyo Bay up to these quieter, greener hills in the west. Here, in Tama Ward, the Fujiko F. Fujio Museum celebrates the creator of Doraemon, the robot cat beloved by generations of Japanese children, and the Ikuta Ryokuchi park has a museum of traditional farmhouses moved from all over Japan, a peaceful place to walk among thatched roofs and old trees.

Riding in Japan requires some adjustments. Traffic drives on the left, roads are generally well maintained and drivers are disciplined, but speed limits are low and enforcement is strict. Larger motorcycles can use the expressways, which are tolled and can be expensive, but the network is efficient. The route to Izu typically follows the Tōmei Expressway or the national roads towards Odawara, and from there into the hills of the Izu Peninsula. The Izu Skyline, a toll road along the volcanic ridge of the peninsula, offers fast, flowing curves and views of Mount Fuji on clear days.

Convenience stores are everywhere, and they are a lifeline for riders, with food, drinks, toilets and sometimes parking for motorcycles. Fuel stations are plentiful, though many close at night in rural areas, and some are full-service, with attendants who will fill your tank. Tokyo traffic can be heavy, so leave early, especially at weekends, when many people head out of the city. The best seasons for riding are spring and autumn; summer is hot and humid, and the rainy season in June and July brings frequent downpours.
t.izu@35.0,138.9:
Shuzenji, the heart of the city of Izu, is one of the oldest hot spring towns in Japan. According to tradition, the great monk Kūkai founded the temple here in the early ninth century and struck a rock in the river with his iron staff, releasing a spring of healing water; a small bath on a rock in the middle of the stream, the Tokko-no-yu, marks the spot. The town has a more sombre history too: in 1204, the second shogun of the Kamakura shogunate, Minamoto no Yoriie, was exiled here and murdered.

Today Shuzenji is a quiet, atmospheric place, with traditional inns along the Katsura River, red bridges, a bamboo forest path and the old temple. A short walk around the town is a peaceful break from the road, and if you have time, a long bath in a hot spring is the classic Japanese way to recover from a day in the saddle.

The roads around Izu are some of the best in the Kanto region. To the south, the road climbs over the Amagi Pass, through dense forests of cedar and beech, and descends towards Kawazu via the Kawazu-Nanadaru Loop Bridge, a double spiral that carries the road down a steep valley. The route was made famous by Yasunari Kawabata's story The Izu Dancer, about a student walking over the pass. To the west, the Nishi-Izu coast road follows the rugged western shore of the peninsula, with cliffs, coves and fishing villages, and on clear evenings the sunset over Suruga Bay, with Mount Fuji rising across the water, is spectacular.

The Amagi area is famous for wasabi, grown in terraced beds fed by cold mountain streams, and a bowl of soba with freshly grated wasabi is a local treat. Fuel and convenience stores are available in Shuzenji and the surrounding towns, but they become scarcer in the mountains and along the west coast, so fill up before setting out. The roads can be narrow and twisty, with tight bends, and they are popular with motorcyclists on weekends.
t.wako@35.8,139.6:
Honda's engineers have tested ideas in Wako for decades; the company's research and development arm grew up here, and the name still turns up on buildings around town. So does RIKEN, Japan's largest research institute, whose headquarters and laboratories occupy a large campus in the city. For a rider ending a long weekend, there is a pleasing symmetry in finishing a ride where so many motorcycles were born on drawing boards.

Wako lies on the north-western edge of Tokyo, just across the boundary in Saitama, where the Arakawa river and the big expressways meet. It is a residential city of apartment blocks, schools and parks, with a small-town feel despite its size. The Arakawa riverbanks, broad and grassy, are popular with joggers, cyclists and baseball teams, and on a clear day you can see Mount Fuji from the levee.

Coming back from the north, the Kan-Etsu expressway and the Gaikan ring road deliver you to Wako, and the final stretch is a short ride through local streets. Traffic can be heavy, especially on Sunday evenings, when the expressways fill with people returning from weekends in the mountains.

Around the station, counters serve ramen, curry and set meals until late, and that is the right way to close a weekend that began on the Bandai Azuma Skyline: elbows on the counter, helmet on the next stool, steam on your glasses.
t.near kumagaya on the way back@36.1,139.4:
In July 2018 Kumagaya recorded 41.1 degrees Celsius, then the highest temperature ever measured in Japan, and the city wears the title of hottest town with something like pride. Banners proclaim it, shops sell heat-themed souvenirs, and in summer the town fills with misting stations. If you are riding through in July or August, take the heat seriously: drink constantly and avoid the middle of the day.

Kumagaya lies on the north bank of the Arakawa, in the flat plain of northern Saitama. In spring the river embankment is lined with cherry trees, and the town fills with people picnicking under the blossoms. The Uchiwa Matsuri, a big summer festival in July, features floats, drums and crowds.

There is no good swimming nearby. The Arakawa is a broad river with strong currents and a stony bed, and while people paddle at the edge in summer, it is not safe for swimming. The town has public pools, which are a better option on a hot day.

Gyōda, a little to the east, has one of Japan's most important groups of ancient burial mounds, the Sakitama Kofun, with large keyhole-shaped tombs from the fifth and sixth centuries. An iron sword found in one of them bears an inscription in gold that is one of the oldest written texts in Japan. Gyōda also has the reconstructed Oshi castle, which held out against a siege in 1590.

The riding is flat and straight, with busy national roads and heavy truck traffic. Route 140 heads west towards Chichibu and the mountains, where the riding becomes much more interesting. Shaved ice has become the town's edible answer to its own climate, and in August there is no more sensible purchase. Pumps and konbini are everywhere along the main roads.
t.yugawara@35.2,139.1:
Yugawara has been soaking tired bodies for well over a thousand years. The hot springs appear in the Man'yōshū, Japan's oldest poetry anthology, and a local legend says that a tanuki, the mischievous raccoon dog of Japanese folklore, was found bathing in the spring to heal its wounds. The town sits where a short, steep valley opens onto Sagami Bay, at the border of Kanagawa and Shizuoka, between Odawara and Atami.

For riders the main attraction is the Tsubaki Line, the prefectural road that climbs from the town to the Hakone pass. It is a famous motorcycle road, with tight bends, steep gradients and views over the bay as you climb. Surfaces are mostly sound, but the road can be busy on weekends, and police are often present. In foggy or wet weather it can be treacherous, as the upper sections are often wrapped in cloud.

The town itself is a quiet onsen resort, with old inns, public baths and a river running through the valley. Many writers stayed here in the twentieth century, drawn by the hot springs and the mild climate. The plum grove at Makuyama park, above the town, blooms in February and early March, a sea of white and pink with the bay below.

As a base it is hard to beat. The coastal road has fuel and konbini, the inns and small restaurants serve fish landed in the bay, and mandarin orchards climb the terraces behind the houses. Several public baths take day visitors, and twenty minutes in hot mineral water undoes a day of hairpins better than any stretching routine.
t.near tokyo@35.7,139.8:
When the poet Bashō set out in 1689 on the journey that became The Narrow Road to the Deep North, he left from Senju, on the Sumida river, where friends saw him off. This finish lies in that same old northern edge of Edo, in Arakawa ward, a neighbourhood of narrow streets, small workshops and wooden houses that still feels more like shitamachi, the old downtown, than the glassy Tokyo of Shinjuku and Roppongi.

The Toden Arakawa line, Tokyo's last surviving streetcar, rattles through the district, and in spring the roses planted along its tracks bloom in great banks of colour. Minowa, at one end, is close to the old Yoshiwara pleasure quarter, and temples in the area tell stories of the city's past, from the Edo period to the fire-bombing of 1945.

Coming back into Tokyo after a day in the Gunma mountains, the final stretch is a test of patience. The expressways are often congested, and the surface streets are a maze of traffic lights, narrow lanes and pedestrians. If you filter, do it gently; cyclists, delivery scooters and pedestrians appear from every side street.

Arakawa ward has convenience stores, small restaurants and izakaya on every corner. The local food is simple and hearty: monjayaki, a runny cousin of okonomiyaki, belongs to the old east side, and the counters near Minowa and Minami-Senju grill skewers late into the night. A beer there, among locals who have never been near Gunma, is a fine way to let the mountains go.
t.kimitsu@35.4,139.9:
Kimitsu runs from the industrial shore of Tokyo Bay deep into the forested hills of the inner Boso peninsula, and the contrast is striking. On the coast, the Nippon Steel works stretches for kilometres, a tangle of furnaces, chimneys and cranes. Inland, within half an hour, you are among steep green hills, narrow valleys and reservoirs, with hardly a building in sight.

The scenic heart of the area is Kanōzan, a low mountain with an old temple at the top and a viewpoint over the Kujūkutani, the ninety-nine valleys. On autumn and winter mornings, mist often fills the valleys below, creating a sea of clouds with the ridges rising like islands. It is a famous sight, and photographers gather at dawn to capture it.

The Kameyama dam lake, further south, is a long, winding reservoir surrounded by forests, and in late November the autumn leaves turn the slopes red and gold. The roads around the lake are narrow and twisty, with little traffic and fine views.

For riders, the inner Boso offers a network of quiet roads with tight bends, steep climbs and tunnels. The tarmac is decent on the whole, though leaves, moss and fallen branches can make the roads slippery, especially in autumn and after rain. Watch out for deer and monkeys, which are common in the forests.

The Aqua-Line, the tunnel and bridge across Tokyo Bay from Kawasaki, lands in nearby Kisarazu, making the area easily accessible from Tokyo. Do your shopping on the coast. The hills are thinly populated, and the stations that do exist inland keep short hours, so leave the bay side with a full tank.
t.near ishige on the way back@36.1,139.9:
The Kinugawa river looks placid enough as it slides through the rice fields of south-western Ibaraki, but in September 2015, swollen by days of torrential rain, it breached its levee at Jōsō and flooded a vast area of the plain, forcing thousands to flee and leaving towns under water for days. Driving the levee road today, high above the fields, you can see how flat and vulnerable the land is.

This stop sits near Ishige, on the plain between the Kinugawa and the Kokai rivers, a landscape of rice paddies, vegetable fields and farmhouses. Mount Tsukuba, with its twin peaks, rises to the north-east, the only high ground in sight, and on clear days it dominates the horizon.

History runs deep here. In the tenth century, Taira no Masakado, a provincial warlord, rebelled against the imperial court and declared himself the new emperor from a base in this area. His rebellion was crushed and he was killed in battle, but he became a legend, and shrines dedicated to him are scattered across the region. His head is said to have flown back to Tokyo, where a shrine still marks the spot.

There is no swimming here: the rivers are wide, fast and muddy, and the levees are steep. The best you can do is sit on the embankment and watch the herons in the fields.

The riding is flat and straight, with long views across the paddies. Watch out for farm vehicles, narrow lanes and sudden junctions. Ishige, a few minutes away, has the pumps, konbini and family restaurants you need, and on a hot day a tray of cold soba with dipping sauce is the lunch Japan invented for exactly this weather.
t.near annaka on the way back@36.3,138.9:
South-west of Takasaki the Kantō plain runs out and the mountains begin, and this stop lies right on that edge, between Annaka and Tomioka. Look west and the strangest skyline in Gunma comes into view: Mount Myōgi, a crown of jagged volcanic spires that looks as if someone took a rasp to an ordinary mountain. It is one of the three famous peaks of the old Jōmō province, and the road that skirts its flanks is a favourite with local riders for its tight, wooded bends.

Tomioka gave Japan its modern silk industry. The silk mill, opened in 1872 with French machinery and French engineers, was the government's showpiece of industrialisation, and its long brick buildings, now a World Heritage site, still stand in the town centre. Silk once paid for much of Japan's modernisation, and mulberry fields covered these hills.

Annaka is the gateway to the old Usui pass towards Karuizawa. At Yokokawa, where the railway once needed extra locomotives to climb the gradient, a railway park preserves old engines, and further up the valley the four-arched brick bridge of Usui, the Megane-bashi, stands in the forest like a Roman aqueduct. Yokokawa station is also famous for its boxed lunch of rice and chicken served in a small clay pot, which travellers have been buying for generations.

For a swim, keep expectations modest. The Usui and Kabura rivers are rocky, fast and cold, good for cooling feet on a hot afternoon but not for real swimming. Gunma's summer heat is fierce, so the shade of the riverbanks may be the best you get.

Fuel is easy in Annaka, Tomioka and Takasaki, and convenience stores are everywhere on the main roads. The roads into the mountains, though, have long stretches with nothing, so leave the plain with a full tank.
t.near dvur kralove nad labem on the way b:
In 1817 a manuscript was found in the church tower of Dvůr Králové, a supposedly medieval collection of Czech epic poems that seemed to prove the antiquity of Czech literature. It became a national treasure, until scholars proved it a forgery decades later, sparking one of the great intellectual battles of the Czech national revival. The town, on the upper Elbe at the foot of the Krkonoše mountains, has never quite lived it down.

Today Dvůr Králové is better known for its safari park, known for its long record of breeding African species, and in particular for the northern white rhinos it once kept, now one of the rarest animals on earth.

Just upstream, the Les Království dam, built in the early twentieth century in an ornate style with towers and statues, holds back a long reservoir in the forest. Swimming is possible in places, but check local rules.

Downstream, at Kuks, the baroque hospital founded by Count Sporck stands above the river, with a famous gallery of statues of the Virtues and Vices by Matthias Braun. It is one of the finest baroque complexes in central Europe.

North of the river the roads climb into the Krkonoše foothills, narrow and bumpy, through villages of timbered cottages with the ridge of Sněžka, the highest Czech summit, showing on clear days. Dvůr Králové handles fuel and a meal easily. Ask for whatever the nearest brewery makes; in this part of Bohemia, there is almost always one within ten kilometres.
t.near chofu@35.6,139.5:
Studio Ghibli's Pom Poko tells the story of raccoon dogs fighting the bulldozers that turned the Tama hills into a new town in the 1960s and 1970s, and this finish lies right in that landscape, between Inagi, Chōfu and Tama. The hills are now covered with apartment blocks, roads and shopping centres, but pockets of woodland and farmland survive, and the Tama River runs through the valley below.

Inagi is known for its pears, grown in orchards on the slopes, and in late summer the farm stands sell them fresh. Chōfu, to the north, has Jindai-ji, an old temple surrounded by soba shops, where buckwheat noodles have been made from spring water for centuries. The botanical garden next to the temple is a fine place for a stroll, with roses in spring and autumn.

The Tama River is a broad, gravelly river with wide banks used for sports, picnics and walking. On summer evenings, families gather by the water, and the river is a cool, open space in the crowded city.

Coming back from the Boso peninsula, the final stretch crosses Tokyo or loops around it on the expressways, and the traffic can be heavy. Plan for delays, especially on Sunday evenings.

If you finish before the soba shops close, ride the few minutes to Jindai-ji and eat a cold tray of noodles under the trees by the temple; it is a far gentler welcome back than any expressway service area. Fuel and konbini are on every main road.
t.chichibu@36.0,139.1:
Every December, on the night of the third, giant wooden floats lit with lanterns are hauled through the streets of Chichibu to the beat of drums and the crackle of fireworks, in a festival that is among the most famous in Japan. The Chichibu Night Festival has been held for centuries, and it draws huge crowds. The rest of the year, Chichibu is a quiet mountain town in a basin west of Tokyo, ringed by forested peaks.

Mount Buko, which looms over the town, has been quarried for limestone for decades, and its summit has been cut away into terraces, a scarred profile that dominates the view. The cement industry was a mainstay of the local economy. Chichibu is also a pilgrimage centre, with a circuit of thirty-four temples dedicated to Kannon, the goddess of mercy, scattered through the valleys.

In spring, Hitsujiyama park is covered with a carpet of pink and white moss phlox, shibazakura, and the crowds come to see it. Nagatoro, to the north, has river boats that shoot the rapids of the Arakawa between flat rock formations.

The food is hearty and local: waraji katsu, a pork cutlet as big as a straw sandal, served over rice, and soba from local buckwheat. Chichibu also makes whisky, and a small distillery has won international prizes.

For riders, the roads around Chichibu are among the best near Tokyo. Route 299 climbs over the mountains to the east, and Route 140 heads west through a long tunnel into Yamanashi. Both are winding, well surfaced and busy with riders on weekends, and the police know it. In winter, watch for ice on shaded corners. Fill the tank in town: once you are on the passes, stations are scarce.
t.near wako@35.8,139.7:
In 1964 the world's best oarsmen raced on a straight, two-kilometre channel dug beside the Arakawa at Toda, a few minutes from this finish. The Toda rowing course was built for the Tokyo Olympics and is still busy with university crews, whose coaches cycle along the bank shouting through megaphones at dawn. Next door, crowds gather to bet on the motorboat races at the Toda kyōtei stadium, one of the few forms of legal gambling in Japan.

This is the low, flat land where Saitama meets Tokyo, between Toda, Wakō and Shimotoda, crossed by the great embankments of the Arakawa and the expressways that carry the weekend traffic home. It is not beautiful, but the river gives it space: the floodplain is a broad green belt of baseball pitches, golf driving ranges, reed beds and cycle paths, and on a clear winter day Mount Fuji appears on the western horizon, framed between the apartment blocks.

The last kilometres after the Bandai Azuma Skyline are rarely relaxing. The Gaikan ring road and the Shuto expressways jam up on Sunday evenings as the whole of Kantō returns at once, and the surface streets are a grid of signals, trucks and scooters. Keep your gaps generous; drivers here are polite but tired.

Practicalities are simple. Petrol stations and konbini line the arterial roads, family restaurants stay open late, and the station areas have counters serving gyōza and beer to salarymen. If it is early enough, a slow walk along the rowing course, with the eights gliding past in the evening light, is a strangely calming way to step off the bike.
t.near uenohara on the way back@35.5,139.1:
Route 413, the Dōshi road, is the motorcycle road of western Kanagawa. It runs from Sagamihara up the long, narrow valley of the Dōshi river to Lake Yamanaka at the foot of Fuji, and on a weekend morning the parade of bikes heading west is almost continuous. This stop lies in that valley, south of Uenohara, where the river runs clear and green between forested slopes and the villages are strung out along the road.

The Dōshi river is famous for its water. It is cold, clean and fast, tumbling over boulders and pooling in deep green basins, and in summer the riverside campsites fill with families from Tokyo who come to paddle, fish and barbecue. For a rider, a riverside stop with boots off and feet in the water is the best kind of break. Swimming is possible in the calmer pools, but the current is strong after rain, and the water is very cold, even in August.

The road itself is a joy, with a rhythm of bends that follow the river, good surfaces and long stretches without junctions. It is also busy and closely watched by police, especially at weekends. Watch for cars stopping suddenly at campsites, cyclists on the climbs, and gravel washed onto the road after storms. In winter, ice lingers on the shaded sections.

Lake Miyagase, the reservoir at the eastern end of the valley, is a popular stop with a large park and views over the water. At the western end, the road climbs to the Yamabushi pass and drops to Lake Yamanaka, with Fuji suddenly filling the view.

Fuel is limited in the valley. Fill up in Sagamihara or at Lake Yamanaka, and do not count on the small stations in between. The roadside stations, michi-no-eki, sell local vegetables, soft ice cream and grilled river fish.
t.near kawaguchi@35.8,139.7:
Kawaguchi was Japan's foundry town. For centuries its workshops cast iron pots, kettles and temple bells from the sand and clay of the Arakawa, and by the twentieth century the town was famous for its cupola furnaces, whose chimneys filled the skyline. A classic 1962 film, set among the foundries, made the town a symbol of working-class Japan. Most of the furnaces have gone, replaced by apartment towers for Tokyo commuters, but a few workshops still cast metal in the old way.

This finish lies on the southern edge of the city, near the Arakawa, where Kawaguchi faces Tokyo across the river. Akabane, on the Tokyo side, is famous for its cheap, cheerful bars, where you can drink and eat for a few coins standing at a counter, and on weekend evenings the narrow lanes near the station are packed.

The Arakawa riverbanks are broad and green, with sports fields, cycle paths and reed beds, and the levee offers views over the city and, on clear days, to Mount Fuji. The river is a reminder of the floods that once threatened the low-lying plain, and the massive embankments were built to keep the water out.

Coming back from the Boso peninsula, the final stretch crosses Tokyo on the expressways or loops around it, and the traffic can be heavy. Plan for delays on Sunday evenings, and take care on the busy surface streets near the river.

Fuel and konbini are easy to find on the main roads. After a long day on the Boso coast, a seat at a counter in Akabane, with a cold beer and a plate of grilled skewers, is a deeply Tokyo way to end the ride.
t.ito@35.0,139.1:
In 1604 an English pilot named William Adams, shipwrecked in Japan a few years earlier and taken into the service of the shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu, built the first Western-style sailing ships in Japan at the mouth of the river in Itō. Adams, known in Japan as Miura Anjin, became a samurai and an adviser to the shogun, and his story inspired the novel Shōgun. Itō remembers him with a festival every August and a memorial by the river.

Itō is a hot-spring town on the east coast of the Izu peninsula, with dozens of inns, public baths and a long promenade along the bay. The Tōkaikan, an old wooden inn on the river, has been preserved and opened to the public, with three storeys of carved wood, tatami rooms and a lookout tower.

South of the town, the Jōgasaki coast is a dramatic shoreline of black lava cliffs formed by an eruption of Mount Ōmuro, a perfectly shaped cinder cone that rises behind the coast. A suspension bridge spans a gorge above the waves, and the coastal path is spectacular. Mount Ōmuro's grass slopes are burned every year in a spring ritual, leaving the cone black for a few weeks.

The beach in Itō is a long, sandy strip in front of the town, open for swimming in summer, with calm water and lifeguards. It is a good place for a dip after a day on the Izu Skyline.

Route 135, the coastal road, is often congested, especially on weekends and holidays. The roads into the hills behind Itō are quieter, winding up to the Izu Skyline and the plateau of Izu Kōgen. In town, the shops along the harbour sell himono, fish split and dried in the sea air, grilled for breakfast all over Izu. Buy a pack for later, top up the tank on the way out, and save the onsen for when the riding is done.
t.near chofu@35.6,139.6:
Doraemon lives here, in a manner of speaking. The museum of Fujiko F. Fujio, the manga artist who created the robot cat, stands in the green hills of Kawasaki's Tama ward, a short ride south of the Tama River, and it is a pilgrimage site for anyone who grew up with the character. Next to it, the Ikuta Ryokuchi park preserves a collection of old farmhouses brought from all over Japan, with thatched roofs, earthen floors and open hearths, a world away from the city.

This finish lies on the edge of Tokyo, between Komae and the Tama River, where the hills of the Tama area rise from the flat plain. The river is broad and gravelly, with wide banks used for sports, picnics and walking, and on summer evenings it is a cool, open space in the crowded city.

Noborito, on the Kawasaki side, is a lively neighbourhood with a station, shops and restaurants, and the hills behind it are covered with woods and parks. The view from the hills over the river and the city is fine on a clear day.

Coming back from Okutama and Chichibu, the last leg runs along the Tama River downstream, through the suburbs of western Tokyo, and the traffic can be heavy. Plan for delays on weekend evenings.

The museum and folk-house park keep daytime hours, so this works best if you are back by mid-afternoon. Otherwise, settle for the river: park near the bank, watch the trains rumble across the bridge, and let the mountains of Okutama replay in your head.
t.kusatsu@35.0,136.0:
Two of the great roads of old Japan met at Kusatsu. The Tōkaidō, running along the Pacific coast from Edo, and the Nakasendō, crossing the mountains of the interior, joined here before the last stretch to Kyoto, and the town grew rich on travellers. The honjin, the official inn where daimyō lords stayed on their journeys, survives as one of the largest and best preserved in Japan, with its long wooden halls, gardens and a register of the famous guests who stayed.

This is not the hot-spring Kusatsu of Gunma, but a busy city on the south-eastern shore of Lake Biwa, in Shiga prefecture, between Kyoto and Nagoya. The lake, the largest in Japan, stretches north to the horizon, and the Lake Biwa Museum, on a peninsula near Kusatsu, tells the story of its ecology and the people who lived around it.

The local sweet is uba-ga-mochi, small rice cakes topped with sweet bean paste, shaped to resemble a nursing mother. They have been sold to travellers here since the Edo period, and the shop near the old junction still sells them.

The riding around Kusatsu is mostly urban, with heavy traffic on the national roads. The lakeshore road offers views over the water, and the hills to the east have quieter roads through forests and tea fields.

Fuel and food are no trouble in a city of this size. Give yourself half an hour in the old post-town street, with its signpost marking the fork of the two great roads, and walk where four centuries of travellers did, then buy a box of uba-ga-mochi for the road. They do not survive a pannier well, so eat them quickly.
t.seto@35.2,137.1:
In Japanese, everyday pottery is called setomono, things from Seto, and that says everything about this town. Potters have worked here for more than a thousand years, using the fine clay of the surrounding hills, and in the Edo period Seto supplied ceramics to the whole country. The kilns still smoke, and the town is full of workshops, galleries and shops selling everything from rice bowls to garden ornaments.

The Kamagaki-no-komichi, a narrow lane in the old pottery district, is lined with walls built from broken kiln furniture and pottery shards, a charming relic of the old industry. The Seto-gura museum tells the story of the town's ceramics, with old kilns, workshops and a reconstructed station.

Seto is also the hometown of Fujii Sōta, the young shogi player who broke record after record and became a national hero. His success brought a wave of visitors and a boom in shogi across Japan.

The town lies in the hills north-east of Nagoya, and the roads around it wind through forests and valleys, with tight bends and little traffic. Sanage-yama, to the south, offers fine views over the Nagoya plain. Fuel and convenience stores are easy in town. The pottery shops are dangerous for anyone with soft luggage: bubble wrap is cheap, and a single handmade cup wrapped in a spare T-shirt has crossed many a mountain pass intact. In September the town holds a big ceramics festival, when the streets fill with stalls.
t.ryuo@35.7,138.5:
In the sixteenth century, the warlord Takeda Shingen built a series of levees and stone barriers along the Kamanashi river at Ryūō to tame its floods, and the system, called Shingen-zutsumi, still protects the Kōfu basin today. The levee is planted with bamboo and trees, and a park along the river commemorates the work. It is a reminder that Shingen, famous as a general, was also a canny administrator.

Ryūō lies on the western side of the Kōfu basin, in Yamanashi, where the flat valley floor is covered with orchards of grapes and peaches. Yamanashi is Japan's fruit bowl, and the roadside stalls sell fruit in summer and autumn. It is also the heart of Japanese wine, with wineries scattered through the valley.

The views are spectacular on a clear day. To the west, the peaks of the Southern Alps rise steeply from the basin, and to the south, Mount Fuji peeks over the hills. The Misaka pass, south of Kōfu, was made famous by the writer Dazai Osamu, who stayed at a tea house there and wrote about the view of Fuji.

The riding around Ryūō is a mix of busy national roads and quiet orchard lanes, with the mountains always in view. Route 52 heads south towards the Fuji river, and the roads into the Southern Alps are steep and winding. Ryūō is a practical stop, with fuel and konbini along the national road. In late summer, pull in at any orchard stall with grapes stacked on the counter; a bunch of Kyohō grapes, dark, sweet and cold from the cooler, is the best thing you will eat all day.
t.tateyama@35.0,139.9:
Tateyama faces west across the mouth of Tokyo Bay, and its bay is so calm that it has long been called Kagami-ga-ura, the mirror bay. On a still evening, Mount Fuji, across the water, is reflected in the sea, and the sunset turns the whole bay gold. Hōjō beach, in front of the town, is one of the best swimming beaches on the Boso peninsula, with calm water, fine sand and lifeguards in summer.

The town is crowned by a reconstructed castle on a hill, the seat of the Satomi clan, who ruled the southern Boso in the sixteenth century. Their story inspired the famous Edo-period novel Nansō Satomi Hakkenden, the tale of eight dog warriors, and the castle museum tells it.

Okinoshima, a small island connected to the shore by a sandbar, is a nature reserve with forest, rock pools and clear water, popular for snorkelling. Warm currents allow corals to grow here, close to their northern limit.

The riding around Tateyama is gentle and scenic, with coast roads and hills. The Boso Flower Line runs south along the coast towards Nojimazaki, and the roads inland are quiet. In summer, aim to arrive in the late afternoon, swim from Hōjō beach as the heat goes out of the day, and then sit on the sea wall for the sunset over Fuji. Fuel and food are close at hand in the town centre.
t.tanashicho@35.7,139.5:
A tall, slender broadcasting tower, Sky Tower Nishitokyo, marks this part of the Musashino plain from miles away, and if you have been riding the Venus Line in the mountains of Nagano all day, it is the first sign that home is close. Tanashi is the eastern half of Nishitokyo city, a quiet suburb of houses, small shops and parks on the Seibu line, west of central Tokyo, where Shin-Ōme Kaidō and Ōme Kaidō run arrow-straight across the flat land towards the city.

Those straight roads are old. The Musashino plain was a dry upland of grass and woods until the Edo period, when the Tamagawa Jōsui, a canal dug in 1653 to bring drinking water from the Tama River to Edo, made settlement possible. The canal still runs a few kilometres south, shaded by cherry trees and zelkovas; the novelist Dazai Osamu drowned in it in Mitaka in 1948, and its banks are now a walking path, lovely in early April.

Tanashi itself is home to the Tama Rokuto Science Museum, whose planetarium is one of the most advanced in Japan, and the Musashino woodland survives in patches around shrines and in the Koganei park nearby, where an open-air museum of old buildings rescued from the city stands among the trees.

The final stretch home from Nagano usually comes in on the Chūō expressway and then along Shin-Ōme Kaidō or Ōme Kaidō, flat, wide and slow, with lights every few hundred metres and trucks heading for the city. It is easy riding, but fatigue is the enemy here. Pull over at a konbini for something cold before the last few kilometres; they are on every corner, and so are fuel stations and family restaurants open late into the night.
t.near nikko@36.7,139.5:
Forty-eight hairpins, each one marked with a sign bearing a letter of the old Japanese alphabet poem, the Iroha: that is Irohazaka, the road that climbs from the town of Nikkō to Lake Chūzenji. There are two roads, one for going up and one for going down, each a series of tight, steep bends through dense forest, and in autumn, when the maples turn red and gold, the scene is so beautiful that the traffic jams stretch for hours.

Nikkō, at the foot of the climb, is famous for the Tōshōgū, the mausoleum of Tokugawa Ieyasu, founder of the shogunate that ruled Japan for two and a half centuries. Its buildings, covered with gold leaf, lacquer and carvings of dragons, monkeys and cats, are a riot of colour and detail, a World Heritage site that draws visitors from all over the world. The red Shinkyō bridge, over the river at the entrance to the shrine area, is one of the symbols of the town.

At the top of the climb, Lake Chūzenji lies at the foot of Mount Nantai, a sacred volcano, and the Kegon falls drop from the lake into a deep gorge, one of the most famous waterfalls in Japan. The Akechidaira ropeway, near the top of the uphill road, offers a view over the lake, the falls and the hairpins.

The local speciality is yuba, the skin that forms on heated soy milk, served fresh, dried or in soups, and the restaurants of Nikkō serve it in many ways.

The road stays open year-round, but in winter the shaded hairpins can be icy and Lake Chūzenji sits well above the town, so expect real cold. In late October, the peak of the foliage, go at first light or not at all. Fill the tank in Nikkō before climbing; options up at the lake are few.
t.near itsukaichi@35.7,139.1:
Itsukaichi takes its name from the market that was once held here on days ending in five, a trading point where charcoal, timber and silk from the mountains of western Tokyo met merchants from the plains. It is now part of the city of Akiruno, a quiet town at the mouth of the Akigawa valley, where the suburbs of Tokyo finally give way to forested hills.

The Akigawa is a clear mountain river, popular for barbecues, swimming and fishing in summer, and its valley leads into the mountains of Hinohara and Okutama, the wild western edge of Tokyo Metropolis. The forests here are dense with cedar and cypress, planted after the war, and mixed with native broadleaf trees that turn red and gold in autumn. Waterfalls, gorges and mountain villages make it a world away from the city.

For riders, the area is a classic escape from Tokyo. The Itsukaichi Kaido leads into the valley, and the roads beyond climb into the mountains, with tight curves, steep grades and spectacular views. The Okutama Shūyū Road, a famous mountain toll-free road, links Hinohara and Okutama over the ridges, and it is very popular with motorcyclists, though it has seen restrictions on motorcycles at night after accidents. Traffic can be heavy on weekends, and the roads are narrow, so ride with care.

Itsukaichi has fuel stations, convenience stores and restaurants, making it a good stop before heading into the mountains, where services become scarce. Local restaurants serve soba noodles, a speciality of the area. The Izu Skyline lies far to the south-west, a long ride across the Kanto plain and around Mount Fuji.
t.near yoshii@36.2,139.0:
One of the oldest written stones in Japan stands near Yoshii. The Tago stele, carved in the early eighth century to commemorate the creation of a new district, is part of a group of three ancient monuments in the area that were added to UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2017. It is a modest stone under a protective roof, but its age and significance give pause in a landscape of fields and low hills.

Yoshii, now part of the city of Takasaki in Gunma Prefecture, sits in the valley of the Kabura river, where the Kanto plain meets the mountains to the west. The landscape is rural, with rice paddies, vegetable fields and orchards, and the hills rise towards the jagged volcanic peaks of Mount Myōgi, one of the three famous mountains of Gunma. The area is known for its silk heritage, and the Tomioka silk mill, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is a short ride away.

On the bike, things are pleasant. The roads in the valley are flat and straight, but those heading into the mountains, towards Myōgi and Shimonita, are winding and steep, with great views. Shimonita is famous for its leeks and konnyaku, and the roads beyond climb towards Nagano. Traffic is light outside the towns, but watch for farm vehicles and for gravel on mountain roads.

Yoshii has fuel, konbini-style convenience stores and plenty of places to eat. A stop at a roadside station, a michi-no-eki, offers local produce, snacks and clean toilets. The Bōsō Peninsula lies far to the south-east, beyond Tokyo, so consider this a pleasant interlude before the long ride across the plain.
t.near satte@36.1,139.8:
Every spring, along an embankment in Satte, about a thousand cherry trees bloom at the same time as fields of yellow rapeseed beneath them, and the combination of pink and yellow draws huge crowds. Gongendō Park, on the levee of an old river, is the place, and if you happen to ride through in late March or early April, it is a sight to remember. The rest of the year, Satte is a quiet town in the flat farmland of north-eastern Saitama.

The Kanto plain here is low and flat, crossed by rivers and canals, with rice paddies, vegetable fields and scattered towns. The Tone River, one of Japan's largest, flows nearby, and the history of the region is a story of floods and the efforts to control them, with levees, channels and pumping stations. The embankments themselves offer the best views in the area, with wide skies and, on clear winter days, the mountains of Nikkō and even Mount Fuji on the horizon.

The riding here is easy but not exciting. Roads are straight and flat, with traffic lights and junctions, and traffic can be heavy on the main routes. The Ken-Ō Expressway passes nearby, offering a fast route around the Tokyo region. In summer, the heat and humidity can be intense, and in winter, a cold, dry wind blows from the mountains.

Satte is well stocked with fuel stations, convenience stores and eateries. A stop at a convenience store for a coffee and a snack is a Japanese riding tradition. Mount Haruna and the hot springs of Ikaho lie to the north-west in Gunma, a much more scenic destination, with winding roads and an onsen bath at the end.
t.near enzan@35.7,138.8:
Takeda Shingen, the warlord who dominated Kai province in the sixteenth century and remains a folk hero in Yamanashi, lies buried at Erin-ji, a Zen temple on the edge of Enzan. Its garden, laid out by the great medieval designer Musō Soseki, is a quiet masterpiece of pond, rocks and moss, and the temple is the spiritual heart of a town that now forms part of the city of Kōshū.

Enzan sits on the north-eastern rim of the Kōfu basin, and the slopes around it are covered with vineyards and peach orchards. This is the fruit bowl of Japan. In spring the peach blossom paints the valley pink, and in late summer and autumn roadside stands sell grapes, peaches and local wine; nearby Katsunuma is the centre of Japanese winemaking. On clear days, Mount Fuji rises to the south across the basin, framed by the Southern Alps to the west.

For riders, Enzan is the gateway to one of the great mountain routes of the region. National Route 411, the Ōme Kaidō, climbs north-east from the town over the Yanagisawa Pass, with steep grades, tight hairpins and views back over the basin, before dropping into the Okutama valley and the lake behind the Ogōchi dam. A side road leads up towards the Daibosatsu Pass, famous from an epic samurai novel. Traffic is light on weekdays, busy with bikes on weekends, and the upper road can be closed or icy in winter.

Enzan offers fuel, convenience stores and cheap restaurants. Try hōtō, the thick noodle stew that is Yamanashi's comfort food, before heading up into the mountains. The Bōsō coast lies far to the east, beyond Tokyo and the bay, a full day's ride from the vines.
t.kukichuo@36.1,139.7:
Kuki is the kind of place that rarely appears in travel guides, a pleasant, low-rise city in the flat farmland of north-eastern Saitama, crossed by railways, rivers and expressways. Kukichūō is its central district, with shops, homes and offices, and it makes a practical stop on the long run north from Tokyo towards the mountains of Gunma and Tochigi.

The area has one unexpected attraction. A short ride away stands Washinomiya Shrine, often described as one of the oldest Shintō shrines in the Kanto region, with a tall torii gate and a quiet grove. In recent years it has become a pilgrimage site for anime fans, after a popular series set some of its scenes there, and you may see votive plaques decorated with cartoon characters alongside traditional offerings.

The landscape around Kuki is the classic Kanto plain: rice paddies, vegetable fields, rivers held in by high embankments, and scattered towns. The Tone River runs to the north, and the levees offer wide views over the plain. The riding here is easy but not particularly exciting, with straight roads, traffic lights and frequent junctions. The Tōhoku Expressway and the Ken-Ō Expressway meet nearby, providing fast access north and around the Tokyo region, though tolls apply.

Kukichūō has fuel stations, convenience stores and restaurants, including the ubiquitous chains serving ramen, gyūdon and curry. A short break here, perhaps with a visit to Washinomiya, is a good way to rest before the climb into the mountains. Gunma's three famous mountains, Haruna, Akagi and Myōgi, rise ahead, with some of the best riding roads in the Kanto region.
t.near ishige@36.1,139.9:
In September 2015, after days of torrential rain, the levee of the Kinu River broke near Ishige, and floodwater spread across a huge area of the city of Jōsō, stranding thousands of people on rooftops while helicopters circled overhead. The images shocked Japan. The levees have since been rebuilt and strengthened, and the landscape has returned to its calm rhythm of rice paddies, villages and river embankments, but the event is a reminder of how much this flat land depends on its defences.

Ishige lies in south-western Ibaraki Prefecture, on the Kanto plain between the Kinu and Kokai rivers. The land is flat and fertile, given over to rice, vegetables and pears, and the twin peaks of Mount Tsukuba rise to the east, a landmark visible from much of the plain. Tsukuba is one of Japan's famous mountains, and the roads that climb its flanks are popular with riders, offering curves and views over the plain.

The riding around Ishige itself is easy and relaxed, with straight roads between the fields, but the roads towards Tsukuba and the hills of eastern Ibaraki are more interesting. Traffic can be heavy on the main routes, and the plain is exposed to wind. In summer, the heat and humidity are intense, while in winter, the air is clear and dry.

Ishige is well stocked with fuel stations, convenience stores and eateries. A local speciality is soba noodles made from buckwheat grown in Ibaraki. A short break here, before continuing towards the Bōsō peninsula to the south, offers a chance to appreciate the quiet beauty of the Kanto plain, its big skies and its wide rivers.
t.near fujisawa@35.3,139.5:
Fujisawa sits on Sagami Bay, south-west of Yokohama, at the heart of the Shonan coast, the stretch of beaches, surf shops and seaside towns that Tokyoites escape to on summer weekends. The town's most famous landmark is Enoshima, a small, steep island linked to the mainland by a bridge, covered with shrines, caves, gardens and seafood restaurants, with a lighthouse observation tower on top.

The Enoshima Electric Railway, the Enoden, rattles along the coast between Fujisawa and Kamakura, sometimes running down the middle of the street, and it has become an icon of the area. Kamakura, a short ride east, was the seat of Japan's first shogunate in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, and it is full of temples and shrines, including the Great Buddha, a huge bronze statue sitting in the open air.
