On clear days, especially in winter, Mount Fuji rises across the bay to the west, its snow-capped cone floating above the water. The view from Enoshima or from the beach at sunset, with the mountain silhouetted against an orange sky, is one of the classic images of Japan.

For riders, Route 134 runs along the coast through Fujisawa, with the sea on one side and pine trees on the other. It is scenic but often congested, especially on weekends and in summer. Fuel and food are plentiful. As a photo stop, the coast near Enoshima with Fuji in the background is unbeatable on a clear day. Go early, before the traffic builds.
t.near noda@35.9,139.9:
Noda is a city in the north-west of Chiba prefecture, between the Edo and Tone rivers, and it smells, faintly, of soy sauce. For more than three centuries, Noda has been one of the main centres of soy sauce brewing in Japan, and it is the home of Kikkoman, whose origins lie in the brewing families of the town. The company's museum offers tours where you can learn about the brewing process and taste the results.

The rivers were the key to Noda's success. The Edo river linked the town with Edo, now Tokyo, and the boats that carried soy sauce down the river to the capital made the brewers rich. The Tone, Japan's largest river by drainage basin, flows to the north, and the land between the rivers is flat and fertile, with fields, woods and residential areas.

The riding around Noda is flat and easy, with roads following the rivers and crossing the plain. The embankments along the Edo river offer long, open views, and the area around the confluence of the rivers, at Sekiyado, has a reconstructed castle tower housing a museum. Traffic can be heavy on the main roads, especially Route 16, the ring road around Tokyo, but the minor roads are quieter.

As a scenic stretch, Noda offers a glimpse of the quieter side of the Kanto plain, with rivers, fields and old breweries. Fuel and food are plentiful. Soy sauce soft-serve ice cream is a local curiosity worth trying.
t.near yokosuka@35.2,139.7:
Yokosuka occupies much of the Miura Peninsula, south of Yokohama, and it has been a naval town since the 1860s, when the Tokugawa shogunate built a shipyard here with French help. Today it is home to the US Navy's Seventh Fleet and a major Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force base, and the mix of cultures gives the town a distinctive feel. Dobuita Street, near the base, is full of bars and shops, and Yokosuka navy curry is a local speciality.

In Mikasa Park, the battleship Mikasa, Admiral Tōgō's flagship at the Battle of Tsushima in 1905, is preserved as a memorial ship. At Kurihama, on the eastern shore of the peninsula, a monument marks the spot where Commodore Perry landed in 1853, an event that led to the opening of Japan to the West. Kannonzaki, on the eastern tip, has a lighthouse that was one of the first Western-style lighthouses in Japan.

As a start and fuel stop, Yokosuka is practical, with plenty of service stations and convenience stores. From Kurihama, the Tokyo Bay Ferry crosses to Kanaya on the Boso Peninsula, a forty-minute crossing that makes a wonderful start to a ride around Boso. Motorcycles are welcome, and the views of the bay from the deck are lovely.

The roads around the Miura Peninsula are winding and scenic, with views over the sea, though traffic can be heavy, especially on weekends. The southern tip of the peninsula, around Misaki, is famous for tuna, and the fishing port has many restaurants serving it fresh.
t.near otsuki@35.7,139.0:
Ōtsuki sits in a deep, narrow valley in the mountains of eastern Yamanashi, where the old Kōshū Kaidō highway from Edo to Kōfu meets the road south towards Mount Fuji and the Fuji Five Lakes. The Katsura river runs through the valley, and steep, forested mountains rise on every side, giving the town a closed-in, mountain feel despite being only about an hour from western Tokyo.

The town is famous for the Saruhashi, the Monkey Bridge, a wooden cantilever bridge spanning a narrow gorge high above the river. According to legend, it was inspired by monkeys forming a chain across the gorge, and it is counted as one of the three strange bridges of Japan. The current bridge is a reconstruction, but the design is centuries old, and the setting is dramatic.

Above the town, the rocky peak of Iwadono was the site of a mountain castle in the Warring States period, and the cliffs are a landmark. The mountains around Ōtsuki are popular with hikers, and the views of Mount Fuji from the ridges are among the best in the region.

For riders, the roads around Ōtsuki are a mix of valley routes and mountain passes. Route 20, the old Kōshū Kaidō, follows the valley with gentle curves, while Route 139 heads south towards Fujiyoshida and the lakes. Smaller roads climb into the mountains with tight bends and steep gradients. Traffic can be heavy on weekends. Fuel and food are available in Ōtsuki.
t.near machida@35.5,139.4:
Machida is a big commuter city on the south-western edge of Tokyo, poking into Kanagawa prefecture like a thumb, so that locals joke about whether it really belongs to Tokyo at all. It is busy, built-up and practical, with department stores, train stations and endless convenience stores, and it makes a straightforward starting point for rides into the mountains to the west.

The city sits in the Tama Hills, a landscape of low, wooded ridges and valleys that has largely been covered by housing estates since the 1960s. Pockets of the old countryside survive, though, in parks and green spaces where satoyama, the traditional mix of woods, fields and ponds, is preserved. The Yakushiike Park, with its pond and lotus flowers, is a pleasant spot.

As a start and fuel stop, Machida is easy, with service stations along the main roads, especially Route 16, the great ring road around greater Tokyo. Convenience stores sell rice balls, coffee and snacks, perfect for a quick breakfast before a ride. From here, the roads west lead towards Sagamihara, Lake Sagami and the mountains of the Tanzawa and the Fuji Five Lakes.

Traffic is heavy in and around Machida, especially on weekdays and at rush hour, and Route 16 is notorious for congestion. An early start, before dawn, is the best way to escape the city. Once you are past Sagamihara, the roads become quieter and the mountains close in.
t.near sagamihara@35.5,139.3:
Sagamihara is a big city on the western edge of the Tokyo sprawl, but it stretches surprisingly far into the mountains. Its western part takes in the Tanzawa foothills, Lake Sagami and Lake Tsukui, two reservoirs on the Sagami river surrounded by forested hills, and the change from suburb to mountain happens quickly.

The city has a space connection: the Sagamihara campus of JAXA, the Japanese space agency, managed the Hayabusa missions that returned samples from asteroids. There is a small exhibition hall open to visitors, and the city is proud of its role in space exploration.

For riders, the high ground west of Sagamihara is the start of some of the best roads near Tokyo. Route 413, the Dōshi road, runs from Sagamihara through the mountains to Lake Yamanaka, near Mount Fuji, a long, winding route through forests and valleys, with countless bends and a few steep climbs. It is hugely popular with motorcyclists, and on weekends you will see many of them, as well as at the roadside rest areas along the way.

Traffic can be heavy, especially on weekends and in the autumn foliage season, and the roads can be narrow, with blind corners. Watch for cyclists, oncoming traffic cutting corners, and wildlife, including deer and monkeys. Fuel is available in Sagamihara and at a few points along the route, but stations are sparse in the mountains, so fill up before you go.
t.ageoshimo@36.0,139.6:
Ageoshimo is a district of Ageo, a commuter city in Saitama prefecture, north of Tokyo, on the flat Omiya plateau between the Arakawa and Ayase rivers. In the Edo period, Ageo was a post town on the Nakasendō, one of the five great highways that radiated from Edo, linking the capital with Kyoto through the mountains of central Japan. Travellers, merchants and feudal lords on their way to and from the capital stayed in its inns.

Today, Ageo is largely residential and suburban, but traces of the old countryside remain in its fields, groves and shrines. The Arakawa river, to the west, has wide floodplains with parks, golf courses and fields, and the embankments offer long views across the plain. On clear winter days, Mount Fuji appears far to the south-west, and the mountains of Chichibu rise to the west.

As a scenic stretch, Ageoshimo is honest about what it is: a passage through the suburbs on the way to the mountains. The roads are flat and straight, with traffic lights and convenience stores, and traffic can be heavy. But once you head west towards Kawagoe and the Chichibu hills, the landscape opens up. Kawagoe, known as Little Edo, has a beautifully preserved district of old merchant houses with thick clay walls and a famous bell tower.

Fuel and food are plentiful in Ageo. An early start helps you beat the traffic and reach the mountains while the roads are still quiet.
t.near sakai@36.1,139.8:
Sakai, in the far south-west of Ibaraki, sits on the Tone river, Japan's largest river by drainage basin, at a point where the river makes a broad sweep across the Kanto plain. In the Edo period, Sakai was a busy river port, where boats loaded with rice, soy sauce and other goods passed on their way to and from Edo, and the town grew rich on the trade.

Across the river, on a narrow tongue of land where the Edo river branches off from the Tone, stands Sekiyado, once a castle town guarding this strategic junction. A reconstructed castle keep there houses the Chiba Prefectural Sekiyado Castle Museum, which tells the story of the rivers and the efforts to control them, including the great Edo-period project that diverted the Tone eastward to protect the capital from floods. The view from the top of the keep over the rivers and the plain is excellent.

Calling this a high point is relative: the land is almost perfectly flat, and the highest ground for miles is the river embankment. But the embankments offer long views across the plain, and on clear days Mount Fuji, Mount Tsukuba and the mountains of Nikkō and Chichibu can all be seen on the horizon.

For riders, the roads around Sakai are flat and straight, with little traffic away from the main routes. The bridges over the Tone offer views of the wide river. Fuel and food are available in Sakai and the surrounding towns. It is a peaceful, unhurried place to pause on the way north.
t.near oiso@35.3,139.3:
Ōiso is a quiet seaside town on Sagami Bay, west of Hiratsuka, and it has an important place in Japanese social history: in 1885 it became the site of Japan's first public sea bathing beach, promoted by an army surgeon who believed that sea bathing was good for health. Wealthy families from Tokyo built villas here, and the town became a fashionable resort for politicians and aristocrats.

Among them was Yoshida Shigeru, prime minister in the years after the Second World War, who lived in Ōiso for many years. His former residence, with its gardens overlooking the sea, has been restored and is open to visitors. Ito Hirobumi, Japan's first prime minister, also had a villa here.

The old Tōkaidō highway, which linked Edo and Kyoto, passes through Ōiso, and a stretch of the old road is still lined with ancient pine trees. Each January, the Hakone Ekiden, a famous university relay race from Tokyo to Hakone and back, runs along this route, and the roadside is lined with spectators.

For riders, Route 1 and the Seishō bypass run along the coast, with views over the sea and, on clear days, Mount Fuji to the west and the Izu Peninsula to the south-west. Traffic can be heavy, especially on weekends. Fuel and food are available in Ōiso and Hiratsuka. As a photo stop, the coast near Ōiso, with the sea and Fuji, is lovely, especially in winter, when the air is clear.
t.zushi@35.3,139.6:
Zushi is a small, relaxed seaside town on the western side of the Miura Peninsula, tucked between Kamakura and Hayama, with a crescent of sandy beach facing Sagami Bay. It has long been a retreat for Tokyo families, and in summer the beach fills with swimmers, windsurfers and stand-up paddlers. Out of season, it is quiet, with dog walkers and joggers on the sand and fishing boats pulled up at the end of the bay.

For a swim, Zushi Beach is one of the most sheltered on this coast, with gentle waves and shallow water, and during the official swimming season in July and August, lifeguards are on duty and beach huts sell food and drinks. Outside that season, swimming is at your own risk. The water is coolest in early summer and warmest in late August and September.

On clear days, especially in winter and early spring, Mount Fuji rises across the bay, and the sunset view from the beach, with the mountain silhouetted against the sky and the sea glowing, is one of the most famous on the Shonan coast. Next door, Hayama is home to an imperial villa, and its coast is lined with rocky coves and small beaches.

As a start, Zushi gives easy access to the coast road around the Miura Peninsula and to Kamakura, with its temples and shrines. Traffic can be heavy, especially on summer weekends, and parking near the beach is limited. Fuel and food are available in Zushi and the surrounding towns. Go early to enjoy the beach in peace.
t.near yashio@35.8,139.9:
Yashio is a flat, workaday city in south-eastern Saitama, just north of Tokyo's Adachi ward, sandwiched between the Nakagawa and Ayase rivers. It is a landscape of small factories, warehouses, apartment blocks and the occasional field of vegetables, crossed by expressways and railway lines. It will not feature in any guidebook, and it does not pretend otherwise.

What it offers a rider is position. The Tokyo Gaikan expressway, the outer ring road, runs past, and the Metropolitan Expressway and Tsukuba Express link it with central Tokyo, so it is a practical place to meet, fill the tank and grab breakfast at a convenience store before heading out. Service stations are plentiful, and the convenience stores sell everything from rice balls and coffee to rain ponchos.

The rivers are the main natural feature. Their embankments, which protect the low-lying land from floods, offer long, open views across the plain, and they are lined with cherry trees in places, beautiful in early April. The land here was once marshy, and the efforts to control the rivers, which began centuries ago, have shaped the whole region.

From Yashio, the roads lead south-west towards Tokyo and the bay, or north towards the open plain and the mountains. Traffic is heavy, especially on weekdays and at rush hour, and the roads are lined with traffic lights. An early start, before the city wakes up, is the best way to escape. Once you are clear of the suburbs, the riding improves quickly.
t.near fujiyoshida@35.4,138.8:
Fujiyoshida sits on the northern foot of Mount Fuji, and the mountain fills the sky above the town so completely that it can feel almost unreal. For centuries, this was the starting point for pilgrims climbing Fuji, and the great shrine of Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Jinja, set in a forest of ancient cedars, marks the traditional beginning of the Yoshida trail. Walking through its huge wooden torii into the dark, quiet forest is a moving experience.

On the hillside opposite, the five-storey Chūreitō pagoda stands above the town, and the view from the platform above it, with the red pagoda in the foreground and Fuji behind, is one of the most photographed in Japan, especially in spring when the cherry trees bloom. Expect crowds and a lot of steps.

Fujiyoshida is also known for its noodles. Yoshida udon is famously thick, firm and chewy, served in a soy and miso broth with cabbage and a dab of spicy sauce. It was once the lunch of the town's weavers, and dozens of small restaurants serve it, many in ordinary houses. It is cheap, filling and perfect after a cold ride.

For riders, the area around Fujiyoshida is superb, with roads around the Fuji Five Lakes, through the forests and up into the surrounding mountains. The Fuji Subaru Line climbs to the fifth station, but private vehicles are restricted during the climbing season, so check before you go. Traffic can be heavy on weekends and holidays. Fuel and food are plentiful in town.
t.near machida@35.6,139.4:
The northern part of Machida climbs into the Tama Hills, where the old ridge roads once linked villages scattered through woods and valleys. Today much of the area is covered by Tama New Town, one of the largest housing developments in Japan, built from the 1960s onwards, but the ridges still offer views, and pockets of woodland, temples and farms survive between the estates.

Machida has a few surprises. The Machida Squirrel Garden lets visitors walk among free-roaming squirrels, a favourite with families. The Tama Hills also hold remnants of satoyama, the traditional landscape of coppice woods, rice terraces and ponds, preserved in parks where volunteers keep the old practices alive. In early summer, fireflies glow along the streams on warm evenings.

As a start and fuel stop, northern Machida is convenient, with service stations and convenience stores along the main roads. The Tama ridge road, which runs along the crest of the hills, offers a pleasant, winding route with views over the estates and the plain, and it leads west towards Hachiōji and the mountains of Okutama and Chichibu.

Traffic is heavy in Machida, especially at rush hour, and the roads are lined with traffic lights. An early start is essential if you want to reach the mountains before the crowds. Once you are past Hachiōji, the roads climb into the hills and the forests close in, and the city feels far away.
t.near oiso@35.4,139.3:
Inland from the coast at Ōiso, the land rises into a line of low, green hills between Hiratsuka and Ninomiya, and from their tops you look out over Sagami Bay, the Shonan coast and, on clear days, Mount Fuji and the Hakone mountains. The Shonan-daira hilltop park, above Hiratsuka, has an observation tower with a panoramic view, and in Ninomiya, Azumayama Park is famous for its early-spring display of rapeseed flowers with Fuji in the background.

Hiratsuka, the nearest big town, is known for its Tanabata festival in early July, one of the largest in the Kanto region, when the shopping streets are hung with huge, colourful streamers. The town was heavily bombed in 1945 and rebuilt after the war.

As a food stop, the area is excellent. The Shonan coast is famous for shirasu, tiny whitebait, served fresh or boiled on a bowl of rice, a dish called shirasu-don. Fishing ports along the coast have restaurants serving the day's catch, and Odawara, a little to the west, is known for kamaboko, fish cake, and for its castle.

For riders, the hill roads are winding and pleasant, with views over the sea, while Route 1 along the coast is busier but scenic. Traffic can be heavy on weekends, especially near the coast. Fuel and food are available in Hiratsuka, Ōiso and Ninomiya. This is a good place for a long lunch on the way to Hakone or the mountains of Gunma.
t.near hadano@35.4,139.2:
Hadano lies in a basin at the southern foot of the Tanzawa mountains, west of Tokyo, and for Kanto riders it means one thing: the Yabitsu Pass. Prefectural Route 70 climbs north from Hadano over the Yabitsu Pass into the Tanzawa and down to Lake Miyagase, a narrow, twisting road through dense forest, with countless tight bends and steep gradients. It is a legendary road among motorcyclists and cyclists, and on weekends it is busy with both.

Hadano has a long agricultural history. It was once famous for tobacco, grown on the slopes of the basin, and today it is known for its peanuts, sold roasted in shops around the town. The Tanzawa mountains are popular with hikers, and the trails up to the peaks of Tōnodake and Ōyama offer views over the Kanto plain and Sagami Bay. Ōyama, to the east, is a sacred mountain with a shrine near its summit, a pilgrimage site since the Edo period.

The Yabitsu Pass road demands respect. It is narrow, with blind corners, damp patches under the trees and gravel washed down from the slopes. Oncoming traffic can cut corners, and cyclists climb slowly. The road is sometimes closed after heavy rain or landslides, so check before you go. Wildlife, including deer, monkeys and wild boar, is common.

As a photo stop and finish, the view over the Hadano basin from the lower slopes, with the town spread out below and the sea beyond, is lovely. Fuel and food are available in Hadano. The local hot spring at Tsurumaki is a good place to soak after a ride.
t.fish river canyon route point 2@-26.8,17:
The map puts this point on the road south of Keetmanshoop, close to Seeheim, a spot whose name appears on road signs long before anything else does. It is the junction where the road to the coast and Lüderitz leaves the main north-south highway, and it lies on the Fish River, the longest river in Namibia, which here is mostly a wide, sandy bed with pools after rain and a thin line of green trees along the banks.

The country between Keetmanshoop and the canyon is open, high and dry. Hills of dark dolerite rise in flat-topped ridges, the plains are covered by low shrub and scattered camelthorn, and the sky seems taller than it is anywhere in Europe. The colours are plain but changeable: ochre in midday light, pink-brown in the evening, and sometimes a sudden, vivid green across the flats after rain. A wide bridge over the Fish River carries the road across the riverbed, and most of the year the river is a faint ghost of itself.

Riding here is about distance and attention. The tarmac is sound, but the long, straight lines invite drifting concentration, and the wind can push a bike sideways with surprising force. Watch for livestock, because goats, donkeys and the occasional cow wander across farm roads, and for baboons and small antelope in the early morning. Trucks run these roads steadily, hauling goods between the south and the coast, so overtaking needs patience and a clear view.

German colonial history left its trace in this part of Namibia. The railway line that parallels the road was a strategic route in the early twentieth century, linking the south to the coast and the capital. The wars between German forces and the Nama people in this region were bitter, and the memory of them is part of the country's present-day conversation about its past. A quiet moment at a roadside stop is a good time to consider that the landscape you admire was contested ground.

Water, shade and a decent breakfast in Keetmanshoop will carry you comfortably through this section, and the larger town behind you holds the shops and workshops if anything goes wrong.
t.fish river canyon route point 3@-27.6,17:
The name sounds like a village, but it is really a small settlement and camping area, and it exists because the canyon's main viewpoint is a short distance away on a gravel track.

What lies beyond is one of the great landscape features of southern Africa. The Fish River Canyon is roughly a hundred and sixty kilometres long, in places up to twenty-seven kilometres wide and around five hundred metres deep, and it is regularly mentioned as the second largest canyon in the world after the Grand Canyon in the United States, though such rankings depend on how you measure. It formed through a combination of rifting and erosion over an immense span of time, the river cutting down through ancient rock layers while the plateau around it was pulled apart.

For a rider the approach is part of the experience. The long run in from the main highway is across empty, stony plains, the colours are all browns and greys, and the canyon comes with no warning at all. The road surface can change from tarmac to graded gravel, with corrugations in dry months and soft patches where drivers have cut the track. Go slowly on the loose parts, keep a loose grip and leave a wide gap from other vehicles to avoid stones.

Hobas is as practical as it is scenic. The campsite has shade from trees and a pool that visitors from many countries have praised after a hot day, and it is a sensible overnight if you want to see the canyon at sunrise or sunset, when the shadows deepen and the walls turn gold and rust. The Hiking Trail through the canyon, about eighty-five kilometres in five days, is open only in the cooler months from roughly May to September, and permits are required, so it is a project for another trip.

Summer heat here is serious. Temperatures climb well above what feels sensible on a motorbike in leather, so winter and the shoulder seasons are kinder. Bring water for the ride in and out, because help is not around the corner.
t.fish river canyon route point 4@-27.6,17:
The main viewpoint at the Fish River Canyon is a slightly strange place to arrive at, because the ground simply stops. You walk or ride the last stretch across flat, stony plateau, a low rail or a few boulders mark an edge, and below you the land falls away in a great meandering gorge. The river you see is a thin green-brown thread at the bottom, wandering in horseshoe bends between buttresses of layered rock.

The scale is hard to absorb in a photo. The canyon is about a hundred and sixty kilometres long and roughly five hundred metres deep at its deepest, and the plateau on the far side looks blue and hazy even on a clear day. The rock is old, some of it hundreds of millions of years, and its horizontal layers catch the light differently as the sun moves, giving the walls bands of rust, grey and cream. In the late afternoon the shadows deepen and the colours warm up so quickly that people who came for a ten-minute look stay for an hour.

Several things are good to know before you go. The viewpoint has a rim path in both directions, and a short walk away from the first platform gives more solitude and a changing angle on the main loop. The rim has no fence in many places, and the wind can gust, so keep children and enthusiasm in check. Baboons and rock hyrax live in the area, and you may hear the bark of the former across the gorge.

For riders the road in is gravel for the last stretch, and an unhurried pace is the right one. Early morning and late afternoon give the best light and the mildest temperatures, and winter is the most comfortable season. Summer midday heat in the canyon area is punishing, and shade is limited to what you carry or find at the camp.

Downstream, the hot springs at Ai-Ais are a popular place to soak aching muscles after the hike, but that is a separate leg of the journey. For now, it is enough to sit on a rock, drink some water and let the size of the thing settle in.
t.tokyo@35.7,139.7:
Every ride from Tokyo begins with a negotiation. The roads are good and the drivers are disciplined, but traffic lights are many and the pace is steady rather than fast, so patience is part of the toolkit. A Sunday dawn is the easiest time to slip away.

Tokyo is a city of more than thirteen million, and the metropolitan area around it is the largest in the world. It was once the fishing village of Edo, and it became the seat of the Tokugawa shogunate in the early seventeenth century, then Japan's capital in 1868. That history is visible in odd places: a small shrine tucked between apartment blocks, a stretch of old canal, a temple with incense drifting over a car park. For a rider, it is worth looking up between traffic lights.

Practicalities are simple, because everything is close. Fuel stations are everywhere, with attendants at many of them, and the city's convenience stores sell hot coffee, rice balls and sandwiches at any hour. The expressways are tolled, and an electronic toll card makes them smoother, though paying at the booth works. Parking for motorcycles is trickier than in many places, so choose a hotel with a bike space in advance and check the rules before leaving the bike anywhere on the street.

Once you reach the open road, the contrast is striking. Heading south-west along the coast toward the Izu Peninsula, the landscape changes from concrete to hills, tangerine groves and sea views, with Mount Fuji appearing on clear days. The best time to ride is autumn, when the air is dry and cool and the visibility is highest, and spring, when the cherry blossom runs up the coast. Summer is hot and humid, and the rainy season in June can be grey and heavy, so pack proper waterproofs.
t.atami@35.1,139.1:
Atami is a hot-spring resort on the eastern coast of the Izu Peninsula, a town that climbs the hillside above Sagami Bay in a tumble of hotels, apartment blocks and narrow streets. It has been a place of rest for centuries, and the shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu is said to have visited for the waters. Today the town is quite easy to reach from Tokyo, with a bullet train stopping here, which makes it a favourite weekend escape, and it still has a faintly retro seaside air, with old inns, souvenir shops and steaming vents.

About forty thousand people live in Atami, so you will have no trouble finding fuel, food or a bed, and Yugawara and Hakone are the neighbouring resort towns. The steepness of the streets is a notable feature: roads switch back and forth up the slope, with sharp turns and tight junctions, and you will find yourself in low gears more than expected. Parking can be limited near the seafront, so check before you leave the bike.

Atami is known for its early-blooming cherry trees, which flower in January and February, long before most of Japan, and for a fireworks display held through the year that reflects across the bay. A reconstructed castle looks over the town from the hill, and a famous art museum stands on a ridge with sea views. The hot springs are the real reason people come, and a soak in an outdoor bath after a day in the saddle does wonders for tired shoulders.

For riders, this town is the doorway to the Izu Skyline and the coastal roads to the south. The surrounding hills hold forests of cedar, camellia and bamboo, and the sea is often visible between the trees. Weather can be changeable, especially in the rainy season and typhoon months, when the roads may be wet and visibility poor. Spring and autumn are best. If you eat here, look for fresh fish from the bay, dried horse mackerel, and the town's sweet shops, which sell steamed buns and hot-spring-style treats.
t.izu skyline@35.1,139.0:
The Izu Skyline is a ridge road, and that one fact explains why motorcyclists have loved it for decades. It runs for tens of kilometres along the high spine of the Izu Peninsula, a toll road that keeps to the crest rather than diving into valleys, so the view changes constantly: on one side the Pacific and Sagami Bay, on the other the deep green slopes toward Suruga Bay, and, on a clear day, the near-perfect cone of Mount Fuji across the water.

The riding is fluent rather than frantic. The road links long curves with gentle rises and falls, the surface is generally good, and traffic is lighter than on the roads below, though weekends bring groups of cars and bikes. Limits are enforced and the road is monitored, so the pleasure is in rhythm and in the views. Morning is usually the best time for Fuji, since haze builds later in the day, while cold, clear winter days give the sharpest outline but also bring a chance of ice at height.

The mountains here were built by volcanic activity, as the Izu Peninsula is the northern tip of the Izu-Bonin arc, which has been colliding with the main island of Honshu for millions of years. That is why the peninsula has so many hot springs and why its slopes are covered in dense forest, with bamboo, cedar and broadleaf trees. Mist drifts in easily, and the ridge can be in cloud while the coast below is sunny, so check the forecast and carry a waterproof.

Fill up in Atami, a short way below, which has everything you need, before you climb onto the ridge. At the lookouts and rest stops you will find vending machines, a few cafes and parking, and the views are well worth the pause. Because this is a toll road, you pay on entering or leaving, and having change or an electronic card ready makes life easier. Autumn gives the clearest air and the best colours.
t.shuzenji@35.0,138.9:
Shuzenji is an onsen town in the middle of the Izu Peninsula, laid out along the Katsura river in a narrow valley of cedar and bamboo, and it is one of the oldest hot-spring settlements in Japan. Legend credits the monk Kobo Daishi with starting it: he is said to have struck a rock in the river with a ritual implement, and the hot water that gushed out became the town's famous open-air bath, which still sits right at the riverside. A temple founded here has given the town its name.

History has also left darker marks. The second Kamakura shogun, Minamoto no Yoriie, was confined at Shuzenji by his Hojo in-laws and killed in 1204, a family story that fed into centuries of drama and theatre. Later, in 1910, the novelist Natsume Soseki came here to recover from a serious stomach illness and nearly died, an episode he wrote about afterwards. These details give the town the feel of a place where people come to recover, and perhaps to be forgotten for a while.

Walking is the main activity: a path through a bamboo grove runs beside the river, lanterns light the bridges in the evening, and the inns serve multi-course dinners of local fish and mountain vegetables. Wasabi grows in clear streams in these hills, and you will find it fresh-grated in the restaurants. For a rider, the town is a place to slow down. The streets are narrow and often busy with walkers in yukata, so park the bike and explore on foot.

The road toward Shuzenji from the surrounding ridges is a pleasure, a series of moderate bends and climbs through forest, with changing views of the valley. The surface is generally good, though leaf litter and damp patches can be slippery in autumn and the rainy season. Itō, about fourteen kilometres away, and Numazu are the larger towns for fuel and supplies, though the town itself has services. In autumn the maples colour the river banks, and in the cooler months a long soak is the best possible ending to a ride.
t.presidio@29.6,-104.4:
Presidio shares its river and most of its life with the Mexican town across the bridge. The Rio Grande runs along the southern edge, Ojinaga stands on the opposite bank, and the border crossing between them is the busiest thing in the area. West Texas is huge, and Presidio is a rare green strip in it, where the Rio Conchos joins the Rio Grande. This confluence, La Junta de los Rios, has been farmed for centuries, and the Spanish gave the place its name, which simply means fortress, after the military post that once stood here.

On the edge of town you can visit Fort Leaton, a large adobe trading post built in the 1840s by a former scalp hunter turned merchant and now a state historic site. The walls are thick, the courtyards are quiet, and the rooms tell the story of a frontier where trade, ranching and border politics all mixed. Presidio is also known for summer heat, regularly among the hottest places in Texas, so do your riding early and take water.

The road you want starts just west of town. Farm-to-Market Road 170, the River Road, follows the Rio Grande towards Lajitas, climbing and dropping over desert hills, with tight bends, steep grades and the famous Big Hill, which has made generations of riders grin. The scenery is raw: the river valley in a ribbon of green, then rock, ocotillo, and the Chinati and Chisos mountains in the distance. Cattle can wander onto the road, rock can fall after storms and the sun is intense, so ride with a clear mind and plenty of water. Spring and autumn are comfortable, summer is brutal and winter mornings can be surprisingly cold.

Presidio has about four thousand residents, and fuel, groceries, a few simple restaurants and motels are available, which is what the road ahead needs. The next large settlements are far apart, so take advantage of the services here and check your tank, tyres and water before heading toward Big Bend. A bridge crossing to Ojinaga is possible with the right papers, but that is a separate trip.
t.near kisarazu@35.4,139.9:
Kisarazu is the Chiba end of the Tokyo Bay Aqua-Line, and for riders that alone makes it special. The Aqua-Line crosses the bay from Kawasaki in two halves: a long tunnel under the water, then a low bridge that skims across the surface for several kilometres into Kisarazu. In the middle sits Umihotaru, an artificial island with a parking area, restaurants and a deck with views over the bay, where on a clear day you can see Mount Fuji to the west and the towers of Tokyo and Yokohama to the north. It is tolled, and crosswinds on the bridge section can be fierce.

The town itself is an old port on the eastern shore of the bay. Its tidal flats are known for clam digging, shiohigari, a favourite family outing in spring and early summer, and asari clams turn up in local dishes. The temple of Shojoji is associated with a well-known folk song about dancing tanuki, the mischievous raccoon dogs of Japanese legend, and you will find tanuki statues around the town.

As a food stop and finish, Kisarazu has plenty to offer, from seafood restaurants near the harbour to family restaurants and convenience stores along the main roads. A bowl of clam ramen or a seafood rice bowl makes a fine end to a day.

The roads inland from Kisarazu lead into the Boso hills, with winding routes through forests and small valleys towards the Pacific coast. The hills are low but steep, and the roads can be narrow and twisting. Traffic is heavy around the Aqua-Line approaches on weekends, especially in the evening, when everyone heads back to Tokyo. Fuel is plentiful.
t.near itsukaichi@35.8,139.0:
Itsukaichi takes its name from the market that was once held here on days ending in five, a trading point where charcoal, timber and silk from the mountains of western Tokyo met merchants from the plains. It is now part of the city of Akiruno, a quiet town at the mouth of the Akigawa valley, where the suburbs of Tokyo finally give way to forested hills.

The Akigawa is a clear mountain river, popular for barbecues, swimming and fishing in summer, and its valley leads into the mountains of Hinohara and Okutama, the wild western edge of Tokyo Metropolis. The forests here are dense with cedar and cypress, planted after the war, and mixed with native broadleaf trees that turn red and gold in autumn. Waterfalls, gorges and mountain villages make it a world away from the city.

For riders, the area is a classic escape from Tokyo. The Itsukaichi Kaido leads into the valley, and the roads beyond climb into the mountains, with tight curves, steep grades and spectacular views. The Okutama Shūyū Road, a famous mountain toll-free road, links Hinohara and Okutama over the ridges, and it is very popular with motorcyclists, though it has seen restrictions on motorcycles at night after accidents. Traffic can be heavy on weekends, and the roads are narrow, so ride with care.

Itsukaichi has fuel stations, convenience stores and restaurants, making it a good stop before heading into the mountains, where services become scarce. Local restaurants serve soba noodles, a speciality of the area. The Izu Skyline lies far to the south-west, a long ride across the Kanto plain and around Mount Fuji.
t.hakone@35.2,139.0:
Hakone is where Tokyo goes to get away from itself. The mountain resort sits in the caldera of an old volcano southwest of the capital, about an hour and a half by road without traffic, with Lake Ashi in the middle and Fuji looming to the northwest on a good day. Odawara, on the coast below, is the practical town, with its castle and its fish markets, while the hot-spring villages scattered through the hills have catered to travellers for centuries. The old Tokaido highway crossed these mountains, and you can still walk stretches of its stone-paved surface and see a reconstructed checkpoint beside the lake, where officials of the Tokugawa shogunate once inspected every traveller's papers.

On a bike, the draw is the mountain road. The Hakone Turnpike climbs from the coast in a long run of bends, open and smooth, with good visibility and a toll that keeps heavy trucks away. The Skyline and the roads around the crater rim offer views over the lake and the Pacific. Expect weekend crowds of cars and motorcycles, especially on fine autumn days, and be careful in fog, which rolls into the caldera quickly and can drop the temperature several degrees. Winter mornings can bring ice on the higher sections.

Landscape matters here as much as the road. Owakudani, the steaming valley of sulphur vents above the lake, is the remains of a violent eruption roughly three thousand years ago, and the smell of rotten eggs drifts across the road. Locals boil eggs in the hot pools there until the shells turn black, and tell you each one adds seven years to your life. The pampas grass fields of Sengokuhara turn silver in autumn, and the cedar avenue along the old highway is cool and dark even in midsummer.

Fuel is straightforward, with stations in Odawara and along the main road up the valley, but the mountain sections have fewer, so fill at the bottom. Konbini stores at the lakeside and along the turnpike sell hot drinks and snacks. A cup of coffee at a mountain cafe, with the lake and the trees outside, is a decent reward after the climb.

Come on a weekday if you can, and early. By midday the lake road is slow, and by evening the mist often comes back down.
t.near tanashicho@35.8,139.5:
The western suburbs of Tokyo go on and on, and Nishitokyo, Kiyose and the old town of Tanashi sit in the middle of them: a quiet, flat, residential belt of low houses, apartment blocks, train stations and shopping streets, about twenty kilometres from the centre. Nishitokyo was formed in 2001 when Tanashi and Hoya merged, and its tallest landmark is a slim tower that carries broadcasting and observation equipment, visible from far away.

Kiyose, just to the north, has an unusual history. In the early twentieth century its clean air and woods made it a centre for tuberculosis sanatoria, and the town became one of Japan's main hospital areas. Many medical institutions remain today, and the woods that once healed the sick still survive in patches, along with the Yanase river valley, where you can walk along the water among fields and groves. Elsewhere, the suburbs are a mix of new houses and old farm plots, where vegetables are still grown in small fields between homes.

It is a logical end to a Tanzawa and Doshi Road day. The Doshi Road, Route 413, runs from Sagamihara through a beautiful forested valley to Lake Yamanaka at the foot of Mount Fuji, with river crossings, tight curves and steep climbs, and it is a favourite with Tokyo riders, though it gets crowded at weekends and police are often present. The ride back usually comes in on the Chuo expressway or along the roads through Hachioji and Tachikawa, and then into the long suburbs. Expect heavy traffic, lots of lights, and slow progress in the late afternoon.

There are plenty of convenience stores, family restaurants, ramen shops and fuel stations around, and many train lines into central Tokyo, which helps if someone is collecting you. It is not a beautiful place, but it is calm, safe and practical, and after a long day in the mountains, a hot bath at a local sento, the public bath that many Tokyo neighbourhoods still have, may be the best end you could wish for.
t.near medora@46.9,-103.4:
The badlands of western North Dakota are where a young Theodore Roosevelt came to recover from grief, and where, he later said, he became the man who could be president. In 1884, after his wife and mother died on the same day, he retreated to his ranches in these rugged hills along the Little Missouri River and spent several years living the life of a cattle rancher.

Roosevelt's Maltese Cross Cabin, which he lived in during his first years in the badlands, has been moved to the visitor centre in Medora, and you can walk through its small rooms. The site of his second home, the Elkhorn Ranch, is further north and much harder to reach. Medora itself is a tiny town of old wooden buildings, revived as a tourist destination, with a summer musical show in an outdoor amphitheatre.

The South Unit scenic loop is one of the best wildlife rides in the West. Bison wander across the road, wild horses graze on the plateaus, and prairie dog towns spread across the flats, with their residents barking at passing traffic. Elk, pronghorn and mule deer are also common. The bison are huge and unpredictable, and you should keep a respectful distance and never approach them, especially on a motorcycle.

The road itself is narrow and winding, with steep gradients and sharp curves, and it climbs to several viewpoints with sweeping views over the badlands. Parts of the loop have been closed in recent years because of landslides and road damage, so check the current situation before you set out. The Painted Canyon Overlook, just off Interstate 94 to the east, offers a stunning view over the colourful badlands.

Medora has fuel, food and lodging in summer, but services are limited in winter. Belfield, about twenty-five kilometres to the east, and Beach, about forty kilometres to the west, have basic services. The nearest larger town is Dickinson, about sixty kilometres east. Early morning and late evening are the hours to be here, when the wildlife is most active and the light is warm.
t.ogrodzieniec@50.5,19.5:
Ogrodzieniec Castle is the biggest ruin on the Eagles' Nests Trail, and the first sight of it is a proper surprise: a long, ragged line of walls and towers sitting along a limestone ridge above the village of Podzamcze, with strange pale rocks poking out of the woods all around it. It looks like a film set, and in fact it has been used as one. The Jura upland here is full of such outcrops, which makes the whole hilltop seem to grow out of the stone.

The castle began as a medieval fortress and then grew under the Boner family, rich bankers and royal officials in the sixteenth century, who turned it into a magnificent Renaissance residence. Its decline came with war: in the seventeenth century Swedish troops did heavy damage during the invasion Poles call the Deluge, and the place was never fully rebuilt. Fire and neglect did the rest, and the ruins stood roofless for generations. Today you can climb through the gate, up the towers and around the courtyard, with views over the village and the forest. Legends cling to it, including a black dog said to roam the grounds and a ghost of Boner's wife, and the guides are happy to tell them.

The ride here from the south is a good one, a quiet run across the upland with long open straights, gentle hills and small villages with whitewashed churches, the road hugging the ridge before it drops toward Podzamcze. Surfaces vary on the secondary roads, and heavy trucks use the main routes near Zawiercie, so keep an eye on your mirrors. The best light is late afternoon, when the limestone turns warm and the shadows of the walls stretch across the grass.

Podzamcze has a busy tourist strip at the foot of the castle, with car parks, stalls, grill bars and ice cream, and it can feel crowded in July and August. Arriving early or on a weekday makes the experience better. The village of Ogrodzieniec has a few thousand inhabitants and shops, and Zawiercie, about ten kilometres away, is the larger town if you need a bigger selection of fuel or repairs.

Rock climbers also love this area, and you may see ropes dangling on the cliffs. Bring sturdy boots if you plan to climb the towers.
t.tokyo@35.7,139.6:
The end of the ride is the beginning of Tokyo again, and it comes in stages. First the hills drop away, and the road widens; then the first signal lights, the first convenience store, the first apartment blocks, and finally the glow of the capital spread across the plain in the dark. Arriving in Chofu at the end of a long day, with the Tama River running quietly beside the road, is a gentle way to come home.

Chofu is an ordinary city of two hundred thousand, quiet in the evening, with a stadium that hosts football and rugby, a long riverside cycle path, and shopping streets where small restaurants serve grilled chicken and cold beer. After a day in the mountains, a plate of yakitori and a noodle soup in a place with a steamed-up window is about as good as it gets. The locals are used to bikers returning in the dusk, and the hospitality is easy.

A few practical points make the last hour smoother. Japan drives on the left, and speed enforcement is strict, with fixed cameras and patrol cars, particularly on the expressways. Rain makes painted lines and manhole covers slippery, and in the city, taxis and delivery vans stop and start without warning. Tolls are charged on most expressways, and an electronic card saves time at the gates. The Chuo Expressway can back up for many kilometres on Sunday evenings, with the Kobotoke tunnel as a notorious bottleneck, so plan to leave the mountains early or accept a slow crawl.

This is also a good place to check the bike over after a long day, look at your tyres, and wipe the bugs from the visor. Park in the places marked for motorcycles, because the rules about street parking are tight and fines can be steep. Then take a deep breath, and let the ride settle.
t.near otsuki on the way back@35.7,138.9:
The Katsura river runs below, cutting a gorge near Ōtsuki that is crossed by Saruhashi, the Monkey Bridge, one of Japan's three great strange bridges, a wooden cantilever construction that has been rebuilt many times since the Middle Ages. Enzan, to the north-west, is the gateway to the Daibosatsu mountains and the Chichibu-Tama-Kai National Park.

This is a landscape of terraced orchards, with grapes, peaches and persimmons ripening along the slopes. The Kōshū grape, grown here for over a thousand years, makes the white wine of Katsunuma, and the vineyards have given the area a growing reputation among wine lovers, with tasting rooms open to visitors. The old Kōshū Kaidō, the road from Edo to Kōfu, ran through here, and Sasago Pass, a long climb to the east, was one of its steepest sections, with checkpoints and inns that have mostly vanished. Mount Fuji appears on the southern horizon from many viewpoints, a huge white shape above the lower hills.

The roads are a pleasure. From Ōtsuki, routes climb the valleys toward Kosuge and Lake Okutama, with sharp bends, narrow sections and a thick cover of forest, and the Matsuhime road in particular has a fine reputation among riders. The surface is mostly good, but narrow in places, and rockfalls, wet leaves and fallen branches are common. In winter, ice persists in the shade, and snow can close the higher roads. Autumn is the best time, with the orchards and forests in colour, and spring brings blossom in the valleys.

Fuel and food are easy in Ōtsuki, Enzan and the Kōfu basin, with convenience stores and restaurants along the main roads. The local dish is hōtō, a thick noodle soup of flat wheat noodles, pumpkin and vegetables, served in an iron pot and perfect for a cold day. Fresh fruit is for sale at roadside stands in season.

The label mentions Bandai Azuma and Shōsenkyō, but the mountains here have their own appeal, quieter and little known to visitors.
t.near sano on the way back@36.3,139.6:
Sano ramen is the first thing to say about this corner of Tochigi. The town is known across Japan for noodles that are flat, springy and kneaded by bamboo poles, served in a clear soy broth that tastes clean and slightly sweet. It also has a famous outlet mall and a temple devoted to warding off bad luck, so the town has a steady flow of visitors.

The terrain is the plain of the Watarase and Tone rivers, marked by drainage channels, levees and rice, with the edge of the Ryōmō hills rising to the north. A few kilometres west, Tatebayashi is known for two things. In spring, the azaleas of Tsutsujigaoka Park bloom in thousands, some of them hundreds of years old, and a festival draws visitors from all over the Kantō. The Morin-ji temple preserves the folk tale of the Bunbuku Chagama, a tanuki that turned into a tea kettle and brought good fortune to a poor priest. It is a cheerful bit of local lore.

South-east of here, the Watarase retention basin is a large wetland where four prefectures meet, built to control flooding and now registered as a Ramsar site, a good place for reeds, herons and migrating birds. In winter, harriers hunt over the reeds and the whole area has a stark beauty. This is not the Japan of mountains and temples but a quiet, productive heartland of vegetables and rice, and the landscape rewards slow looking.

For riders, the roads are flat and straight, which suits an early start from Tokyo before heading to the hills. Fuel is easy, with Sano, Tatebayashi and Fujioka all within a short ride and plenty of stations along the main roads. Ride with attention to crossings, since farm traffic and local drivers do not always look. Pick a hot day and the plain can be oppressive, so take your time and keep water on the bike. In November, when the harvest is done and the air is clear, the views to the mountains are some of the best of the year.
t.near kimitsu@35.3,139.9:
Kimitsu runs from the industrial shore of Tokyo Bay deep into the forested hills of the inner Boso peninsula, and the contrast is striking. On the coast, the Nippon Steel works stretches for kilometres, a tangle of furnaces, chimneys and cranes. Inland, within half an hour, you are among steep green hills, narrow valleys and reservoirs, with hardly a building in sight.

The scenic heart of the area is Kanōzan, a low mountain with an old temple at the top and a viewpoint over the Kujūkutani, the ninety-nine valleys. On autumn and winter mornings, mist often fills the valleys below, creating a sea of clouds with the ridges rising like islands. It is a famous sight, and photographers gather at dawn to capture it.

The Kameyama dam lake, further south, is a long, winding reservoir surrounded by forests, and in late November the autumn leaves turn the slopes red and gold. The roads around the lake are narrow and twisty, with little traffic and fine views.

For riders, the inner Boso offers a network of quiet roads with tight bends, steep climbs and tunnels. The tarmac is decent on the whole, though leaves, moss and fallen branches can make the roads slippery, especially in autumn and after rain. Watch out for deer and monkeys, which are common in the forests.

The Aqua-Line, the tunnel and bridge across Tokyo Bay from Kawasaki, lands in nearby Kisarazu, making the area easily accessible from Tokyo. Do your shopping on the coast. The hills are thinly populated, and the stations that do exist inland keep short hours, so leave the bay side with a full tank.
t.near hachioji@35.6,139.3:
Mount Takao stands at the edge of Hachiōji like a patient dog, a green hill of about six hundred metres that Tokyoites climb in their hundreds of thousands. For a rider, it is a start and finish point, a convenient place for fuel, parking and a good bowl of ramen before the mountains begin. The city sits at the foot of the Tama hills, and the climate here is a few degrees cooler than central Tokyo.

Hachiōji has a clear identity. The local ramen is a shoyu broth with chopped onions floating on top, a simple, comforting bowl that sells at counters across the city. The city was an important silk centre, and its merchants traded in bales of silk that travelled to Yokohama along a road still called the Silk Road. In the sixteenth century, the Hōjō clan of Odawara held a castle on a hill here, which fell to Toyotomi Hideyoshi's army in 1590, and the remains of its walls can still be walked. In late November, the avenue of ginkgo trees along the road to Mount Takao turns a brilliant yellow, and the city holds a festival beneath them.

The riding that starts here goes west. Route 20, the old Kōshū Kaidō, climbs past the foot of Mount Takao and through the long Kobotoke tunnel, then continues toward Sagamiko, Ōtsuki and the Chūō corridor. Other roads lead north-west to Ōme and the Okutama valley, or south-west to the Tanzawa foothills. The early morning is the best time, when the city is quiet and the mountains are cool. Sunday traffic is heavy on the way out.

Fuel and food are everywhere. The city has hundreds of stations and restaurants, and the area around Hachiōji station is lively with cafés and small bars. If you finish here at the end of the day, plan to arrive before the evening rush, when the roads back into central Tokyo are slow. A bowl of ramen after a long ride is hard to beat, and the soy broth, rich and salty, is just what a tired rider needs.
t.near miura@35.1,139.7:
At the very tip of the Miura Peninsula, south of Yokosuka, the land ends in low cliffs, rocky shelves, cabbage fields and a fishing harbour that has supplied Tokyo with tuna for generations. Misaki port is the heart of Miura, and that is where you go to eat. The city has around fifty thousand people, but it feels like a coastal country town, with the sea always close and the smell of salt and fish on the wind.

Misaki maguro is the dish. The harbour is lined with restaurants serving tuna in every form, raw on rice in a big bowl, grilled, fried, as sashimi or as rich slices of fatty toro, and the long queues at lunchtime on weekends tell you how famous it is. Miura is also known for its vegetables, especially its big white radishes, the daikon, and its cabbages, grown in fields that stretch right to the edge of the cliffs, with the sea glittering behind them. In winter you will see daikon hanging to dry on frames by farmhouses.

Just across a bridge from the harbour lies Jogashima, a small island with a lighthouse, a park and rocky shores carved into strange shapes by the waves. The walk along the southern cliffs is lovely, with views across the mouth of Tokyo Bay to the Boso peninsula and, on clear days, Mount Fuji to the west and the island of Oshima to the south. Kites, hawks and cormorants ride the wind. The poet Hakushu Kitahara lived here and wrote a famous song about the rain on Jogashima, and there is a monument to him on the island.

The ride down the peninsula follows Route 134 and the coast roads past Hayama, where the imperial family has a seaside villa, and then through hills, tunnels and farmland. Expect traffic on weekends, especially in summer, when beaches like Miura Kaigan fill with Tokyo families. Early morning is the best time, when the light is soft and the roads are quiet, and the wind off the sea can be strong in winter and spring.

Fuel, convenience stores and food are easy to find in Miura and in Yokosuka on the way back. If you only do one thing here, eat a tuna bowl by the harbour, then sit on the rocks on Jogashima and watch the waves come in from the Pacific.
t.near hanno@35.8,139.3:
Hanno is where Saitama's flat suburbs run out and the green ridges begin, at about 100 metres above the sea, on the Iruma river at the mouth of the valley that leads up toward Okutama and Chichibu. It is a city of about eighty-six thousand people, so a fuel stop is easy, and it has a long history as a timber town. For centuries the cedar and cypress felled in the mountains upstream were floated or hauled down here to supply the building boom of Edo, and the old lumber trade gave the place much of its wealth.

Today Hanno is better known for something gentler. Moomin Valley Park, beside Lake Miyazawa, is a Finnish-inspired village with a theme dedicated to the beloved trolls of Tove Jansson, and it is a favourite family outing. The lake itself is a quiet reservoir surrounded by woods, with a path around its shore, and it is often the starting point for walking and cycling trips into the hills. Cherry blossom in early April and the autumn colours bring crowds.

The Hanno riding starts the moment you leave the town. Routes 299 and 70 climb into the valley through cedar forest and small hamlets, with tight bends, shade and occasional mossy patches, and it is known among riders as the gateway to the best roads west of Tokyo. The Shomaru and Tokigawa areas have cheerful, winding roads, and the Chichibu basin lies just over the hills. At weekends, the road is thick with bikes and cars, so a weekday or a very early start is a good idea.

Convenience stores and petrol stations are plentiful in town, but they become sparse as you climb, and some mountain stations close early in the evening, so fill up before you head into the hills. Many riders gather at a few popular stops near the foothills, particularly on Sunday mornings, and the atmosphere can be quite sociable.

Check your tyre pressures, warm up the engine gently and enjoy the long, shaded climb. After the grey suburbs, the green of the mountains feels like a reward.
t.near nagatoro@36.1,139.2:
Nagatoro is a small town in the hills of western Saitama where the Arakawa river squeezes through a gorge of layered grey-green rock, and that rock is the reason the place is famous. Along the riverbank lies the Iwadatami, a broad flat terrace of crystalline schist, worn smooth by the water and split into slabs like stepping stones, and it is a national natural monument. Japanese geologists have studied it since the late nineteenth century, and Nagatoro calls itself the birthplace of Japanese geology, with the Saitama Museum of Natural History right in town.

The river is the show. Flat-bottomed wooden boats, steered by boatmen with long poles, carry visitors down the rapids between the rock walls, and in summer there is rafting and canoeing. The water is clear and green, and on hot days families sit on the rocks with their feet in it. In autumn, the maples along the gorge turn red, and in spring cherry blossoms line the river and the road. Above the town, a ropeway climbs Mount Hodo, where wintersweet flowers bloom in January and February, and the Hodosan shrine sits among old trees at its foot.

As a food stop, Nagatoro and the Chichibu area have their own specialities. Kakigori, shaved ice, is a summer ritual here, made from natural ice harvested in winter from ponds in the mountains, light and fluffy and topped with syrups. Chichibu is also known for miso potatoes, fried and coated in sweet miso sauce, and for waraji katsu, huge breaded pork cutlets shaped like straw sandals. Soba noodles made from local buckwheat are another good choice, cold on a hot day or hot in winter.

The riding to and from Nagatoro is a pleasure. Route 140 follows the Arakawa valley from Yorii, with gentle bends, good surfaces and views of the river, and the roads up into the Chichibu mountains climb through forests to passes and lookout points, with tight corners and very little traffic on weekdays. Chichibu Muse Park, on a ridge above the city of Chichibu, has wide views over the basin and the mountains. On weekends, the main roads can be busy with day-trippers from Tokyo.

Nagatoro has fuel, convenience stores and many small restaurants and cafés along the main street near the station. Arrive early, before the tour buses, and watch the boats glide through the gorge in the morning light.
t.near chichibu@36.0,139.0:
Every December, on the night of the third, giant wooden floats lit with lanterns are hauled through the streets of Chichibu to the beat of drums and the crackle of fireworks, in a festival that is among the most famous in Japan. The Chichibu Night Festival has been held for centuries, and it draws huge crowds. The rest of the year, Chichibu is a quiet mountain town in a basin west of Tokyo, ringed by forested peaks.

Mount Buko, which looms over the town, has been quarried for limestone for decades, and its summit has been cut away into terraces, a scarred profile that dominates the view. The cement industry was a mainstay of the local economy. Chichibu is also a pilgrimage centre, with a circuit of thirty-four temples dedicated to Kannon, the goddess of mercy, scattered through the valleys.

In spring, Hitsujiyama park is covered with a carpet of pink and white moss phlox, shibazakura, and the crowds come to see it. Nagatoro, to the north, has river boats that shoot the rapids of the Arakawa between flat rock formations.

The food is hearty and local: waraji katsu, a pork cutlet as big as a straw sandal, served over rice, and soba from local buckwheat. Chichibu also makes whisky, and a small distillery has won international prizes.

For riders, the roads around Chichibu are among the best near Tokyo. Route 299 climbs over the mountains to the east, and Route 140 heads west through a long tunnel into Yamanashi. Both are winding, well surfaced and busy with riders on weekends, and the police know it. In winter, watch for ice on shaded corners. Fill the tank in town: once you are on the passes, stations are scarce.
t.near jicin@50.5,15.3:
Jičín owes its looks to one very ambitious man. Albrecht von Wallenstein, the general who made a fortune in the Thirty Years' War, took over the estate in the 1620s and set out to turn a modest market town into the capital of his own duchy. He built a palace, a church, a grand arcaded square and a gate, and brought in Italian architects to do it, so the centre of Jičín today has an unexpectedly Renaissance and early baroque air for a town in the middle of northern Bohemia. The great square, Valdštejnovo náměstí, is lined with arcades and pastel house fronts, and the Valdice Gate, a tall tower with a narrow arch, still marks the way out toward the north.

Wallenstein did not live to enjoy it for long; he was murdered in Cheb in 1634. His body was taken to the Carthusian monastery he had founded at Valdice, a few kilometres from town, which later became a prison, and the old monastery buildings can still be seen from the road. Locals have a gentler hero in Rumcajs, the good-natured robber of a Czech children's tale by Václav Čtvrtek, who lived in the forest near here with his wife and son, and the town celebrates him with statues, shops and an annual festival.

Jičín is known as the gateway to the Bohemian Paradise, the Český ráj, a protected landscape of sandstone towers, deep forests and castle ruins perched on rocky crags. The rock formations stand in green woods in all kinds of odd shapes, and the roads between them wind and climb in a way that suits a motorbike. They are narrow and often patched, with farm traffic and cyclists, so keep to a modest pace and expect surprises around the blind corners. Spring and autumn are good times, when the forest is bright and the crowds thin.

The town, with about sixteen thousand people, is a full service stop, with petrol stations, supermarkets and a good choice of cafés and pubs around the square. Czech pub food is hearty, with roast pork, dumplings, and a very decent pilsner. Regional specialities include the sweet Jičín cakes and the fruit orchards that surround the town, and in late summer the plums and cherries are sold at roadside stalls. It is an excellent place to finish a day, and the arcades give shelter if it rains, which in Bohemia it often does.
